prompt: What is a design pattern?
optionA: A rule about how code must be structured
optionB: A diagram produced before coding
optionC: A name for a solution shape that keeps recurring
optionD: A library you install
correctAnswerText: A name for a solution shape that keeps recurring
explanation: A name, not a rule. Code arrives at these shapes on its own; the name is what lets two engineers discuss one in a word.

prompt: What does the strategy pattern let you change?
optionA: How two interfaces that were never meant to meet connect
optionB: Which class is created
optionC: Which algorithm runs, without changing the caller
optionD: How objects are notified of events
correctAnswerText: Which algorithm runs, without changing the caller
explanation: The algorithm varies; the caller does not. That separation is the whole pattern.

prompt: What does a factory do?
optionA: Puts the decision about which object to make in one place
optionB: Guarantees only one instance exists
optionC: Converts one interface into another
optionD: Creates objects faster than calling a constructor directly
correctAnswerText: Puts the decision about which object to make in one place
explanation: One place that decides. Speed has nothing to do with it, and a single instance is a different pattern.

prompt: What problem does the observer pattern solve?
optionA: Telling interested parties that something happened
optionB: Choosing which class to instantiate
optionC: Restricting a class to one instance
optionD: Making two incompatible types work together
correctAnswerText: Telling interested parties that something happened
explanation: The thing that changed does not need to know who cares. That is what it buys.

prompt: What is an adapter for?
optionA: Making something usable through an interface it does not implement
optionB: Notifying subscribers of a change
optionC: Adding behaviour to an object at runtime
optionD: Creating the right objects without naming their concrete class
correctAnswerText: Making something usable through an interface it does not implement
explanation: Usually around a library you cannot change. It translates, and nothing else needs to know.

prompt: Is using more design patterns a sign of better code?
optionA: Yes, for anything above a small project
optionB: Yes, patterns are best practice
optionC: Only in object-oriented languages
optionD: No — each one has to earn its place
correctAnswerText: No — each one has to earn its place
explanation: Every pattern is machinery the next reader must hold. Unearned, it is cost without benefit.

prompt: What is the main practical benefit of a pattern having a name?
optionA: It makes the code shorter
optionB: Two engineers can discuss the design in one word
optionC: The compiler can optimise it
optionD: It proves the design is correct before anything is written
correctAnswerText: Two engineers can discuss the design in one word
explanation: Communication. "Make it a strategy" replaces a paragraph, and both people picture the same thing.

prompt: What do most design patterns separate?
optionA: Tested code from untested code
optionB: Fast code from slow code
optionC: Public code from private code
optionD: What changes from what stays the same
correctAnswerText: What changes from what stays the same
explanation: Almost every pattern is an answer to "what varies here, and what must not be disturbed when it does".

prompt: What does a singleton guarantee?
optionA: That the object is created lazily
optionB: That the object is thread-safe
optionC: That only one instance of the class exists
optionD: That the class cannot be subclassed
correctAnswerText: That only one instance of the class exists
explanation: One instance. Laziness and thread safety are implementation choices, and neither is implied.

prompt: Why do some patterns look unnecessary in some languages?
optionA: The patterns only apply to compiled languages
optionB: Those languages actively discourage object-oriented design
optionC: The patterns were written for older hardware
optionD: The language already provides what the pattern works around
correctAnswerText: The language already provides what the pattern works around
explanation: Strategy is a class in one language and a function argument in another. The need is the same; the machinery is not.

prompt: What does strategy replace, in code that has grown without it?
optionA: A function with too many parameters
optionB: A loop that does several things
optionC: A class hierarchy that is too deep
optionD: A conditional that keeps gaining branches
correctAnswerText: A conditional that keeps gaining branches
explanation: The signal is a switch on a type that gets edited every time a case is added. Strategy turns editing into adding.

prompt: Why put object creation behind a factory?
optionA: It removes the need for constructors
optionB: Objects end up being created rather more efficiently
optionC: The choice lives in one place instead of every caller
optionD: It makes the objects immutable
correctAnswerText: The choice lives in one place instead of every caller
explanation: When the rule changes, one place changes. Callers that each decided for themselves are the problem it solves.

prompt: What does observer stop you from having to do?
optionA: Store the same piece of state in more than one place
optionB: Edit the source of the event every time a new listener appears
optionC: Pass data through several layers
optionD: Write code that runs concurrently
correctAnswerText: Edit the source of the event every time a new listener appears
explanation: Without it, adding a fifth thing that cares about an order means editing the order code. With it, the order code never changes again.

prompt: Why is an adapter often the right answer around a third-party library?
optionA: It means you can skip reading the library documentation entirely
optionB: It removes the dependency entirely
optionC: You cannot change the library, and it keeps its shape out of your code
optionD: It makes the library faster
correctAnswerText: You cannot change the library, and it keeps its shape out of your code
explanation: It also means swapping the library later touches one file rather than forty.

prompt: Why is singleton the most criticised of the common patterns?
optionA: It always causes memory leaks
optionB: It is measurably slower than creating objects normally
optionC: It cannot be used in modern languages
optionD: It is global state, which makes testing and reasoning harder
correctAnswerText: It is global state, which makes testing and reasoning harder
explanation: A singleton is a global with better manners. Two tests sharing one now share its state as well.

prompt: Why does applying a pattern early often make code worse?
optionA: A pattern cannot be refactored away once it is in place
optionB: You are guessing at which axis will actually change
optionC: Early code has no tests
optionD: Patterns are slower to execute
correctAnswerText: You are guessing at which axis will actually change
explanation: The flexibility gets built along the wrong axis, and then both the machinery and the real change have to be paid for.

prompt: Why do most patterns favour composition over inheritance?
optionA: Inheritance is slower
optionB: Composition uses less memory
optionC: Inheritance is not supported in every language you might use
optionD: Composed parts can be changed at runtime and independently
correctAnswerText: Composed parts can be changed at runtime and independently
explanation: Inheritance fixes the relationship when the code is written. Composition leaves it changeable when the program runs.

prompt: A class is called OrderFactory but only ever returns one fixed type. What is the harm?
optionA: The name promises a flexibility the code does not have
optionB: A factory is required to return several different types
optionC: The class will be slower
optionD: The compiler cannot inline it
correctAnswerText: The name promises a flexibility the code does not have
explanation: A reader trusts the name and goes looking for the variation. Misleading vocabulary is worse than none.

prompt: How does strategy usually affect testability?
optionA: It removes the need for tests
optionB: It has no effect on testing
optionC: It worsens it — there are simply more classes to cover
optionD: It improves it — each algorithm can be tested alone
correctAnswerText: It improves it — each algorithm can be tested alone
explanation: Behaviour behind an interface is behaviour you can substitute, which is most of what makes something testable.

prompt: Where did the catalogued design patterns come from?
optionA: They were designed as a standard for the industry
optionB: They were observed in code people had already written
optionC: They were defined by language committees
optionD: They came from mathematical proofs
correctAnswerText: They were observed in code people had already written
explanation: Catalogued, not invented. Which is why "refactor towards a pattern once the need appears" is the natural order.

prompt: Shipping cost is calculated by a switch on carrier, and a fourth carrier is being added. What fits?
optionA: Strategy — one implementation per carrier
optionB: Observer — notify carriers of orders
optionC: Adapter — wrap each carrier API
optionD: Singleton — one calculator for the application
correctAnswerText: Strategy — one implementation per carrier
explanation: The algorithm varies by carrier and the caller does not care which. Adding a carrier becomes adding a file.

prompt: Placing an order must send an email, update stock and log analytics — and more will be added. What fits?
optionA: Strategy — swap the order algorithm
optionB: Factory — create the right order type
optionC: Observer — the order publishes, others subscribe
optionD: Adapter — wrap each downstream service interface
correctAnswerText: Observer — the order publishes, others subscribe
explanation: The list of things that care will keep growing, and none of them should require editing the order code.

prompt: You are replacing one payment provider with another, and their SDKs differ. What limits the damage?
optionA: An observer notified of payments
optionB: An adapter, so your code talks to one interface either way
optionC: A singleton holding whichever provider is currently active
optionD: Nothing — the call sites must change
correctAnswerText: An adapter, so your code talks to one interface either way
explanation: Done before the migration it is one file; done after, it is every call site twice.

prompt: Which report object to build depends on the user plan, and the rule is repeated in six places. What fits?
optionA: An adapter over the report types
optionB: A factory holding the rule once
optionC: A singleton report builder
optionD: A strategy for each report
correctAnswerText: A factory holding the rule once
explanation: The repetition is the signal. The rule changing in five places out of six is the bug waiting to happen.

prompt: A function formats a date one way and nothing suggests it will ever do otherwise. What should you apply?
optionA: An adapter around the date library
optionB: Nothing — leave it as a function
optionC: Strategy, in case formats are added
optionD: A factory for formatters
correctAnswerText: Nothing — leave it as a function
explanation: Flexibility nobody asked for is the commonest way patterns make code worse. Add it when the second format arrives.

prompt: When is the right moment to introduce a pattern?
optionA: During the first implementation
optionB: Only during a dedicated refactoring sprint
optionC: At the design stage, well before any code has been written
optionD: When the need has appeared, usually the second or third time
correctAnswerText: When the need has appeared, usually the second or third time
explanation: Once is an instance, twice is a coincidence, three times is a shape. Refactoring towards a pattern beats guessing at one.

prompt: You need one database connection pool for the application. What is usually better than a singleton?
optionA: A new pool per request
optionB: Create it once at startup and pass it where it is needed
optionC: A global variable
optionD: A static class that exposes nothing but static methods
correctAnswerText: Create it once at startup and pass it where it is needed
explanation: Same single instance, without the global reach — and a test can hand in a different one.

prompt: A class calls a live email service directly and cannot be tested. What change helps most?
optionA: Make the sender a singleton
optionB: Take the sender as a dependency behind an interface
optionC: Add a flag that skips actually sending while under test
optionD: Move the call into a private method
correctAnswerText: Take the sender as a dependency behind an interface
explanation: A test then hands in a fake. The flag is the same idea done worse: test-only branches in production code.

prompt: A notification can be email, SMS, or both at once, and combinations keep being requested. What fits?
optionA: A singleton notifier with flags
optionB: A separate subclass for every possible combination
optionC: Compose notifiers, so a combination is a list of them
optionD: A switch on notification type
correctAnswerText: Compose notifiers, so a combination is a list of them
explanation: Subclassing combinations explodes: three channels is seven classes. Composition makes a combination a list.

prompt: Two implementations of one behaviour are needed, in a language with first-class functions. What is usually enough?
optionA: A factory returning the implementation
optionB: A strategy interface with two classes
optionC: An abstract base class
optionD: Pass a function
correctAnswerText: Pass a function
explanation: The same separation with none of the machinery. The pattern is the idea, not the class diagram.

prompt: Following one request through the code passes seven interfaces, each with one implementation. What is the problem?
optionA: Indirection that buys nothing
optionB: Poor naming
optionC: Missing documentation
optionD: Not enough abstraction
correctAnswerText: Indirection that buys nothing
explanation: An interface with one implementation is a layer to read through, not a seam. Seven of them is a codebase nobody can follow.

prompt: A strategy was built for payment methods, but every change so far has been to currency handling. What happened?
optionA: Currency should also be a strategy
optionB: Strategy was the wrong pattern for this problem entirely
optionC: The flexibility was built along an axis that does not change
optionD: The strategies were implemented badly
correctAnswerText: The flexibility was built along an axis that does not change
explanation: The cost is paid and the benefit never arrives. Which is the argument for adding a pattern once the change has shown itself.

prompt: Tests pass alone and fail when run together. The code uses a singleton cache. What is the likely cause?
optionA: Singletons are not safe to use across threads
optionB: The tests run too quickly
optionC: State from one test is still there in the next
optionD: The cache is too small
correctAnswerText: State from one test is still there in the next
explanation: The classic symptom of global state. It also means the tests now depend on the order they run in.

prompt: Saving a record triggers effects nobody can locate. The system is event-driven throughout. What has been traded away?
optionA: The ability to add new listeners without editing the source
optionB: Performance
optionC: Traceability — you cannot see what happens next by reading
optionD: Type safety
correctAnswerText: Traceability — you cannot see what happens next by reading
explanation: Decoupling is exactly what makes the consequences invisible. That is observer’s real cost, and it grows with the listeners.

prompt: A codebase is full of classes named Manager, Helper and Processor. What does that usually indicate?
optionA: Responsibilities were never really decided
optionB: The team follows a naming convention
optionC: The code is heavily patterned
optionD: The classes are utilities
correctAnswerText: Responsibilities were never really decided
explanation: A class you cannot name precisely is usually a class doing several things. The vague name is the symptom, not the fault.

prompt: A pricing rule must change, and the same conditional appears in eleven files. What was missing?
optionA: More tests around pricing
optionB: A faster algorithm
optionC: Better variable names
optionD: One place that owned the rule
correctAnswerText: One place that owned the rule
explanation: Whether that place is called a factory or a function hardly matters. The absence of it is the defect.

prompt: Adding a fourth option doubled the number of subclasses. What is the underlying mistake?
optionA: Independent choices were modelled as inheritance
optionB: The base class is too large
optionC: The subclasses are poorly named
optionD: The hierarchy is missing a common interface
correctAnswerText: Independent choices were modelled as inheritance
explanation: Each independent choice doubles a hierarchy and adds one to a composition. That growth rate IS the diagnosis.

prompt: A class is almost impossible to test. What does that usually say about its design?
optionA: It decides its own collaborators instead of being given them
optionB: It is simply not using enough of the established patterns
optionC: It has too many methods
optionD: It needs more comments
correctAnswerText: It decides its own collaborators instead of being given them
explanation: Difficulty testing is a design signal rather than a testing problem. Something it constructs internally cannot be substituted.

prompt: Every class ends in Factory, Strategy or Builder. What does that suggest?
optionA: The codebase is mature
optionB: The design is well documented
optionC: Patterns are being applied as a goal rather than a solution
optionD: The team is unusually disciplined about its naming
correctAnswerText: Patterns are being applied as a goal rather than a solution
explanation: A name should say what the thing is FOR. A codebase named after its machinery has forgotten what it does.

prompt: A Python codebase has abstract base classes with single methods, one implementation each. What is happening?
optionA: The classes are placeholders
optionB: A pattern is being carried over that the language already handles
optionC: Python requires this for polymorphism
optionD: The code has been correctly designed for future extension
correctAnswerText: A pattern is being carried over that the language already handles
explanation: In a language with first-class functions, that is a function. The shape was imported from a language that needed the class.

prompt: What is the test of whether a pattern earns its place?
optionA: Whether it appears in the catalogue
optionB: Whether the change it anticipates actually happens
optionC: Whether it reduces the number of lines
optionD: Whether everybody on the team recognises the pattern
correctAnswerText: Whether the change it anticipates actually happens
explanation: Unused flexibility is pure cost, paid by every reader forever. The change arriving is what redeems it.

prompt: A codebase solves a problem one way throughout; you know a better pattern. What matters most?
optionA: Whether the team has heard of it
optionB: Whether your pattern is, in the abstract, objectively better
optionC: Whether it is in the original catalogue
optionD: Whether the whole codebase will move, or only your corner
correctAnswerText: Whether the whole codebase will move, or only your corner
explanation: One island of a better approach is a second convention. Better alone does not beat consistent.

prompt: A pattern and a plain conditional both solve the problem today. Which should you choose?
optionA: The pattern, because it is more extensible
optionB: The pattern, because a conditional will not scale later on
optionC: The conditional, until a second reason to change appears
optionD: Whichever the team used last
correctAnswerText: The conditional, until a second reason to change appears
explanation: Refactoring a conditional into a strategy later is easy. Removing machinery that turned out unnecessary rarely happens.

prompt: Does it matter that a pattern is unfamiliar to most of the team?
optionA: No, they should learn it
optionB: Yes — code is read far more often than written
optionC: Only for very large teams
optionD: No, these patterns are standard professional knowledge
correctAnswerText: Yes — code is read far more often than written
explanation: Not an argument against ever using one — an argument for explaining it, and for weighing the cost honestly.

prompt: When is making a system event-driven throughout the wrong call?
optionA: When events are frequent
optionB: When the system is distributed across many separate services
optionC: When there are many listeners
optionD: When the flow is essentially a sequence somebody needs to follow
correctAnswerText: When the flow is essentially a sequence somebody needs to follow
explanation: Events buy decoupling and spend traceability. For a linear process, calling the next step is clearer and honest.

prompt: A pattern has been in place two years and its flexibility was never used. What should happen?
optionA: Add more implementations so that it justifies itself
optionB: Document why it exists
optionC: Leave it, in case it is needed
optionD: Consider removing it — unused indirection is a cost
correctAnswerText: Consider removing it — unused indirection is a cost
explanation: Two years of evidence beats the original guess. Taking machinery out is a legitimate refactoring and rarely done.

prompt: In a design discussion, what makes a pattern suggestion convincing?
optionA: Citing where it is commonly used
optionB: Describing its class structure
optionC: Naming the change it protects against
optionD: Naming the pattern correctly
correctAnswerText: Naming the change it protects against
explanation: "Strategy, because carriers are added twice a year" is an argument. "Strategy" on its own is a word.

prompt: You genuinely cannot tell which axis will change. What is the best response?
optionA: Choose whichever axis seems most likely today and commit to it fully
optionB: Delay the work until it is clearer
optionC: Keep it simple and easy to change, rather than flexible in one direction
optionD: Add flexibility on every axis
correctAnswerText: Keep it simple and easy to change, rather than flexible in one direction
explanation: Simple code can become anything. Code made flexible along the wrong axis has to be undone first.

prompt: Why is the second or third occurrence usually the right moment, rather than the first?
optionA: By then you can see the actual shape of the variation
optionB: Teams only approve refactoring after repetition
optionC: Two cases are easier to refactor than one
optionD: One occurrence cannot be abstracted
correctAnswerText: By then you can see the actual shape of the variation
explanation: One example tells you nothing about what varies. Three tell you where the seam belongs — and that it belongs.

prompt: What does knowing design patterns well actually give an engineer?
optionA: A reliable way of making almost any codebase more extensible
optionB: A standard structure for new projects
optionC: A vocabulary for design, and judgement about when not to use it
optionD: A catalogue of solutions to apply
correctAnswerText: A vocabulary for design, and judgement about when not to use it
explanation: The vocabulary is the easy half and the restraint is the valuable one. Somebody who knows all twenty-three and uses all of them is worse than somebody who knows four.

prompt: What is a layer in an application?
optionA: A group of code with one kind of responsibility
optionB: A separate process the application runs
optionC: A version of the app released to users
optionD: A folder that keeps related files together
correctAnswerText: A group of code with one kind of responsibility
explanation: Responsibility, not location. A folder is how you store it; a layer is what it is allowed to be about.

prompt: In a layered application, which way should dependencies point?
optionA: Inward, towards the business rules
optionB: Outward, towards the database
optionC: Downward, towards the framework
optionD: Both ways, so layers can cooperate
correctAnswerText: Inward, towards the business rules
explanation: The rules are the thing you keep. Everything else is a detail that should be replaceable around them.

prompt: What does a boundary in a system represent?
optionA: A wall between two development teams
optionB: A point where the language changes
optionC: A limit on how much code a file may hold
optionD: A promise about what can change independently
correctAnswerText: A promise about what can change independently
explanation: That promise is the whole value. A boundary nothing can change across independently is only a folder.

prompt: What does separation of concerns mean in practice?
optionA: One piece of code is about one thing
optionB: Business code is kept in one folder
optionC: Each developer owns a separate module
optionD: Concerns are documented before coding
correctAnswerText: One piece of code is about one thing
explanation: Said plainly rather than abstractly: if you cannot name what a file is about in a phrase, it is about several things.

prompt: What does adding a layer cost?
optionA: Something more for every reader to hold
optionB: A longer build and deployment time
optionC: More memory used while the app runs
optionD: Measurably slower execution at runtime
correctAnswerText: Something more for every reader to hold
explanation: The cost is comprehension, paid by everybody who reads it afterwards. That is why a layer has to buy something.

prompt: Which kind of decision deserves the most thought up front?
optionA: One that is expensive to reverse later
optionB: One that affects the most files today
optionC: One the team disagrees about most
optionD: One that takes longest to implement
correctAnswerText: One that is expensive to reverse later
explanation: Cheap to undo means decide quickly and move on. The expensive ones are where the thinking belongs.

prompt: What belongs in the domain layer?
optionA: The queries that read the database
optionB: The rules of the business itself
optionC: The endpoints the client calls
optionD: The settings the app starts with
correctAnswerText: The rules of the business itself
explanation: What the business would still be true about if you rewrote the whole application in another language.

prompt: Two modules are tightly coupled. What does that mean?
optionA: They are written by the same team
optionB: They are stored in the same source folder
optionC: Changing one usually forces changing the other
optionD: They run inside the same process
correctAnswerText: Changing one usually forces changing the other
explanation: Coupling is measured by what a change costs, not by where the files sit or who wrote them.

prompt: What usually sits at a boundary between layers?
optionA: An interface describing what is needed
optionB: A shared file of helper functions
optionC: A comment explaining the split
optionD: A database table both layers read
correctAnswerText: An interface describing what is needed
explanation: The interface is stated by the layer that NEEDS the work, which is what keeps the dependency pointing inward.

prompt: Is a diagram of boxes and arrows the architecture?
optionA: No — the decisions behind it are
optionB: Yes, if it is kept up to date
optionC: Yes, that is what the word means
optionD: Only for systems above a certain size
correctAnswerText: No — the decisions behind it are
explanation: A diagram records an architecture. Two teams can draw the same boxes and have made opposite decisions.

prompt: Why should the business rules not import the database code?
optionA: So the rules can be written in any language
optionB: So the database can be queried more quickly
optionC: So the database schema stays simpler
optionD: So they can be tested and kept when it changes
correctAnswerText: So they can be tested and kept when it changes
explanation: Rules that import a database need one to run, so every test needs one too — and swapping it rewrites them.

prompt: What does a well-placed boundary let you do?
optionA: Change one side without reading the other
optionB: Deploy the two halves separately
optionC: Assign the two sides to different teams
optionD: Write the two sides in different styles
correctAnswerText: Change one side without reading the other
explanation: Separate deployment is sometimes a consequence; not having to understand both sides is the point.

prompt: Why is tight coupling expensive over time?
optionA: Each change spreads further than intended
optionB: It makes the codebase larger on disk
optionC: It prevents the use of design patterns
optionD: Coupled code runs more slowly than split code
correctAnswerText: Each change spreads further than intended
explanation: A one-line change that touches nine files is the symptom. The cost is paid on every change, forever.

prompt: Why is "add another layer" not automatically an improvement?
optionA: Layers make automated testing harder
optionB: Layers always slow the application down
optionC: Most languages limit how many you can have
optionD: Indirection that buys nothing still has to be read
correctAnswerText: Indirection that buys nothing still has to be read
explanation: Following one request through seven hops is a real cost. Each hop has to earn itself against that.

prompt: Why is a hard-to-test class usually an architecture problem?
optionA: It has too many methods to cover
optionB: It decides its own collaborators internally
optionC: It lacks an interface of its own
optionD: Its tests were written after the code
correctAnswerText: It decides its own collaborators internally
explanation: Something built inside cannot be substituted from outside. Difficulty testing is a design signal, not a testing one.

prompt: Why is choosing a logging library a cheap decision?
optionA: It sits at the edge and can be swapped
optionB: Logs are not important to the product
optionC: It only affects the operations team
optionD: Logging libraries are broadly identical
correctAnswerText: It sits at the edge and can be swapped
explanation: Cheap because of WHERE it sits. The same choice made in the middle of the domain would not be cheap at all.

prompt: Why keep framework types out of the domain layer?
optionA: Frameworks change their names often
optionB: Frameworks are usually badly designed
optionC: It keeps the domain layer smaller
optionD: The framework will outlive its welcome first
correctAnswerText: The framework will outlive its welcome first
explanation: Business rules outlast frameworks. Rules written in a framework’s types are rewritten when it goes.

prompt: What is the benefit of putting things that change together in one place?
optionA: A change stays inside one module
optionB: Fewer modules exist overall
optionC: The code is faster to compile
optionD: The module can be deployed separately
correctAnswerText: A change stays inside one module
explanation: Cohesion and coupling are the same question asked twice: what does one change have to touch.

prompt: Does a small application have an architecture?
optionA: No, architecture begins at a certain size
optionB: Only once more than one team works on it
optionC: Yes — one that was chosen or one that happened
optionD: Only if it was designed before coding
correctAnswerText: Yes — one that was chosen or one that happened
explanation: There is no such thing as no architecture. There is only one nobody decided, which is usually the expensive kind.

prompt: Why record WHY an architectural decision was taken?
optionA: Because reviewers ask for documentation
optionB: So the original author can be identified
optionC: Otherwise it gets undone by somebody reasonable
optionD: To prove the design was considered
correctAnswerText: Otherwise it gets undone by somebody reasonable
explanation: A constraint nobody can see looks like an accident, and the person who removes it is usually acting sensibly.

prompt: Your pricing rules call the database directly. How do you point the dependency inward?
optionA: Cache the query so the rules call it less
optionB: Have the rules declare an interface the data layer implements
optionC: Move the database calls into a shared helper module
optionD: Put the pricing rules inside the data layer
correctAnswerText: Have the rules declare an interface the data layer implements
explanation: The inner layer states what it needs; the outer one supplies it. That inversion is the whole technique.

prompt: Where should you put a boundary in a growing application?
optionA: Where the code uses two different libraries
optionB: Where the file has grown beyond a size limit
optionC: Where two different teams want to work
optionD: Where the two sides change for different reasons
correctAnswerText: Where the two sides change for different reasons
explanation: Different reasons to change is the signal. Splitting by size alone leaves both halves changing together.

prompt: One function validates input, applies a discount and writes a row. What should it become?
optionA: A class with the three as methods
optionB: Three files in the same folder
optionC: One function with clearer comments
optionD: Three pieces, each about one of those
correctAnswerText: Three pieces, each about one of those
explanation: Three reasons to change is three concerns. A class holding all three still changes for all three reasons.

prompt: Your domain objects carry the web framework’s request types. What do you change?
optionA: Move the domain objects into the web layer
optionB: Document the coupling for future readers
optionC: Upgrade to a framework with better types
optionD: Translate to your own types at the edge
correctAnswerText: Translate to your own types at the edge
explanation: One translation at the boundary. Otherwise the framework reaches into every rule you own.

prompt: A small script reads a file and prints a total. What architecture does it need?
optionA: A service class holding the logic
optionB: A domain layer and a data layer
optionC: None beyond being readable
optionD: An interface for the file reading
correctAnswerText: None beyond being readable
explanation: Layering something with one reason to change adds cost and buys nothing. Structure answers a problem.

prompt: A service builds its own HTTP client inside its constructor. What is the fix?
optionA: Make the client a module-level singleton
optionB: Move the construction into a static method
optionC: Accept the client as a constructor argument
optionD: Add a test-only flag that skips the calls
correctAnswerText: Accept the client as a constructor argument
explanation: Given rather than built, it can be substituted. The flag is the same idea done worse — test branches in production code.

prompt: The team has spent two days choosing a date library. What should happen?
optionA: Continue until everyone genuinely agrees
optionB: Pick one and move on — it is easy to change
optionC: Write an adapter and defer the choice
optionD: Escalate the decision to an architect
correctAnswerText: Pick one and move on — it is easy to change
explanation: Two days on a reversible decision is two days not spent on the data model nobody can change later.

prompt: Should you group files by technical type or by feature?
optionA: By feature, since a change is usually one feature
optionB: By type, because most frameworks expect it
optionC: By type, so similar code sits together
optionD: By author, so ownership stays clear
correctAnswerText: By feature, since a change is usually one feature
explanation: Grouping by type means every feature change touches four folders. Grouping by feature keeps a change local.

prompt: Which side of a boundary should define the interface?
optionA: The side that needs the work done
optionB: A shared module between the two
optionC: The side that performs the work
optionD: Whichever side was written first
correctAnswerText: The side that needs the work done
explanation: Defined by the consumer, the dependency points at it rather than at the implementation. That is what inverts it.

prompt: What belongs in a record of an architectural decision?
optionA: A list of the files the change touched
optionB: The names of everybody who agreed to it
optionC: The context, the options, the choice, the consequences
optionD: A diagram showing the resulting system structure
correctAnswerText: The context, the options, the choice, the consequences
explanation: The rejected options matter most. Without them the next reader re-argues a case somebody already lost.

prompt: Adding one field to an order touches eleven files. What does that say?
optionA: The team needs better refactoring tooling
optionB: The concept is spread across the codebase
optionC: The field was badly named
optionD: The codebase is simply large
correctAnswerText: The concept is spread across the codebase
explanation: Every one of those files knows the shape of an order. The concept has no single place that owns it.

prompt: Every unit test needs a running database. What has gone wrong architecturally?
optionA: There are not enough mocks in the suite
optionB: The database is too slow for testing
optionC: The rules depend on the database rather than the reverse
optionD: The tests were written at the wrong level entirely
correctAnswerText: The rules depend on the database rather than the reverse
explanation: You cannot test rules alone because they cannot run alone. The test pain is reporting the dependency direction.

prompt: A request passes six classes that each call one method on the next. What is the problem?
optionA: The team has not documented the flow
optionB: The classes are too small to be useful
optionC: Method calls are slowing the request
optionD: Layers that pass work along without adding any
correctAnswerText: Layers that pass work along without adding any
explanation: A layer that only forwards is a layer with no responsibility. Six of them is a codebase nobody can follow.

prompt: One class is imported by almost every file and changes weekly. What does that indicate?
optionA: It is doing several unrelated jobs
optionB: It needs to be split by team
optionC: It is a well-used shared utility
optionD: It should be made a singleton
correctAnswerText: It is doing several unrelated jobs
explanation: Changing weekly for unrelated reasons is the tell. A cohesive shared type changes rarely.

prompt: Replacing the web framework turns out to require rewriting the business rules. Why?
optionA: The framework was an unusually invasive one
optionB: The migration was planned badly
optionC: The rules were never covered by tests
optionD: The rules were written in the framework’s terms
correctAnswerText: The rules were written in the framework’s terms
explanation: The framework reached past the edge. A detail that got into the middle stops being cheap to change.

prompt: A service returns the database row straight to the client. What has that cost you?
optionA: The service is harder to unit test
optionB: The schema is now part of the public contract
optionC: The database has to stay available
optionD: The response is larger than it needs to be
correctAnswerText: The schema is now part of the public contract
explanation: Renaming a column is now a breaking API change. The boundary is drawn but nothing is translated across it.

prompt: A new product was split into six services and every feature touches four. What happened?
optionA: The team is too small for six services
optionB: The boundaries were guessed before the domain was known
optionC: The services were each implemented inconsistently
optionD: The services need a shared library
correctAnswerText: The boundaries were guessed before the domain was known
explanation: Boundaries drawn early are drawn in ignorance, and a wrong boundary costs more across a network than in a file.

prompt: The discount rule lives in a database query and in the front end. What is the risk?
optionA: The front end will be harder to style
optionB: The two will disagree and nobody will know
optionC: The query will run more slowly than before
optionD: The rule cannot be changed at all
correctAnswerText: The two will disagree and nobody will know
explanation: A rule in two places is two rules. They agree until one is changed, and the disagreement is silent.

prompt: The architecture diagram no longer matches the code. Which is the architecture?
optionA: Whichever the team agreed most recently
optionB: The diagram, which the code should match
optionC: The code — the diagram is now a wish
optionD: Neither, until they are reconciled
correctAnswerText: The code — the diagram is now a wish
explanation: The system behaves as the code says. A diagram that disagrees is documentation of an intention.

prompt: A choice made in week one now cannot be undone. What made it expensive?
optionA: It came from an outside consultant
optionB: Everything was allowed to depend on it
optionC: It was made before the team was complete
optionD: Nobody wrote down why it was chosen
correctAnswerText: Everything was allowed to depend on it
explanation: Reversibility is about how much depends on it, not how old it is. Isolated choices stay cheap forever.

prompt: What makes one architecture better than another?
optionA: It follows the most established pattern
optionB: It has the fewest layers and files
optionC: It suits what this system must do and change
optionD: It is the one the team knows best
correctAnswerText: It suits what this system must do and change
explanation: There is no best architecture in the abstract. There is one that fits these constraints, and it expires.

prompt: When is splitting into services usually the right call?
optionA: At the start, so the split never has to happen later
optionB: Once the boundaries have proved themselves in one codebase
optionC: When the team grows past a certain number
optionD: When the application becomes slow to deploy
correctAnswerText: Once the boundaries have proved themselves in one codebase
explanation: A boundary inside one codebase is cheap to move. The same boundary across a network is not.

prompt: A design can swap its database, its queue and its cache. Is that good?
optionA: No — such designs are always over-built
optionB: Yes, provided the interfaces are clean
optionC: Only if any of those are likely to be swapped
optionD: Yes — flexibility is always worth having
correctAnswerText: Only if any of those are likely to be swapped
explanation: Three unused seams are three abstractions everybody reads through forever. Likelihood is the whole question.

prompt: You join a team whose architecture you would not have chosen. What comes first?
optionA: Documenting everything wrong with it
optionB: Isolating your work from the rest
optionC: Understanding what it was solving for
optionD: Proposing the design you would prefer
correctAnswerText: Understanding what it was solving for
explanation: Most odd architectures are answers to a constraint that is not visible in the code. Find it before you argue.

prompt: An architecture that fitted three years ago no longer does. What does that mean?
optionA: The team failed to maintain it
optionB: It was never properly documented
optionC: The system’s constraints changed, as they do
optionD: The original design was a poor one to begin with
correctAnswerText: The system’s constraints changed, as they do
explanation: Architectures have a shelf life because the problem moves. Expecting one to last forever is the actual mistake.

prompt: Why do full rewrites so often go badly?
optionA: The old code holds years of unrecorded knowledge
optionB: The new technology is usually immature
optionC: Rewrites always take longer than estimated
optionD: Teams lose interest partway through them
correctAnswerText: The old code holds years of unrecorded knowledge
explanation: Every strange branch is a bug somebody once hit. A rewrite discards the record and rediscovers them in production.

prompt: What makes a design answer convincing in an interview?
optionA: Drawing a complete component diagram
optionB: Naming what you gave up and why
optionC: Using well-known architectural patterns
optionD: Covering every requirement given
correctAnswerText: Naming what you gave up and why
explanation: Every design gives something up. An answer with no trade-off named has not understood the question.

prompt: How is an architecture usually changed safely?
optionA: By building the replacement alongside it
optionB: In a dedicated project with a feature freeze
optionC: By documenting the target state and migrating to it
optionD: One boundary at a time, with the system working throughout
correctAnswerText: One boundary at a time, with the system working throughout
explanation: The same rule as refactoring, at a larger scale: every step keeps the system running, so any step can be the last.

prompt: With genuine uncertainty about what the system will become, what should you build?
optionA: A design that covers the likeliest future
optionB: The most flexible structure you can manage
optionC: Whatever the last successful project used
optionD: The simplest thing that is easy to change
correctAnswerText: The simplest thing that is easy to change
explanation: Simple code can become anything. Flexibility built along the wrong axis has to be removed before you can move.

prompt: What is an architecture, in the end?
optionA: The set of technologies chosen
optionB: The diagram the team agreed on
optionC: The structure of folders and modules
optionD: The decisions that are hard to change later
correctAnswerText: The decisions that are hard to change later
explanation: Which is why so little of it is on the diagram, and why the expensive decisions deserve nearly all the thought.

prompt: What question does authentication answer?
optionA: Whether this request is safe to run
optionB: Who is making this request
optionC: Where this request came from
optionD: What this request is allowed to do
correctAnswerText: Who is making this request
explanation: Identity only. What they may do is authorization, and keeping the two apart is the first thing to learn.

prompt: How should a password be kept in the database?
optionA: As a slow one-way hash of it
optionB: In plain text, on a locked table
optionC: Encrypted with the application key
optionD: As a SHA-256 digest of the text
correctAnswerText: As a slow one-way hash of it
explanation: One-way so it cannot be read back, slow so guessing costs. SHA-256 is one-way but far too fast.

prompt: What is a salt?
optionA: A second password the user sets
optionB: Random data mixed in before hashing
optionC: Extra characters added to the input
optionD: A secret key kept by the server
correctAnswerText: Random data mixed in before hashing
explanation: Random and per-user. It is stored beside the hash and is not a secret — its job is to make each hash unique.

prompt: What is a session?
optionA: The time a user spends on the site
optionB: A record of the pages a user saw
optionC: A connection held open to the server
optionD: A remembered login across later requests
correctAnswerText: A remembered login across later requests
explanation: HTTP forgets between requests, so something has to carry the fact that this person already proved who they are.

prompt: What does it mean that a token is a bearer token?
optionA: It carries the user’s details inside it
optionB: It is issued by a trusted authority
optionC: Whoever holds it counts as that user
optionD: It must be sent on every request
correctAnswerText: Whoever holds it counts as that user
explanation: Like cash. A stolen bearer token needs no password to use, which is why transport and expiry matter so much.

prompt: What makes two authentication factors genuinely different?
optionA: They are different kinds of thing entirely
optionB: They are checked at two separate times
optionC: They are stored in two separate systems
optionD: They are chosen by two different parties
correctAnswerText: They are different kinds of thing entirely
explanation: Something you know, have or are. Two passwords are two of the same kind, so they are one factor twice.

prompt: How must credentials travel between browser and server?
optionA: Over an encrypted connection, always
optionB: Hashed by the browser before sending
optionC: In the request body rather than the URL
optionD: Encoded so they are not human-readable
correctAnswerText: Over an encrypted connection, always
explanation: Encoding is not encryption and a client-side hash just becomes the new password. TLS is not optional.

prompt: Why do access tokens carry an expiry time?
optionA: So the token stays a small size
optionB: So users are reminded to log in
optionC: So the server can free its memory
optionD: So a stolen one stops working soon
correctAnswerText: So a stolen one stops working soon
explanation: Expiry is damage limitation. It does not prevent theft; it bounds how long theft is useful.

prompt: What is a password reset flow, from a security point of view?
optionA: A way of changing a stored credential
optionB: Another way of logging in entirely
optionC: A convenience built on top of email
optionD: A support feature for locked-out users
correctAnswerText: Another way of logging in entirely
explanation: It grants access without the password, so it is a login route — and it deserves the same care as the main one.

prompt: What does "log in with Google" let your application avoid?
optionA: Checking who the user actually is
optionB: Holding a password of its own
optionC: Keeping any user records at all
optionD: Running its own session handling
correctAnswerText: Holding a password of its own
explanation: You still have users and sessions. What you no longer have is a password database worth stealing.

prompt: Why must a password hash be deliberately slow?
optionA: Fast hashes produce more collisions
optionB: Slow hashing rate-limits the login endpoint
optionC: Slower hashes produce longer output
optionD: A stolen table is guessed at offline, at speed
correctAnswerText: A stolen table is guessed at offline, at speed
explanation: Once the table is stolen your rate limits are irrelevant. The only remaining brake is the cost per guess.

prompt: What does a per-user salt actually prevent?
optionA: An attacker guessing a weak password
optionB: Two users choosing the same password
optionC: Reading a password back out of the hash
optionD: Cracking every account with one effort
correctAnswerText: Cracking every account with one effort
explanation: Without it, one precomputed table breaks every matching password at once. Salts force per-account work.

prompt: Why is keeping a token in browser local storage risky?
optionA: Any injected script on the page can read it
optionB: Other sites on the browser can read it
optionC: It survives longer than the token expiry
optionD: Local storage is written to disk unencrypted
correctAnswerText: Any injected script on the page can read it
explanation: One cross-site scripting bug anywhere on the origin turns into a stolen identity. A cookie can be closed to scripts.

prompt: Why should a failed login not say which field was wrong?
optionA: It exposes the validation rules used
optionB: It makes the error harder to translate
optionC: It confirms whether an account exists
optionD: It helps an attacker guess the password
correctAnswerText: It confirms whether an account exists
explanation: "No such user" is an account enumeration oracle. The attacker learns your customer list before trying a password.

prompt: Why does a second factor help even with a weak password?
optionA: It encrypts the password in transit
optionB: A remote attacker has only the one half
optionC: It makes the password harder to guess
optionD: It forces the user to change passwords
correctAnswerText: A remote attacker has only the one half
explanation: Most attacks are remote and at scale. A factor tied to a physical thing does not scale for the attacker.

prompt: What does rate limiting the login endpoint protect against?
optionA: Someone stealing the password database
optionB: A user forgetting their own password
optionC: Tokens being reused after expiry
optionD: Trying many passwords against one account
correctAnswerText: Trying many passwords against one account
explanation: It is the only defence that works while the password is still secret, which makes it the cheapest one you own.

prompt: Why issue a short access token and a long refresh token rather than one long token?
optionA: Refresh tokens cannot be stolen at all
optionB: The one sent everywhere expires quickly
optionC: It reduces the number of login requests
optionD: Two tokens are harder to steal than one
correctAnswerText: The one sent everywhere expires quickly
explanation: The access token is exposed on every call; the refresh token is exposed rarely and can be revoked centrally.

prompt: Why should a password reset link stop working after an hour?
optionA: It sits in an inbox that may be read later
optionB: Long links are harder for users to copy
optionC: It keeps the token table from growing
optionD: Email providers delete old messages
correctAnswerText: It sits in an inbox that may be read later
explanation: The link is a login credential sitting in plain text somewhere you do not control. Short life is the only mitigation.

prompt: Why is deleting the token in the browser not really a logout?
optionA: A copy taken earlier still works
optionB: Other tabs keep their own copy
optionC: The browser may restore it later
optionD: The server still has the session open
correctAnswerText: A copy taken earlier still works
explanation: Client-side logout is a UI gesture. Until the server refuses that token, the credential is still live.

prompt: What is the main security argument for delegating login to a provider?
optionA: It removes the need for session handling
optionB: You no longer hold the thing worth stealing
optionC: Users pick stronger passwords with them
optionD: Providers use stronger encryption than you
correctAnswerText: You no longer hold the thing worth stealing
explanation: You cannot leak a password table you do not have. That is the whole argument, and it is a strong one.

prompt: You are storing passwords for a new service. What do you use?
optionA: SHA-256 with a random salt per user
optionB: AES encryption with a server-side key
optionC: SHA-256 applied several thousand times
optionD: An established password hashing function
correctAnswerText: An established password hashing function
explanation: bcrypt, scrypt or argon2 — designed for this, tuned for cost. Hand-rolled iteration is how people get it wrong.

prompt: What should a failed login return to the user?
optionA: A message if the user exists, else nothing
optionB: One message covering both possibilities
optionC: A generic message plus a support code
optionD: A message naming the field that failed
correctAnswerText: One message covering both possibilities
explanation: "Email or password is incorrect." One message, one response time, no signal about which half was wrong.

prompt: Someone requests a reset for an email that has no account. What do you show?
optionA: Nothing, and no email is sent at all
optionB: A note that no such account exists
optionC: The same message as for a real account
optionD: An invitation to create an account
correctAnswerText: The same message as for a real account
explanation: Same message either way, or the reset form becomes the account enumeration tool the login form refused to be.

prompt: Where should a browser keep a session token?
optionA: A cookie that scripts cannot read
optionB: A cookie readable by the front end
optionC: Local storage, read by the API client
optionD: Memory only, refetched on reload
correctAnswerText: A cookie that scripts cannot read
explanation: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite. It survives a reload and an injected script cannot read it out.

prompt: You rate limit login by IP address. What does that miss?
optionA: One password tried across many accounts
optionB: A user who keeps mistyping their password
optionC: Attempts made through your own API
optionD: Requests arriving from a mobile network
correctAnswerText: One password tried across many accounts
explanation: Password spraying spreads across accounts and addresses. Limit per account as well as per source.

prompt: How do you make logout actually end the session?
optionA: Set the token expiry to the present
optionB: Clear the cookie from the browser
optionC: Have the server stop accepting that token
optionD: Redirect the user to the login page
correctAnswerText: Have the server stop accepting that token
explanation: Revoke server-side. Everything on the client is a request the holder of a stolen copy simply will not make.

prompt: What password rule actually improves security?
optionA: A forced change every ninety days for everyone
optionB: A generous minimum length, checked against known leaks
optionC: A maximum length so hashing stays fast
optionD: One uppercase, one digit and one symbol required
correctAnswerText: A generous minimum length, checked against known leaks
explanation: Composition rules produce Password1!. Length plus a breach list removes the passwords attackers actually try.

prompt: How should you compare a submitted token against the stored one?
optionA: With a comparison that always takes the same time
optionB: By hashing both and comparing the hashes
optionC: By comparing lengths first, then contents
optionD: With the language’s standard equality operator
correctAnswerText: With a comparison that always takes the same time
explanation: Ordinary comparison stops at the first wrong byte, and that timing difference is measurable across many tries.

prompt: A refresh token is used. What is the safer thing to do next?
optionA: Extend its expiry by the same period
optionB: Keep it valid until its expiry time
optionC: Issue a new access token and nothing more
optionD: Issue a new one and retire the used one
correctAnswerText: Issue a new one and retire the used one
explanation: Rotation makes theft detectable: if the old one is presented again, two parties hold it and you can cut both off.

prompt: Which second factor is the weakest of these in practice?
optionA: A push approval in a trusted app
optionB: A hardware security key
optionC: A code from an authenticator app
optionD: A code sent by text message
correctAnswerText: A code sent by text message
explanation: SIM swapping moves the number to the attacker. Still far better than nothing, but the weakest of the four.

prompt: Your login returns one message, but unknown emails fail in 5ms and known ones in 300ms. What leaks?
optionA: How many users the system has
optionB: The hashing algorithm being used
optionC: Which email addresses have accounts
optionD: Whether the password was close
correctAnswerText: Which email addresses have accounts
explanation: The message is identical and the timing is not. Hash a dummy password when the user is missing.

prompt: A system can email users their forgotten password. What does that prove?
optionA: The passwords are hashed with a weak function
optionB: The email system stores them separately
optionC: The passwords are recoverable, not hashed
optionD: The reset flow was implemented incorrectly
correctAnswerText: The passwords are recoverable, not hashed
explanation: If they can show it to you, they can show it to whoever takes the database. Hashing makes recovery impossible by design.

prompt: The session id stays the same before and after login. Why is that dangerous?
optionA: An id planted beforehand becomes a logged-in one
optionB: Two users may end up sharing one session
optionC: The session cannot then be expired properly
optionD: The id can be guessed from the previous one
correctAnswerText: An id planted beforehand becomes a logged-in one
explanation: Session fixation. Give the browser a fresh id at the moment privilege changes, which is exactly login.

prompt: Reset tokens are built from the user id and the current timestamp. What is wrong?
optionA: Two users could receive the same token
optionB: Both inputs are known, so it can be forged
optionC: The token cannot be expired reliably
optionD: The token will be longer than necessary
correctAnswerText: Both inputs are known, so it can be forged
explanation: A token derived from known values is not a secret. Reset tokens come from a cryptographic random source.

prompt: A token is passed as a query parameter over HTTPS. What is still exposed?
optionA: Server logs, browser history and referrers
optionB: The token contents to network observers
optionC: The token to any script on the page
optionD: The user identity to the receiving site
correctAnswerText: Server logs, browser history and referrers
explanation: TLS protects the wire, not what happens at either end. URLs get written down in several places automatically.

prompt: A service decodes a JWT and trusts the user id inside without checking the signature. What can an attacker do?
optionA: Claim to be anybody they like
optionB: Learn the server’s signing key
optionC: Extend their own token expiry
optionD: Read other users’ token contents
correctAnswerText: Claim to be anybody they like
explanation: A JWT body is encoded, not protected. The signature is the only thing separating a claim from a fact.

prompt: Accounts lock permanently after three failures. What has that enabled?
optionA: Sessions stay open after the lock
optionB: Attackers learn which accounts exist
optionC: Passwords can be guessed more cheaply
optionD: Anyone can lock anyone else out
correctAnswerText: Anyone can lock anyone else out
explanation: A defence that anybody can trigger against anybody is a denial of service. Prefer delays that decay over time.

prompt: A user reports their account was accessed. You reset the password, but access continues. Why?
optionA: The new password was also compromised
optionB: The reset only applied at next login
optionC: Existing tokens were never invalidated
optionD: The attacker reset the password back
correctAnswerText: Existing tokens were never invalidated
explanation: A password change must revoke every live session. Otherwise the attacker never needs the password again.

prompt: Signup never verifies the email address. What breaks later?
optionA: Reset depends on an address nobody proved
optionB: Marketing emails will bounce frequently
optionC: Users will mistype and lose their account
optionD: Two accounts may share one address
correctAnswerText: Reset depends on an address nobody proved
explanation: The reset flow is a login route keyed on that address. Unverified, it is a login route keyed on a guess.

prompt: You match provider logins to accounts by email address alone. What is the risk?
optionA: Users with two providers get two accounts
optionB: A provider that does not verify email grants entry
optionC: Email addresses change and break the link
optionD: The provider may stop returning the email
correctAnswerText: A provider that does not verify email grants entry
explanation: You are trusting somebody else’s verification. Match on the provider’s stable subject id, and check the verified flag.

prompt: When is writing your own authentication the right call?
optionA: For any system holding sensitive data
optionB: When the team has security experience
optionC: Whenever the product has unusual requirements
optionD: Rarely — the failure modes are subtle and known
correctAnswerText: Rarely — the failure modes are subtle and known
explanation: Not because you are incapable, but because the bugs are invisible until exploited and everyone hits the same ones.

prompt: A security measure makes login so awkward that users write passwords down. Is it a good measure?
optionA: Yes, provided users are trained properly
optionB: Yes, the system itself is more secure
optionC: No, but only because users dislike it
optionD: No — it moved the weakness somewhere worse
correctAnswerText: No — it moved the weakness somewhere worse
explanation: Security that people route around is security you have lost while believing you have it. Behaviour is part of the system.

prompt: What should decide how long a session lasts?
optionA: The default the framework provides
optionB: What a stolen session could do here
optionC: How often the average user returns
optionD: What competing products tend to use
correctAnswerText: What a stolen session could do here
explanation: A bank and a recipe site have the same technology and opposite answers, because the loss on theft differs.

prompt: When is it worth asking a logged-in user for their password again?
optionA: Every time the session has been idle
optionB: Whenever the user changes device
optionC: Before an action that is hard to undo
optionD: At a fixed interval during the session
correctAnswerText: Before an action that is hard to undo
explanation: Step-up spends friction where the loss is greatest — changing the email, deleting the account, moving money.

prompt: The password table has leaked, well hashed. What is the right response?
optionA: Tell users and force a reset anyway
optionB: Monitor for unusual login activity
optionC: Increase the hashing cost factor
optionD: Nothing — the hashes are strong
correctAnswerText: Tell users and force a reset anyway
explanation: Good hashing buys time, not safety, and weak passwords in the set will fall. Time is what you spend telling people.

prompt: What do you give up by making a third party your only login route?
optionA: Access for anyone they lock out or lose
optionB: Control over your own session lengths
optionC: The ability to identify your own users
optionD: The option of adding a second factor
correctAnswerText: Access for anyone they lock out or lose
explanation: Their outage is your outage and their account closure is your customer’s. Usually worth it — but it is a real cost.

prompt: Why did guidance turn against forcing regular password changes?
optionA: It conflicted with multi-factor rollouts
optionB: It increased the load on support teams
optionC: People made small, predictable edits instead
optionD: Attackers moved to other techniques
correctAnswerText: People made small, predictable edits instead
explanation: Summer2024! becomes Summer2025!. The measured behaviour was worse than the problem the rule was aimed at.

prompt: Which attack should a typical web application plan for first?
optionA: Credentials reused from another site’s leak
optionB: An insider reading the password table
optionC: A targeted attempt to break its hashing
optionD: Interception of traffic on the network
correctAnswerText: Credentials reused from another site’s leak
explanation: Credential stuffing is where the volume is. Nobody breaks your cryptography when people reuse passwords.

prompt: A team replaces passwords with emailed login links. What changed?
optionA: A second factor is no longer needed
optionB: Login became strictly more secure overall
optionC: The email account is now the whole security
optionD: Sessions can no longer be stolen at all
correctAnswerText: The email account is now the whole security
explanation: Not more secure or less — moved. Whether that is an improvement depends on how well that inbox is protected.

prompt: Why keep authentication and authorization as separate concerns in code?
optionA: Identity is settled once; permissions are checked everywhere
optionB: Authorization is the more complex of the two
optionC: They are usually maintained by entirely different teams
optionD: Standards require the two to be separated
correctAnswerText: Identity is settled once; permissions are checked everywhere
explanation: One happens at the edge, once. The other happens at every decision point, and mixing them leaves gaps at both.

prompt: What question does authorization answer?
optionA: Who is making this request
optionB: Whether the user is logged in
optionC: Whether the request is well formed
optionD: May this identity do this thing
correctAnswerText: May this identity do this thing
explanation: Permission, not identity. Being logged in is an input to the question, not an answer to it.

prompt: What is a role?
optionA: A named bundle of permissions
optionB: A level of access, from low to high
optionC: A group of users in the system
optionD: A job title stored on the account
correctAnswerText: A named bundle of permissions
explanation: The bundle is the point: you grant one name instead of twenty permissions, and change it in one place.

prompt: What should happen to a request no rule covers?
optionA: It is logged and allowed
optionB: It is passed to an administrator
optionC: It is refused
optionD: It is allowed
correctAnswerText: It is refused
explanation: Deny by default. A new endpoint added next year is then closed until somebody deliberately opens it.

prompt: Where must an authorization check run?
optionA: In the client, before the request
optionB: At the network edge, once
optionC: On the server, for every request
optionD: In both, to catch it early
correctAnswerText: On the server, for every request
explanation: Anything in the client is a suggestion, because the client is a program the user controls entirely.

prompt: What does least privilege mean?
optionA: Only the access the job needs
optionB: Access that expires after each use
optionC: Permissions granted one at a time
optionD: The lowest role available to assign
correctAnswerText: Only the access the job needs
explanation: Scoped to the work, not to the person’s seniority. It bounds the damage of any single account being taken.

prompt: What is an ownership check?
optionA: Confirming the record still exists
optionB: Confirming the record belongs to this user
optionC: Confirming the user has the right role
optionD: Confirming the user is still logged in
correctAnswerText: Confirming the record belongs to this user
explanation: Distinct from a role check, and the one people forget. Every customer has the "customer" role.

prompt: What does a scope on an API token express?
optionA: The subset of actions it may take
optionB: The user account it belongs to
optionC: How long the token remains valid
optionD: The services it is allowed to reach
correctAnswerText: The subset of actions it may take
explanation: A narrowing. The user may be able to do far more than the token they issued to some integration can.

prompt: What does hiding a button from a user achieve?
optionA: The same effect as a server check
optionB: A tidier interface, and nothing more
optionC: A record that access was refused
optionD: Protection of the action behind it
correctAnswerText: A tidier interface, and nothing more
explanation: The endpoint is still there and still reachable with any HTTP client. Hiding is courtesy; the check is security.

prompt: What does an attribute-based rule decide on?
optionA: The group the user has been placed in
optionB: The role assigned to the user account
optionC: Facts about the user, the thing and the context
optionD: The permissions listed on the endpoint
correctAnswerText: Facts about the user, the thing and the context
explanation: Department, record status, time of day, amount. It expresses rules roles alone cannot reach.

prompt: What does an audit log record?
optionA: Who did what, and when
optionB: The requests that were refused
optionC: Every error the system raised
optionD: Changes made to the source code
correctAnswerText: Who did what, and when
explanation: Including the allowed actions. A log of refusals alone cannot answer what an abused account actually did.

prompt: Why can a client-side check never be trusted?
optionA: The user can send the request without it
optionB: The check may run before data loads
optionC: Browsers may disable the script entirely
optionD: Client code may be an outdated version
correctAnswerText: The user can send the request without it
explanation: Your interface is one way to call your API. Nothing obliges anybody to use it.

prompt: Why is a list of what is allowed safer than a list of what is forbidden?
optionA: The allowed list is shorter to write
optionB: Forbidden lists are harder to read
optionC: Allowed lists are faster to check
optionD: The allowed list can be complete
correctAnswerText: The allowed list can be complete
explanation: You can enumerate what should work. You can never finish enumerating what should not, especially next year.

prompt: Why is "the user has the customer role" not enough to show them an invoice?
optionA: The role may have expired by now
optionB: Every customer has that same role
optionC: Invoices need a higher role than that
optionD: Roles can be changed by the user
correctAnswerText: Every customer has that same role
explanation: The role says what kind of user they are. It says nothing about whose invoice this particular one is.

prompt: What does least privilege buy you when an account is compromised?
optionA: The compromise is detected more quickly
optionB: The account can be disabled more easily
optionC: The attacker inherits only that much reach
optionD: Fewer accounts are affected in total
correctAnswerText: The attacker inherits only that much reach
explanation: It assumes compromise rather than preventing it, and bounds what any single stolen account is worth.

prompt: Why express permission rules in one place rather than inline everywhere?
optionA: A rule change then cannot be half-applied
optionB: Inline checks cannot be unit tested
optionC: It reduces the total lines of code
optionD: Centralised checks run more efficiently
correctAnswerText: A rule change then cannot be half-applied
explanation: Scattered rules drift. The one endpoint nobody updated is exactly where the hole ends up.

prompt: Why give an integration a read-only token rather than your own credentials?
optionA: Read-only tokens are harder to steal
optionB: It keeps the integration simpler to build
optionC: Its compromise then cannot change anything
optionD: It avoids sharing your account password
correctAnswerText: Its compromise then cannot change anything
explanation: Third-party code runs where you cannot see it. The scope decides what a bad day over there costs you.

prompt: Why might you return "not found" instead of "forbidden" for another user’s record?
optionA: Forbidden invites the user to retry
optionB: Forbidden confirms the record exists
optionC: Not found is easier to cache safely
optionD: Not found is the more accurate code
correctAnswerText: Forbidden confirms the record exists
explanation: Existence is itself information. Whether it matters depends on the data, which is why this is a judgement call.

prompt: Why log actions that were permitted, not only those refused?
optionA: Auditors require a complete history
optionB: An abused account is doing permitted things
optionC: Permitted actions are easier to record
optionD: Refusals are rare and less informative
correctAnswerText: An abused account is doing permitted things
explanation: The insider and the stolen session both pass every check. A refusal log cannot see either of them.

prompt: Why do role systems tend to grow dozens of near-identical roles?
optionA: Every new feature requires its own role
optionB: Teams forget which roles already exist
optionC: Roles cannot be deleted once created
optionD: Each exception becomes a new role
correctAnswerText: Each exception becomes a new role
explanation: manager-except-refunds. Roles cannot express conditions, so every condition becomes another bundle.

prompt: In a system serving many organisations, what must every query carry?
optionA: The permissions the endpoint requires
optionB: The identity of the logged-in user
optionC: The organisation the request belongs to
optionD: The role of the user making it
correctAnswerText: The organisation the request belongs to
explanation: One missing tenant filter shows another company their competitor’s data, and the user was fully authorized.

prompt: An endpoint returns /orders/:id. What check does it need beyond being logged in?
optionA: That the order id is a valid format
optionB: That the user has the customer role
optionC: That the order belongs to this user
optionD: That the session has not expired
correctAnswerText: That the order belongs to this user
explanation: Without it, changing the number in the URL walks through everybody’s orders. This is the classic hole.

prompt: A list endpoint fetches all records then filters them in code. What is the better shape?
optionA: Cache the filtered list for the next request
optionB: Ask the database only for what they may see
optionC: Filter in code but add a second check after
optionD: Paginate before filtering to limit the rows
correctAnswerText: Ask the database only for what they may see
explanation: Filtering after fetching means one forgotten path leaks the lot. The constraint belongs in the query itself.

prompt: Where is the safest layer to enforce record-level permission?
optionA: In the route handler for each endpoint
optionB: In the client, before the call is made
optionC: As close to the data access as possible
optionD: In middleware before any handler runs
correctAnswerText: As close to the data access as possible
explanation: Middleware sees the URL, not the record. The layer that loads the row is the one that can judge it.

prompt: Should code check "is an admin" or "may delete invoices"?
optionA: The role, since it is simpler to read
optionB: The role, as permissions change often
optionC: Both, so either grant path works
optionD: The permission, so the roles can change
correctAnswerText: The permission, so the roles can change
explanation: Check the capability and the role becomes a configuration detail. Check the role and every change is a code change.

prompt: How do you stop one organisation ever reading another’s rows?
optionA: Review every query for the filter
optionB: Check the tenant in the route handler
optionC: Put each tenant in its own table
optionD: Make the tenant filter impossible to omit
correctAnswerText: Make the tenant filter impossible to omit
explanation: A scoped repository or a row-level policy. Anything relying on memory fails the first time somebody is in a hurry.

prompt: Should the front end hide actions the user may not take?
optionA: Yes, for usability, on top of a server check
optionB: No, it duplicates the server’s logic
optionC: No, users should see what they cannot do
optionD: Yes, and the server check is then optional
correctAnswerText: Yes, for usability, on top of a server check
explanation: Both, with different jobs. The hidden button saves a pointless refusal; the server check is what enforces it.

prompt: What must a permission test assert that people usually skip?
optionA: That the wrong user is actually refused
optionB: That the error message is worded well
optionC: That the check runs before the handler
optionD: That the right user is allowed through
correctAnswerText: That the wrong user is actually refused
explanation: The happy path passes even with no check at all. Only the refusal test can prove the check exists.

prompt: Support needs admin access to investigate one incident. What do you grant?
optionA: Permanent admin, revoked afterwards
optionB: A shared admin account for the team
optionC: Access that expires on its own
optionD: Read access to the whole database
correctAnswerText: Access that expires on its own
explanation: Time-boxed by default. Access that has to be remembered to be removed is access that never gets removed.

prompt: "A manager may approve, but not their own request." How do you express that?
optionA: A rule comparing the requester and the approver
optionB: A check in the UI that hides the button
