optionC: A second role for managers who may approve
optionD: A separate endpoint for self-approval
correctAnswerText: A rule comparing the requester and the approver
explanation: The rule depends on a relationship between two parties, which no bundle of permissions can capture.

prompt: A logged-in user requests a document belonging to a different company. What do you return?
optionA: Forbidden, with the owner named
optionB: Not found, revealing nothing about it
optionC: Unauthorized, prompting a new login
optionD: Forbidden, so the refusal is honest
correctAnswerText: Not found, revealing nothing about it
explanation: Across a tenant boundary, even existence is somebody else’s information. Within your own account, forbidden is kinder.

prompt: Changing the id in /api/profile/42 shows another user’s profile. What is missing?
optionA: Authentication on that endpoint
optionB: Rate limiting on profile requests
optionC: A check that the record is the caller’s
optionD: Validation of the id parameter
correctAnswerText: A check that the record is the caller’s
explanation: Authentication worked perfectly. The request is from a real, logged-in user asking for something not theirs.

prompt: The delete button is hidden for normal users, but the DELETE endpoint works for them. What happened?
optionA: The endpoint was deployed before the UI
optionB: The role was not applied to that user
optionC: The control was put only in the interface
optionD: Middleware was skipped for that route
correctAnswerText: The control was put only in the interface
explanation: Extremely common and usually found by accident. The interface expressed the intention; nothing enforced it.

prompt: A report endpoint filters by tenant, but a joined table is not filtered. What is the effect?
optionA: The report fails for smaller tenants
optionB: The query returns fewer rows than expected
optionC: Rows from other tenants appear in the results
optionD: The join runs more slowly than it should
correctAnswerText: Rows from other tenants appear in the results
explanation: The filter has to cover every table the data comes from. One unscoped join is a cross-tenant leak.

prompt: A profile update copies the whole request body onto the user record. What can a user do?
optionA: Set fields they should never control, like role
optionB: Overwrite another user’s profile entirely
optionC: Bypass the authentication on that route
optionD: Delete fields by omitting them from the body
correctAnswerText: Set fields they should never control, like role
explanation: Mass assignment. Authorization is per field as well as per record; accept a named list, never the whole body.

prompt: Nineteen endpoints check permission and one does not. How did that happen?
optionA: The last endpoint was written in a hurry
optionB: The team lacked a code review process
optionC: That route was added by a different team
optionD: The check is opt-in rather than automatic
correctAnswerText: The check is opt-in rather than automatic
explanation: A check somebody must remember is a check somebody will forget. Make the default closed and opening explicit.

prompt: The server reads the user’s role from a header the client sends. What is wrong?
optionA: The header may be stripped by a proxy
optionB: The client decides its own permissions
optionC: Roles should be sent in the body instead
optionD: Headers are not encrypted in transit
correctAnswerText: The client decides its own permissions
explanation: Anything the client sends is a claim. The role must come from the server’s own record of that identity.

prompt: Over three years, most staff have ended up with the admin role. Why?
optionA: Staff requested it to do their jobs faster
optionB: Granting was easy and removal never happened
optionC: The company grew faster than the role model
optionD: The admin role gained too many permissions
correctAnswerText: Granting was easy and removal never happened
explanation: Privilege creep is a ratchet. Without periodic review it only ever turns one way.

prompt: A per-user page is cached by a shared proxy. What can go wrong?
optionA: The page becomes stale for everybody
optionB: The cache grows larger than expected
optionC: One user is served another user’s page
optionD: Logged-out users see a login prompt
correctAnswerText: One user is served another user’s page
explanation: The check ran once, for somebody else. Authorized responses need cache headers that say private.

prompt: A user’s admin role is removed, but they keep admin access for hours. Why?
optionA: The role is carried inside a long-lived token
optionB: The cache of roles was not cleared
optionC: The change did not save to the database
optionD: Their session was not expired on change
correctAnswerText: The role is carried inside a long-lived token
explanation: A token is a snapshot of permissions at issue time. Anything self-contained is stale the moment reality changes.

prompt: An internal service performs no checks because "only our own services call it". What is the flaw?
optionA: Internal services can be called externally
optionB: Other teams may misuse the interface
optionC: Any foothold inside the network reaches it
optionD: The service cannot log who called it
correctAnswerText: Any foothold inside the network reaches it
explanation: Network position is not identity. One compromised service turns into everything that service can reach.

prompt: When are simple roles the right choice over a richer model?
optionA: When the team is new to authorization
optionB: Whenever the system is still small
optionC: When the real rules genuinely fit them
optionD: When performance is a concern
correctAnswerText: When the real rules genuinely fit them
explanation: Roles are not a beginner model; they are the right model when permission really does follow the job.

prompt: What decides whether a refusal should admit the resource exists?
optionA: How the front end wants to show it
optionB: Whether the user is inside the company
optionC: Which status code the standard prefers
optionD: Whether existence is itself sensitive here
correctAnswerText: Whether existence is itself sensitive here
explanation: Knowing a patient record exists can be the leak. Knowing a colleague’s document exists usually is not.

prompt: Permissions are so tight that staff share accounts to get work done. What is the verdict?
optionA: The model failed — accountability is now gone
optionB: The model is working and staff need training
optionC: The model is right but needs more roles
optionD: The model should be relaxed for everyone
correctAnswerText: The model failed — accountability is now gone
explanation: Shared accounts destroy the audit trail, which is worse than the over-permission you were avoiding.

prompt: Why review who has what access on a schedule?
optionA: Grants accumulate; nothing removes them
optionB: Roles change meaning over time
optionC: Permissions can be lost silently
optionD: Auditors ask for the evidence
correctAnswerText: Grants accumulate; nothing removes them
explanation: People change teams and keep the old access. Only a deliberate review ever turns the ratchet back.

prompt: Permissions in the token are fast; looking them up is fresh. How do you choose?
optionA: By how often permissions actually change
optionB: By how bad a few minutes of stale access is
optionC: By whether the token format supports it
optionD: By how many requests the system handles
correctAnswerText: By how bad a few minutes of stale access is
explanation: The real question is the cost of the gap, not the frequency of change. Sometimes minutes are fine; sometimes not.

prompt: What is the argument for services checking each other’s identity internally?
optionA: One breach then does not become all of them
optionB: External standards increasingly require it
optionC: It makes the services easier to test
optionD: It removes the need for network controls
correctAnswerText: One breach then does not become all of them
explanation: Containment. The perimeter will be crossed eventually, and what matters then is how far the intruder gets.

prompt: Support staff can view the app as a customer. What must that feature include?
optionA: A read-only restriction on all actions
optionB: The customer’s consent before each use
optionC: A record of who acted, not just as whom
optionD: A time limit on each viewing session
correctAnswerText: A record of who acted, not just as whom
explanation: Without the real actor in the log, every impersonated action is attributed to the customer. That is the whole risk.

prompt: What gives the most confidence that no endpoint is unprotected?
optionA: An annual penetration test of the API
optionB: A checklist reviewers work through
optionC: A test per endpoint for the happy path
optionD: A test that every route is denied by default
correctAnswerText: A test that every route is denied by default
explanation: Enumerate the routes and assert refusal. A new endpoint then fails the suite until somebody opens it deliberately.

prompt: A permission model is so intricate that nobody can say who can do what. What is the risk?
optionA: Nobody can tell whether it is correct
optionB: The checks become slow to evaluate
optionC: New roles take longer to create
optionD: The rules are hard to document
correctAnswerText: Nobody can tell whether it is correct
explanation: Security you cannot reason about is security you are hoping for. Comprehensibility is a property of the control.

prompt: What question should you ask at every endpoint you write?
optionA: Is this user logged in properly
optionB: Whose data is this, and is it theirs
optionC: Does this user hold the right role
optionD: Has this input been validated fully
correctAnswerText: Whose data is this, and is it theirs
explanation: The role question is answered once at the door. The ownership question has to be asked at every single record.

prompt: What is a graph made of?
optionA: Values arranged in a parent-child order
optionB: Items stored one after another in memory
optionC: Nodes and the connections between them
optionD: Keys paired with the values they point to
correctAnswerText: Nodes and the connections between them
explanation: Vertices and edges. Everything else — trees, grids, linked lists — is a graph with a restriction added.

prompt: What makes a graph directed?
optionA: It contains no cycles at all
optionB: The nodes are kept in an order
optionC: An edge goes one way only
optionD: It has a single starting node
correctAnswerText: An edge goes one way only
explanation: Following somebody is directed; being friends is not. The distinction decides what a traversal can reach.

prompt: What structure does breadth-first search use to hold nodes it has yet to visit?
optionA: A heap
optionB: A stack
optionC: A queue
optionD: A set
correctAnswerText: A queue
explanation: First in, first out, which is what keeps it exploring one whole distance before starting the next.

prompt: What does depth-first search use, explicitly or through recursion?
optionA: A stack
optionB: A queue
optionC: A priority queue
optionD: A sorted list
correctAnswerText: A stack
explanation: Recursion is a stack you did not write. That is why deep graphs overflow it and iterative versions do not.

prompt: What is the visited set for?
optionA: Recording the order nodes were seen
optionB: Stopping the traversal revisiting nodes
optionC: Counting how many nodes were reached
optionD: Storing the path back to the start
correctAnswerText: Stopping the traversal revisiting nodes
explanation: Without it, any cycle makes the traversal run forever. It is part of the algorithm, not a speed-up.

prompt: What does a weight on an edge represent?
optionA: How important that node is
optionB: How many times it has been used
optionC: The order edges should be taken in
optionD: The cost of using that connection
correctAnswerText: The cost of using that connection
explanation: Distance, time, price, risk. Once edges cost different amounts, counting them stops answering the question.

prompt: What does an adjacency list store for each node?
optionA: Its position in the graph
optionB: The nodes it connects to
optionC: Whether it has been visited
optionD: Its distance from the start
correctAnswerText: The nodes it connects to
explanation: Neighbours only. The whole graph is then one list per node, which is small when most pairs are unconnected.

prompt: What is a cycle?
optionA: A node connected to every other node
optionB: A path that returns to where it began
optionC: A pair of nodes joined twice over
optionD: A graph with more edges than nodes
correctAnswerText: A path that returns to where it began
explanation: Cycles are what make graphs harder than trees, and what makes the visited set non-negotiable.

prompt: What is a connected component?
optionA: A group of nodes that can all reach each other
optionB: A set of nodes with the same number of edges
optionC: A part of the graph with no cycles in it
optionD: The largest group of nodes in the graph
correctAnswerText: A group of nodes that can all reach each other
explanation: One traversal reaches exactly one component, which is why counting components means restarting from unvisited nodes.

prompt: What is a directed acyclic graph?
optionA: A directed graph shaped like a tree
optionB: A graph with exactly one path each way
optionC: A directed graph with no cycles
optionD: A graph where all edges point down
correctAnswerText: A directed graph with no cycles
explanation: Dependencies, build steps, course prerequisites. The absence of cycles is what makes an ordering possible.

prompt: What does breadth-first search guarantee about the first time it reaches a node?
optionA: It arrived by the fewest edges possible
optionB: It arrived by the cheapest route there
optionC: It arrived along the only path to it
optionD: It arrived before any other traversal would
correctAnswerText: It arrived by the fewest edges possible
explanation: Fewest edges, not cheapest. The two coincide only when every edge costs exactly the same.

prompt: Why does depth-first search not find shortest paths?
optionA: It stops as soon as the target is found
optionB: It commits to one branch before trying others
optionC: It does not keep track of the distances
optionD: It may visit some nodes more than once
correctAnswerText: It commits to one branch before trying others
explanation: It follows one route to its end. The first arrival is simply the first route tried, not the shortest.

prompt: In BFS, when should a node be marked visited?
optionA: When the traversal has finished
optionB: When it is put into the queue
optionC: When all its neighbours are explored
optionD: When it is taken out of the queue
correctAnswerText: When it is put into the queue
explanation: Marking on removal lets the same node be queued several times before it is ever processed.

prompt: Why is an adjacency matrix a poor choice for a sparse graph?
optionA: It stores a cell for every possible pair
optionB: It has to be rebuilt when nodes are added
optionC: It cannot represent weighted edges well
optionD: It makes finding neighbours much slower
correctAnswerText: It stores a cell for every possible pair
explanation: A million nodes means a trillion cells, nearly all of them empty. The list stores only what exists.

prompt: Why is a full traversal described as O(V + E) rather than O(V)?
optionA: Edges must be sorted before the traversal
optionB: Every edge is examined as well as every node
optionC: The queue operations each cost extra time
optionD: Some nodes are examined more than once
correctAnswerText: Every edge is examined as well as every node
explanation: You touch each node once and look down each of its edges once. Both terms are real work.

prompt: Why can BFS not be used for shortest paths on a weighted graph?
optionA: Weighted graphs usually contain cycles
optionB: BFS visits the nodes in the wrong order
optionC: BFS cannot read the weights at all
optionD: A longer route may cost less overall
correctAnswerText: A longer route may cost less overall
explanation: Three cheap hops can beat one expensive one. Counting hops answers a different question entirely.

prompt: Why does a topological order require the graph to have no cycles?
optionA: Cycles make the ordering ambiguous
optionB: Cycles mean some nodes are unreachable
optionC: Cycles make the traversal run indefinitely
optionD: A cycle means each must come before the other
correctAnswerText: A cycle means each must come before the other
explanation: The requirement is contradictory, not merely difficult. That is why a failed sort detects a dependency cycle.

prompt: In what sense is a grid of cells a graph?
optionA: The grid can be flattened into a list
optionB: Grids and graphs are both two-dimensional
optionC: Each cell is a node joined to its neighbours
optionD: The rows and columns form the edges
correctAnswerText: Each cell is a node joined to its neighbours
explanation: Seeing this is most of the skill. Half of all graph problems in interviews arrive drawn as a grid.

prompt: On a wide, shallow graph, which traversal uses less memory?
optionA: Whichever one visits fewer nodes
optionB: Breadth-first, since it holds one level
optionC: Depth-first, since it holds one path
optionD: Both hold the same number of nodes
correctAnswerText: Depth-first, since it holds one path
explanation: BFS holds a whole level at once, and on a wide graph a level is enormous. DFS holds only the current path.

prompt: Why might one traversal not reach every node?
optionA: The graph may be in separate pieces
optionB: The visited set may fill up early
optionC: The traversal may stop at a cycle
optionD: Some nodes may have no edges at all
correctAnswerText: The graph may be in separate pieces
explanation: A traversal reaches one component. Covering the graph means restarting from every node still unvisited.

prompt: You need the fewest moves from one square to another on an unweighted board. What do you use?
optionA: Depth-first search from the start
optionB: Breadth-first search from the start
optionC: A topological ordering of the squares
optionD: A shortest-path algorithm with weights
correctAnswerText: Breadth-first search from the start
explanation: Unweighted and asking for fewest steps is precisely what BFS promises. Anything heavier is wasted.

prompt: Roads have different travel times and you want the quickest route. What do you use?
optionA: Breadth-first search counting the roads
optionB: A topological ordering of the junctions
optionC: Depth-first search keeping the best found
optionD: A shortest-path search using a priority queue
correctAnswerText: A shortest-path search using a priority queue
explanation: Dijkstra: always expand the cheapest known node next. The priority queue is what makes that possible.

prompt: Courses have prerequisites and you need a valid order to take them. What do you use?
optionA: Breadth-first search from the first course
optionB: A shortest-path search across the courses
optionC: A topological sort of the dependency graph
optionD: Depth-first search recording the depth
correctAnswerText: A topological sort of the dependency graph
explanation: And if the sort cannot finish, the prerequisites contain a cycle — which is the other answer it gives you.

prompt: How do you count separate islands of land cells in a grid?
optionA: Check each cell against its four neighbours
optionB: Count the land cells and divide by the average size
optionC: Traverse once from the first land cell found
optionD: Traverse from each unvisited land cell, counting runs
correctAnswerText: Traverse from each unvisited land cell, counting runs
explanation: Each traversal consumes one whole island. The number of times you had to start is the answer.

prompt: How do you detect a cycle in a directed graph with DFS?
optionA: Check whether any node has two parents
optionB: Look for a node already on the current path
optionC: Count whether edges outnumber the nodes
optionD: Look for a node already in the visited set
correctAnswerText: Look for a node already on the current path
explanation: Visited-anywhere is not enough; a diamond hits that with no cycle. Cycles need the path you are currently on.

prompt: BFS found the target. How do you produce the actual path taken?
optionA: Re-run the traversal recording each step
optionB: Store the full path with every queued node
optionC: Keep the whole queue and read it in order
optionD: Record each node’s predecessor and walk back
correctAnswerText: Record each node’s predecessor and walk back
explanation: One parent pointer per node, then walk backwards from the target. Storing whole paths costs far more memory.

prompt: You are given a list of connected pairs. What is the first thing to build?
optionA: A sorted list of all the pairs given
optionB: A matrix of every possible connection
optionC: A map from each node to its neighbours
optionD: A set of all the nodes that appear
correctAnswerText: A map from each node to its neighbours
explanation: The pair list cannot be traversed. Almost every graph solution starts by turning it into an adjacency map.

prompt: How do you check whether people can be split into two groups with no conflicts inside either?
optionA: Try every possible split and test each one
optionB: Traverse, colouring each neighbour the opposite way
optionC: Sort the people by how many conflicts they have
optionD: Count the conflicts and halve the total
correctAnswerText: Traverse, colouring each neighbour the opposite way
explanation: A two-colouring. It fails exactly when a neighbour already carries the colour you were about to assign.

prompt: What must a grid traversal check before stepping to a neighbour?
optionA: That it is inside the grid and not yet seen
optionB: That it holds the value being searched for
optionC: That it is closer to the target than now
optionD: That it has not been queued this round
correctAnswerText: That it is inside the grid and not yet seen
explanation: Bounds first, then visited. Off-by-one on the bounds check is the single most common grid bug.

prompt: You need each cell’s distance to its nearest of many sources. What is the efficient approach?
optionA: Run BFS from each cell towards the sources
optionB: Compute every pair of distances and compare
optionC: Run a separate BFS from each of the sources
optionD: Put every source in the queue and run BFS once
correctAnswerText: Put every source in the queue and run BFS once
explanation: Multi-source BFS. Seeding all of them at distance zero spreads one wave, and the first arrival is the nearest.

prompt: A traversal never finishes on a graph that has cycles. What is missing?
optionA: The check for nodes already seen
optionB: A limit on how deep it will go
optionC: A check for the target node
optionD: The base case in the recursion
correctAnswerText: The check for nodes already seen
explanation: It is going round the cycle forever. The visited set is not an optimisation; it is the termination condition.

prompt: A BFS marks nodes visited only when dequeued, and runs far slower than expected. Why?
optionA: Nodes are being processed out of order
optionB: The distances recorded become incorrect
optionC: The same node is queued many times over
optionD: The queue is being searched on each step
correctAnswerText: The same node is queued many times over
explanation: Between queueing and dequeueing, every other neighbour queues it again. On a dense graph that is ruinous.

prompt: BFS returns a route with three hops costing 90; another route has five hops costing 30. What went wrong?
optionA: The graph should be directed instead
optionB: BFS minimised hops, not cost
optionC: The BFS implementation has a bug
optionD: The weights were read incorrectly
correctAnswerText: BFS minimised hops, not cost
explanation: Nothing is broken. BFS did exactly what it promises, and what it promises was not the question being asked.

prompt: A cycle detector reports a cycle in a graph shaped like a diamond, which has none. Why?
optionA: It follows edges in the wrong direction
optionB: It fails to mark nodes as visited at all
optionC: It treats any revisited node as a cycle
optionD: It starts the traversal from a leaf node
correctAnswerText: It treats any revisited node as a cycle
explanation: Two paths reaching the same node is not a cycle. The test is whether the node is on the CURRENT path.

prompt: A recursive DFS crashes on a long chain of a hundred thousand nodes. What is the cause?
optionA: The recursion missed its base case
optionB: The visited set grew beyond memory
optionC: The graph contains a hidden cycle
optionD: The call stack ran out of room
correctAnswerText: The call stack ran out of room
explanation: Correct algorithm, wrong machine limit. The fix is an explicit stack, which puts the frames on the heap.

prompt: A friendship graph built from pairs finds A reaches B but B never reaches A. What was missed?
optionA: Each pair had to be added in both directions
optionB: Some pairs appeared in the input twice
optionC: The pairs were added in the wrong order
optionD: The visited set was shared between runs
correctAnswerText: Each pair had to be added in both directions
explanation: Friendship is undirected; the adjacency map was built as though it were not. Add each edge both ways.

prompt: Dijkstra gives a wrong answer on a graph containing a negative-cost edge. Why?
optionA: It assumes a settled node cannot improve
optionB: It cannot compare negative numbers correctly
optionC: Negative edges always create cycles
optionD: The priority queue orders them incorrectly
correctAnswerText: It assumes a settled node cannot improve
explanation: Once it finalises a node it never revisits it, and a negative edge is exactly what would have made it cheaper.

prompt: A traversal scans the whole edge list to find each node’s neighbours. What does that cost?
optionA: A factor of the edge count on every node
optionB: A slower result only on dense graphs
optionC: Nothing — the total work is unchanged
optionD: Extra memory proportional to the edges
correctAnswerText: A factor of the edge count on every node
explanation: O(V·E) instead of O(V+E). Building the adjacency map once is the difference between passing and timing out.

prompt: An island counter resets the visited set before each new start and reports far too many islands. Why?
optionA: The traversal never reaches the whole island
optionB: Cells of one island get counted repeatedly
optionC: The count is incremented in the wrong place
optionD: Some cells are skipped by the outer loop
correctAnswerText: Cells of one island get counted repeatedly
explanation: The visited set must span the whole outer loop. Resetting it makes each cell of an island look like a new one.

prompt: A topological sort produces fewer nodes than the graph holds. What does that tell you?
optionA: Some nodes had no edges at all
optionB: Those left over sit in a cycle
optionC: The graph has separate components
optionD: The sort visited nodes in a bad order
correctAnswerText: Those left over sit in a cycle
explanation: Nodes in a cycle never reach zero remaining dependencies. The shortfall is the cycle detector.

prompt: What most often decides whether someone solves a graph problem?
optionA: Noticing that it is a graph problem
optionB: Writing the traversal without bugs
optionC: Choosing the right representation
optionD: Knowing the algorithms by heart
correctAnswerText: Noticing that it is a graph problem
explanation: The algorithms are few and learnable. The translation from word problem to nodes and edges is the hard part.

prompt: Both BFS and DFS would answer the question. How do you choose?
optionA: By whether the graph is directed
optionB: By the shape of the graph and the memory
optionC: By whichever is simpler to write
optionD: By which one runs faster in general
correctAnswerText: By the shape of the graph and the memory
explanation: Same asymptotic cost, opposite memory profiles. Wide and shallow favours DFS; deep and narrow favours BFS.

prompt: A candidate reaches for Dijkstra on an unweighted graph. What is the issue?
optionA: The priority queue will not terminate
optionB: BFS answers it with less machinery
optionC: Dijkstra will give the wrong answer
optionD: Dijkstra cannot handle equal weights
correctAnswerText: BFS answers it with less machinery
explanation: It works, and it signals not having noticed that equal weights collapse the problem into a simpler one.

prompt: The graph is too large to hold in memory. What changes?
optionA: The graph must first be split into pieces
optionB: The traversal must generate nodes as it goes
optionC: Only depth-first search remains possible
optionD: The algorithms no longer apply at all
correctAnswerText: The traversal must generate nodes as it goes
explanation: An implicit graph: neighbours computed on demand rather than stored. Chess positions are never held as a list.

prompt: A puzzle asks for the fewest moves to reach a target state. What is a node?
optionA: One position on the board
optionB: One whole state of the puzzle
optionC: One move that can be made
optionD: One piece that can be moved
correctAnswerText: One whole state of the puzzle
explanation: States are nodes and moves are edges. This inversion is what turns puzzles into ordinary shortest-path problems.

prompt: The same graph will be queried thousands of times. What is worth considering?
optionA: Using a faster traversal each time
optionB: Computing answers once and reusing them
optionC: Keeping the graph in a matrix instead
optionD: Reducing the number of edges stored
correctAnswerText: Computing answers once and reusing them
explanation: A cost paid once against a cost paid per query. The shape of the workload, not the graph, decides this.

prompt: What should you establish before writing any graph code in an interview?
optionA: Whether it is directed, weighted and connected
optionB: Whether recursion is allowed here
optionC: Which traversal the interviewer expects
optionD: How large the input is likely to be
correctAnswerText: Whether it is directed, weighted and connected
explanation: Those three facts determine the algorithm. Writing before asking is choosing the tool before knowing the job.

prompt: A BFS between two known points explores an enormous number of nodes. What can help?
optionA: Searching from both ends until they meet
optionB: Processing the queue in a different order
optionC: Switching to a depth-first traversal
optionD: Reducing the size of the visited set
correctAnswerText: Searching from both ends until they meet
explanation: Bidirectional search. Two halves of the depth explore vastly fewer nodes than one full one.

prompt: Which test case catches the most graph bugs?
optionA: A graph where every node joins every other
optionB: A large graph with many thousand nodes
optionC: A disconnected graph containing a cycle
optionD: A straight chain of connected nodes
correctAnswerText: A disconnected graph containing a cycle
explanation: It catches the two classic failures at once: forgetting to restart, and forgetting the visited set.

prompt: Why are graphs worth learning properly rather than memorising?
optionA: Most real problems become one once translated
optionB: The algorithms are the hardest to recall
optionC: Interviewers ask about them most often
optionD: They appear in every kind of system
correctAnswerText: Most real problems become one once translated
explanation: Dependencies, routes, permissions, social ties, state machines. Memorising the code does not help you see that.

prompt: What is dynamic programming, in one sentence?
optionA: Making a locally best choice at each step
optionB: Trying every option and keeping the best one
optionC: Breaking a problem into independent halves
optionD: Solving subproblems once and reusing the answers
correctAnswerText: Solving subproblems once and reusing the answers
explanation: Recursion plus remembering. The other three describe divide and conquer, brute force and greedy.

prompt: What does it mean for subproblems to overlap?
optionA: Solving one changes the answer to another
optionB: The same subproblem is reached many times
optionC: Subproblems can be solved in any order
optionD: Subproblems share some of their inputs
correctAnswerText: The same subproblem is reached many times
explanation: Reached repeatedly by different routes. That repetition is the only thing a cache can save you.

prompt: What does optimal substructure mean?
optionA: The best answer is built from best sub-answers
optionB: Every subproblem has exactly one answer
optionC: The subproblems do not depend on each other
optionD: The problem can be split into equal parts
correctAnswerText: The best answer is built from best sub-answers
explanation: It is what makes the recurrence valid. Without it, combining the best pieces need not give the best whole.

prompt: What is memoisation?
optionA: Caching a function’s result against its arguments
optionB: Storing the whole recursion tree in memory
optionC: Writing results into a table from the bottom up
optionD: Keeping the best answer found so far
correctAnswerText: Caching a function’s result against its arguments
explanation: Top-down. You keep the recursion you already wrote and add a lookup before doing the work.

prompt: What is tabulation?
optionA: Caching results as the recursion returns them
optionB: Filling a table from the smallest case upward
optionC: Sorting the subproblems before solving them
optionD: Storing the inputs alongside their answers
correctAnswerText: Filling a table from the smallest case upward
explanation: Bottom-up. Same recurrence, no recursion, and no risk of exhausting the call stack.

prompt: What is the state in a dynamic programming solution?
optionA: The values still left to be computed
optionB: The order the subproblems are solved in
optionC: The answer computed for a subproblem
optionD: What a subproblem’s answer depends on
correctAnswerText: What a subproblem’s answer depends on
explanation: The arguments, not the result. Getting this wrong is the single most common way a DP solution fails.

prompt: What is a base case in a DP recurrence?
optionA: The case the recursion starts from
optionB: The first entry written into the table
optionC: A case whose answer is known outright
optionD: The smallest input the problem allows
correctAnswerText: A case whose answer is known outright
explanation: Known without recursing. Everything else is defined in terms of it, so a wrong base is wrong everywhere.

prompt: What does a transition express?
optionA: How many states the problem has in total
optionB: Which state the problem should start from
optionC: How the table is filled in from left to right
optionD: How one state’s answer follows from smaller ones
correctAnswerText: How one state’s answer follows from smaller ones
explanation: The recurrence itself. State plus transition plus base case is the whole of a DP solution.

prompt: How do you work out the cost of a DP solution?
optionA: The size of the input, squared
optionB: The number of base cases needed
optionC: States multiplied by the work per state
optionD: The depth of the recursion tree
correctAnswerText: States multiplied by the work per state
explanation: Each state is solved once. So the count of states, times what each one costs, is the whole calculation.

prompt: Why is naive recursive Fibonacci the standard example?
optionA: It cannot be written iteratively
optionB: It has no base case of its own
optionC: It recomputes the same values constantly
optionD: It uses more memory than it needs
correctAnswerText: It recomputes the same values constantly
explanation: fib(30) computes fib(10) thousands of times. One cache turns exponential into linear, visibly.

prompt: Why does caching turn an exponential recursion into a fast one?
optionA: The distinct subproblems are far fewer than the calls
optionB: Recursion becomes iteration once results are stored
optionC: The recursion tree is pruned to a single branch
optionD: The cache lookup is faster than the computation
correctAnswerText: The distinct subproblems are far fewer than the calls
explanation: The tree has billions of nodes but only a few thousand distinct ones. You pay for the distinct ones.

prompt: Why does DP need optimal substructure and not just overlap?
optionA: Otherwise the best pieces need not make the best whole
optionB: Otherwise the table cannot be filled in order
optionC: Otherwise the recursion will not terminate
optionD: Otherwise the subproblems cannot be cached safely
correctAnswerText: Otherwise the best pieces need not make the best whole
explanation: Overlap says caching pays. Substructure says the recurrence is true. Both are required, for different reasons.

prompt: What goes wrong if the state leaves out something the answer depends on?
optionA: Some subproblems are never computed at all
optionB: The table ends up larger than necessary
optionC: The recursion never reaches its base case
optionD: A cached answer is reused where it does not apply
correctAnswerText: A cached answer is reused where it does not apply
explanation: Two genuinely different situations look identical to the cache, so one of them gets the other’s answer.

prompt: What goes wrong if the state carries more than it needs to?
optionA: The recursion depth grows beyond the limit
optionB: The answers become incorrect for edge cases
optionC: The base cases can no longer be defined
optionD: Nothing repeats, so nothing can be reused
correctAnswerText: Nothing repeats, so nothing can be reused
explanation: Put the whole path in the state and every state is unique. The cache never hits and you are back to brute force.

prompt: What does top-down memoisation give you that tabulation does not?
optionA: It runs faster on every kind of input
optionB: It handles larger inputs without failing
optionC: It computes only the states actually reached
optionD: It uses less memory for the same problem
correctAnswerText: It computes only the states actually reached
explanation: Tabulation fills the table whether or not each cell is needed. When most are not, top-down wins.

prompt: What does tabulation give you that memoisation does not?
optionA: No recursion, so no stack limit to hit
optionB: The ability to skip unused subproblems
optionC: A smaller table for the same problem
optionD: Correct answers on more input shapes
correctAnswerText: No recursion, so no stack limit to hit
explanation: Deep recursion on a large input overflows. The loop version of the same recurrence never does.

prompt: Why does a greedy choice fail on problems that need DP?
optionA: The choices cannot be made in any order
optionB: Greedy algorithms cannot handle large inputs
optionC: The best local step can lead to a worse total
optionD: Greedy algorithms do not have base cases
correctAnswerText: The best local step can lead to a worse total
explanation: DP tries every choice and keeps the best outcome. Greedy commits, which only works when committing is safe.

prompt: Why can some DP tables be reduced to a couple of rows?
optionA: Only the final row is ever read back
optionB: Most of the table holds identical values
optionC: Each row depends only on the row before
optionD: The earlier rows can be recomputed cheaply
correctAnswerText: Each row depends only on the row before
explanation: Look at what the transition actually reads. If it never reaches back further than one row, nothing older is needed.

prompt: The table gives the best total but not the choices that produced it. Why?
optionA: Each cell stores a value, not a decision
optionB: The table was reduced to save memory
optionC: The transitions were applied out of order
optionD: The choices were overwritten as it filled
correctAnswerText: Each cell stores a value, not a decision
explanation: The value is what you asked it to store. Getting the choices back means recording them or walking the table again.

prompt: Why does adding one dimension to the state matter so much?
optionA: The number of states multiplies by its size
optionB: The recursion grows one level deeper
optionC: More base cases have to be defined
optionD: Each state then costs more work to solve
correctAnswerText: The number of states multiplies by its size
explanation: States multiply rather than add. A third dimension of size a thousand is a thousand times the work.

prompt: Counting ways to climb n stairs taking one or two at a time. What is the state?
optionA: The last step size that was used
optionB: The number of stairs remaining
optionC: The steps taken so far in order
optionD: The total ways found up to now
correctAnswerText: The number of stairs remaining
explanation: How you arrived does not change what remains. That is precisely why the subproblems overlap.

prompt: For the stairs problem, what is the transition?
optionA: Ways(n) is Ways(n-1) times two
optionB: Ways(n) is Ways(n-1) plus Ways(n-2)
optionC: Ways(n) is Ways(n-1) plus one
optionD: Ways(n) is the larger of the two below
correctAnswerText: Ways(n) is Ways(n-1) plus Ways(n-2)
explanation: Every route ends with a one-step or a two-step, so the counts from those two positions add up.

prompt: Choosing items to maximise value within a weight limit. What is the state?
optionA: The heaviest item that is still available
optionB: The total value collected so far
optionC: Which item you are at and the capacity left
optionD: The set of items already chosen
correctAnswerText: Which item you are at and the capacity left
explanation: Two dimensions. The set of chosen items would be complete but unique per path, so nothing would reuse.

prompt: Comparing two strings for their longest common subsequence. What is the state?
optionA: The length of the longer string
optionB: A position in each of the two strings
optionC: The characters matched so far
optionD: The difference between the positions
correctAnswerText: A position in each of the two strings
explanation: Two indices. Nearly every two-string DP has this shape, which is why recognising it is worth so much.

prompt: For minimum coins to make an amount, what should the value at amount zero be?
optionA: Zero, since no coins are needed
optionB: Infinity, since it cannot be made
optionC: Undefined, since it never happens
optionD: One, since one coin is the least
correctAnswerText: Zero, since no coins are needed
explanation: Zero coins make zero. Getting this wrong shifts every other answer by exactly one.

prompt: Your table is n by m but the transition only reads the previous row. What can you do?
optionA: Store the table on disk rather than memory
optionB: Reduce the table to a single value
optionC: Keep two rows instead of the whole table
optionD: Compute the earlier rows again as needed
correctAnswerText: Keep two rows instead of the whole table
explanation: Two rows, swapped each iteration. O(n·m) memory becomes O(m) with the same running time.

prompt: You have a correct but slow recursion. What is the smallest change that fixes it?
optionA: Sort the inputs before the recursion starts
optionB: Look up the arguments before doing the work
optionC: Reduce how deep the recursion can go
optionD: Rewrite the recursion as a bottom-up loop
correctAnswerText: Look up the arguments before doing the work
explanation: Two lines. Check the cache, and store before returning. The recursion you already trust is unchanged.

prompt: You need which items were chosen, not just the best value. What do you add?
optionA: A record of which branch each cell took
optionB: A re-run of the algorithm per item
optionC: A second table holding the item lists
optionD: A counter of how many items were used
correctAnswerText: A record of which branch each cell took
explanation: One decision per cell, then walk back from the answer. Storing whole lists multiplies the memory.

prompt: In what order must a tabulated DP fill its cells?
optionA: In the order the recursion would visit them
optionB: From the largest subproblem downward
optionC: From the first index to the last, always
optionD: So each cell’s dependencies are already filled
correctAnswerText: So each cell’s dependencies are already filled
explanation: Dependencies first. Some tables fill backwards, some diagonally — the transition decides, not convention.

prompt: Which phrasing most often signals a DP problem?
optionA: The first item satisfying a given condition
optionB: Whether two collections share any element
optionC: The items appearing more than once
optionD: The number of ways, or the best possible total
correctAnswerText: The number of ways, or the best possible total
explanation: Counting arrangements or optimising over choices. Both mean exploring choices, which means repeated subproblems.

prompt: A memoised solution is right without the cache and wrong with it. What does that mean?
optionA: The base case is defined incorrectly
optionB: The state omits something the answer depends on
optionC: The cache is being cleared between the calls
optionD: The recursion is going too deep to finish
correctAnswerText: The state omits something the answer depends on
explanation: The clearest signal in DP. The recursion is fine; the key is not distinguishing cases that genuinely differ.

prompt: A memoised solution is correct but no faster than the plain recursion. Why?
optionA: The base case is reached too rarely
optionB: The cache is too small to hold the states
optionC: The lookups cost as much as the work
optionD: The key includes something unique per call
correctAnswerText: The key includes something unique per call
explanation: Usually the path or the chosen set has crept into the key, so no two calls ever share one.

prompt: A tabulated DP reads cells that are still at their initial value. What is wrong?
optionA: The transition reads the wrong neighbouring cells
optionB: The table is one row smaller than it needs
optionC: The fill order does not respect the dependencies
optionD: The table was not initialised to the right value
correctAnswerText: The fill order does not respect the dependencies
explanation: The recurrence is right and the loops run the wrong way round. Some tables must fill from the far end.

prompt: A knapsack that should use each item once is using some of them twice. What caused it?
optionA: The capacity loop runs in the wrong direction
optionB: The value table was initialised to zero
optionC: The base case allows an empty selection
optionD: The item loop starts at the wrong index
correctAnswerText: The capacity loop runs in the wrong direction
explanation: In the one-row version, ascending capacity reads a cell this item already updated. Descending fixes it.

prompt: Every answer is exactly one more than it should be. Where do you look first?
optionA: The base case value
optionB: The order of the loops
optionC: The table dimensions
optionD: The transition formula
correctAnswerText: The base case value
explanation: A constant error everywhere comes from the one value everything is built on, not from the recurrence.

prompt: A memoised solution passes small tests and crashes on a large input. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The cache has grown larger than memory
optionB: The recursion is deeper than the stack allows
optionC: The answer overflows the number type
optionD: The base case is never reached at all
correctAnswerText: The recursion is deeper than the stack allows
explanation: Correct and unscalable. The same recurrence written bottom-up has no stack to exhaust.

prompt: A minimum-coins DP returns strange small numbers for impossible amounts. What went wrong?
optionA: The impossible marker was added to as a number
optionB: The base case was set to one instead of zero
optionC: The table was too small for the amount
optionD: The coin values were not sorted beforehand
correctAnswerText: The impossible marker was added to as a number
explanation: A large sentinel plus one wraps or competes as a real answer. Impossible states must be checked, not arithmetic.

prompt: A DP gives answers that are consistently good but not optimal. What should you suspect?
optionA: The base case is slightly too large
optionB: The table is being filled too early
optionC: The recurrence does not actually hold
optionD: The cache is returning stale values
correctAnswerText: The recurrence does not actually hold
explanation: Plausible-but-wrong is the signature of a broken recurrence. The best sub-answers are not composing correctly.

prompt: There are n² states but the solution runs in cubic time. Where did the extra factor come from?
optionA: Each state is computed more than once
optionB: Each state loops over its options
optionC: The cache lookup is not constant time
optionD: The table is allocated inside the loop
correctAnswerText: Each state loops over its options
explanation: States times work per state. A transition with an inner loop adds a factor the state count does not show.

prompt: A cache keyed on an array that the code keeps modifying behaves unpredictably. Why?
optionA: Arrays cannot be used as keys at all
optionB: The stored key changes after it is stored
optionC: The comparison is by value, not identity
optionD: The cache grows faster than expected
correctAnswerText: The stored key changes after it is stored
explanation: A key that mutates points at an entry describing something else. Keys must be immutable values.

prompt: When should you prefer greedy over DP, given both produce an answer?
optionA: When the greedy version is simpler to write
optionB: When the greedy choice is provably always safe
optionC: When the input is too large for a table
optionD: When the answer need not be exactly optimal
correctAnswerText: When the greedy choice is provably always safe
explanation: The proof is the requirement. Greedy that merely looks right is the most common wrong answer in interviews.

prompt: A candidate builds a DP table for a problem a single loop solves. What is the issue?
optionA: The table will use too much memory
optionB: Machinery was added where none was needed
optionC: DP cannot be applied to simple problems
optionD: The DP answer will be subtly incorrect
correctAnswerText: Machinery was added where none was needed
explanation: Correct but unreadable. Reaching for DP because it was the topic is a habit interviewers notice.

prompt: How do you decide between memoisation and tabulation for a given problem?
optionA: By recursion depth and how many states are used
optionB: By which one the interviewer asked for
optionC: By whichever gives the smaller constant factor
optionD: By whether the problem is one or two dimensional
correctAnswerText: By recursion depth and how many states are used
explanation: Deep recursion argues for bottom-up; a sparse state space argues for top-down. Otherwise they are the same thing.

prompt: What is the most reliable way to arrive at a DP solution under pressure?
optionA: Write the plain recursion first, then cache it
optionB: Draw the table and work out how to fill it
optionC: Identify the dimensions before anything else
optionD: Recall a similar problem and adapt its code
correctAnswerText: Write the plain recursion first, then cache it
explanation: The recursion forces you to name the state honestly. Starting from the table means guessing at it.

prompt: When is the rolling-array space optimisation worth making?
optionA: When the table has two dimensions
optionB: When the full table genuinely will not fit
optionC: When the interviewer mentions memory
optionD: Whenever the transition allows it
correctAnswerText: When the full table genuinely will not fit
explanation: It costs readability and the ability to reconstruct the answer. Pay that when the memory is actually a problem.

prompt: Knapsack runs in O(n·W). Why is that not as good as it sounds?
optionA: W can be huge while its input is tiny
optionB: The constant factor is unusually large
optionC: It only holds for sorted item lists
optionD: The memory grows faster than the time
correctAnswerText: W can be huge while its input is tiny
explanation: A capacity of a billion is ten digits to type and a billion columns to fill. That is why it is pseudo-polynomial.

prompt: What makes a DP answer convincing to an interviewer?
optionA: Stating the complexity of the solution
optionB: Naming the standard problem it matches
optionC: Writing the code without any errors
optionD: Saying in words what one cell means
correctAnswerText: Saying in words what one cell means
explanation: "dp[i][w] is the best value using the first i items within w." Someone who can say that has actually solved it.

prompt: Your state space works out to 10¹² entries. What does that tell you?
optionA: The table should be stored on disk
optionB: The state needs rethinking, not a bigger table
optionC: The problem requires a faster language
optionD: Memoisation will avoid most of the entries
correctAnswerText: The state needs rethinking, not a bigger table
explanation: An impossible state count means the formulation is wrong. Look for a dimension that is not really needed.

prompt: A DP solution ships to production. What does it need that the interview version did not?
optionA: A fallback for very large inputs
optionB: A comment saying what a cell holds
optionC: A rewrite into a simpler algorithm
optionD: Tests covering every input size
correctAnswerText: A comment saying what a cell holds
explanation: DP code is unreadable without its state definition. One sentence saves every future reader an hour.

prompt: What is the hard part of dynamic programming?
optionA: Remembering the standard problems
optionB: Working out the complexity
optionC: Writing the table-filling loops
optionD: Deciding what a subproblem is
correctAnswerText: Deciding what a subproblem is
explanation: Once the state is right, the rest is mechanical. Everybody who fails a DP question fails at the state.

prompt: What does a min heap guarantee?
optionA: The items form a balanced search tree
optionB: The items are held in sorted order
optionC: The smallest item is at the root
optionD: Each level is smaller than the last
correctAnswerText: The smallest item is at the root
explanation: The root, and only the root. Everything below it is unordered relative to its siblings.

prompt: What does it cost to look at the smallest item in a min heap?
optionA: Logarithmic time
optionB: Linear time
optionC: Linearithmic time
optionD: Constant time
correctAnswerText: Constant time
explanation: It is the root. Looking costs nothing; it is removing it that requires the heap to reorganise.

prompt: What do inserting and removing cost on a heap of n items?
optionA: Constant to insert, linear to remove
optionB: Constant time each
optionC: Logarithmic time each
optionD: Linear time each
correctAnswerText: Logarithmic time each
explanation: Both walk one path from root to leaf, and the tree is balanced, so that path is log n long.

prompt: How is a heap usually stored?
optionA: As two arrays, one for each half of the tree
optionB: As nodes holding pointers to their children
optionC: As a sorted list rebuilt after each change
optionD: In a plain array, with positions implying the tree
correctAnswerText: In a plain array, with positions implying the tree
explanation: A child of position i sits at 2i+1 and 2i+2. No pointers exist, which is why heaps are so fast in practice.

prompt: What is the relationship between a heap and a priority queue?
optionA: A heap is a priority queue with fixed size
optionB: A heap is how a priority queue is usually built
optionC: They are two names for the same structure
optionD: A priority queue is a heap kept sorted
correctAnswerText: A heap is how a priority queue is usually built
explanation: The priority queue is the interface; the heap is the implementation. Most languages give you the former.

prompt: What order do you get by iterating a heap’s underlying array?
optionA: Descending order of the items
optionB: Ascending order of the items
optionC: No useful order at all
optionD: The order they were inserted in
correctAnswerText: No useful order at all
explanation: Only the parent-child relation holds. Reading the array out is one of the most common heap mistakes.

prompt: What does finding an arbitrary value in a heap cost?
optionA: Linearithmic time
optionB: Constant time
optionC: Logarithmic time
optionD: Linear time
correctAnswerText: Linear time
explanation: You must check everything. A heap is not a search structure, which is the main thing it is not.

prompt: What does building a heap from n existing items cost?
optionA: Constant time
optionB: Linearithmic time
optionC: Linear time
optionD: Quadratic time
correctAnswerText: Linear time
explanation: O(n), not O(n log n). Most nodes are near the bottom and barely sink at all.

prompt: How does a max heap differ from a min heap?
optionA: It uses a different underlying structure
optionB: It supports removal from either end
optionC: It stores the items in the opposite order
optionD: The comparison is reversed, nothing else
correctAnswerText: The comparison is reversed, nothing else
explanation: One comparison. Languages with only a min heap get a max heap by negating, or by passing a comparator.

prompt: What shape is a heap always kept in?
optionA: A tree where each node has two children
optionB: A tree with every leaf at the same depth
optionC: A tree where both sides hold equal counts
optionD: A tree filled level by level, left to right
correctAnswerText: A tree filled level by level, left to right
explanation: Complete. That is what keeps the depth at log n and lets the array indexing work with no gaps.

prompt: Why is inserting into a heap logarithmic rather than linear?
optionA: Only half the items need to be compared
optionB: The new item rises at most the tree’s height
optionC: The comparison is made just once per level
optionD: The array does not need to be resized
correctAnswerText: The new item rises at most the tree’s height
explanation: It swaps upward while it is smaller than its parent, and a complete tree of n items is log n deep.

prompt: Why is building a heap from an array linear rather than n log n?
optionA: The build skips the items that are leaves
optionB: Each item is compared only with its parent
optionC: Most items sit near the bottom and barely move
optionD: The array is already partly in heap order
correctAnswerText: Most items sit near the bottom and barely move
explanation: Half the nodes are leaves and sink zero levels. The sum across all depths comes out linear.

prompt: Why is a heap not fully sorted?
optionA: The array layout cannot express an order
optionB: Full sorting is more work than it needs to do
optionC: Items arrive too quickly to be sorted
optionD: Sorting would break the tree’s shape
correctAnswerText: Full sorting is more work than it needs to do
explanation: Partial order is cheaper to maintain and answers the only question a heap is asked. That is the trade.

prompt: Why use a heap rather than sorting, when you need the smallest few?
optionA: Sorting cannot handle arriving items
optionB: You never pay to order the rest
optionC: Heaps use less memory than sorting
optionD: Sorting is slower on every input
correctAnswerText: You never pay to order the rest
explanation: Sorting orders all n. If you only ever look at k of them, most of that work was thrown away.

prompt: Why does a heap suit data that arrives over time?
optionA: It processes the items in arrival order
optionB: It absorbs a new item without redoing the rest
optionC: It discards items that are no longer needed
optionD: It can store an unlimited number of items
correctAnswerText: It absorbs a new item without redoing the rest
explanation: A sorted list has to find the insertion point and shift; a heap just sifts one path.

prompt: For the k largest items, why is a MIN heap of size k the right structure?
optionA: It keeps the largest item easy to read
optionB: It sorts the k items as they arrive
optionC: Its root is the weakest of the current best
optionD: It discards small items automatically
correctAnswerText: Its root is the weakest of the current best
explanation: The root is the one to evict. You compare each newcomer against it and drop whichever is smaller.

prompt: Why can you not binary search a heap?
optionA: The heap is not stored as a real tree
optionB: The items may contain duplicate values
optionC: The heap changes its shape while you search it
optionD: A node tells you nothing about which side to take
correctAnswerText: A node tells you nothing about which side to take
explanation: In a search tree, smaller goes left. In a heap both children are simply larger, so there is no direction.

prompt: How does heapsort produce a sorted array?
optionA: By removing the root repeatedly
optionB: By sifting every item into place once
optionC: By comparing each pair of siblings
optionD: By merging the two halves of the heap
correctAnswerText: By removing the root repeatedly
explanation: n removals at log n each. The heap gives you the next item in order every time, which is a sort.

prompt: Why does Dijkstra’s algorithm use a priority queue?
optionA: It repeatedly needs the cheapest node not yet settled
optionB: It needs to remove nodes from both ends
optionC: It needs the nodes kept in sorted order
optionD: It needs to look nodes up by their given name
correctAnswerText: It repeatedly needs the cheapest node not yet settled
explanation: Take the cheapest, relax its edges, repeat. That single operation is exactly what a heap is for.

prompt: Two items have the same priority. Which comes out first?
optionA: The one inserted first
optionB: The one nearer the root
optionC: Either — the heap makes no promise
optionD: The one inserted most recently
correctAnswerText: Either — the heap makes no promise
explanation: Heaps are not stable. If arrival order matters, the tiebreak has to be part of the key you compare.

prompt: You need the 10 largest of a million numbers. What do you do?
optionA: Keep a max heap of all million numbers
optionB: Keep a min heap of ten and compare each one
optionC: Scan for the largest, ten times over
optionD: Sort the million and take the last ten
correctAnswerText: Keep a min heap of ten and compare each one
explanation: O(n log k) with ten items in memory, against O(n log n) with a million. The gap is enormous.

prompt: How do you track the median of a stream of numbers?
optionA: A running total divided by the count
optionB: A sorted list rebuilt as each arrives
optionC: Two heaps, one for each half, kept balanced
optionD: One heap holding every number seen
correctAnswerText: Two heaps, one for each half, kept balanced
explanation: A max heap of the low half and a min heap of the high half. The median sits at one root or between them.

prompt: How do you merge k already-sorted lists efficiently?
optionA: Concatenate them all and sort the result
optionB: Compare all k fronts on every step
optionC: Merge them two at a time, in pairs
optionD: Heap the front of each list, take the smallest
correctAnswerText: Heap the front of each list, take the smallest
explanation: The heap holds k items and always names the next output. O(n log k) rather than O(n·k).

prompt: Tasks arrive with urgencies and must run most urgent first. What do you use?
optionA: A priority queue keyed on urgency
optionB: A queue, with urgent tasks at the front
optionC: A stack, so the newest runs first
optionD: A list sorted after each arrival
correctAnswerText: A priority queue keyed on urgency
explanation: This is the definition of the structure. Re-sorting a list on each arrival does the same job far slower.

prompt: Your language only provides a min heap and you need a max heap. What do you do?
optionA: Insert the values negated, and negate on the way out
optionB: Keep a separate record of the largest seen
optionC: Remove all items and re-insert them reversed
optionD: Insert everything and read the array backwards
correctAnswerText: Insert the values negated, and negate on the way out
explanation: Or pass a reversed comparator where one is supported. Negation is the trick for libraries that take neither.

prompt: You need a heap of task objects ordered by their deadline. What do you supply?
optionA: The deadlines only, with a lookup table
optionB: A comparison that reads the deadline field
optionC: A wrapper class holding just the deadline
optionD: A pre-sorted list of the tasks by deadline
correctAnswerText: A comparison that reads the deadline field
explanation: The heap needs one thing: a way to say which of two items comes first. Everything else stays as it is.

prompt: Equal-priority tasks must run in arrival order. How do you arrange that?
optionA: Compare an arrival counter when priorities match
optionB: Insert equal items in reverse arrival order
optionC: Adjust the priorities so no two are equal
optionD: Use a queue instead of a heap entirely
correctAnswerText: Compare an arrival counter when priorities match
explanation: A monotonic counter as the second key. The heap now has a total order and behaves stably.

prompt: An item already in the heap needs a new priority. What is the usual practical approach?
optionA: Search the heap and update it where it sits
optionB: Push the new version and ignore the stale one later
optionC: Remove every item until that one appears
optionD: Rebuild the entire heap from the items
correctAnswerText: Push the new version and ignore the stale one later
explanation: Lazy deletion. Finding the item costs linear time, so most code skips the old entry when it surfaces.

prompt: You have all n items already. How should you build the heap?
optionA: Sort them first, then load them in order
optionB: Insert them one at a time into an empty heap
optionC: Insert the smallest half, then the rest
optionD: Heapify the array in place, in one pass
correctAnswerText: Heapify the array in place, in one pass
explanation: O(n) against O(n log n). When everything is present up front, heapify is strictly the better option.

prompt: You need the k most common words in a document. What is the approach?
optionA: Sort the whole document and count the runs
optionB: Heap the words as they are read from the text
optionC: Keep a heap of every word seen so far
optionD: Count with a map, then heap the counts by k
correctAnswerText: Count with a map, then heap the counts by k
explanation: Two structures, each doing what it is good at. The map answers "how many"; the heap answers "which k".

prompt: Code reads a heap’s array to list items in order and the list is wrong. Why?
optionA: The array includes some empty slots
optionB: The heap was built in the wrong order
optionC: The array holds the items reversed
optionD: Only the root position is guaranteed
correctAnswerText: Only the root position is guaranteed
explanation: Sorted output means popping repeatedly. Reading the array is reading a structure that was never sorted.

prompt: Someone keeps a MAX heap of size k to find the k largest items, and gets wrong answers. Why?
optionA: The comparison must be reversed on output
optionB: The root is the one they should be keeping
optionC: A max heap cannot be limited in size
optionD: The heap needs to hold every item seen
correctAnswerText: The root is the one they should be keeping
explanation: To evict you need the weakest of the current best at hand, and in a max heap it is buried in the leaves.

prompt: A Dijkstra using lazy deletion sometimes processes a node twice. What is missing?
optionA: A limit on how many entries may be pushed
optionB: A check that the popped distance is still current
optionC: A removal of the old entry when pushing
optionD: A separate heap for the settled nodes
correctAnswerText: A check that the popped distance is still current
explanation: Stale entries remain in the heap by design. You skip them on the way out, which is the price of laziness.

prompt: An object’s priority field is changed while it sits in the heap. What happens?
optionA: The heap order silently becomes invalid
optionB: The heap reorders itself on the next read
optionC: The object moves to the end of the array
optionD: The change is ignored until it is popped
correctAnswerText: The heap order silently becomes invalid
explanation: The structure was arranged around the old value and nothing told it to move. Corruption with no error.

prompt: Code checks "is this value in the heap?" on every iteration and runs slowly. What is wrong?
optionA: The heap has grown larger than expected
optionB: A heap cannot answer membership quickly
optionC: The heap is being rebuilt on each check
optionD: The comparison function is too costly
correctAnswerText: A heap cannot answer membership quickly
explanation: Membership is a set question. Keep a set alongside the heap rather than scanning it.

prompt: A top-k solution over a huge stream runs out of memory. What was the mistake?
optionA: Every item was pushed and none evicted
optionB: The heap was built before the stream ended
optionC: The heap was rebuilt on each new item
optionD: The items were larger than anticipated
correctAnswerText: Every item was pushed and none evicted
explanation: The whole point of the k-sized heap is the eviction. Without it you have stored the entire stream.

prompt: Equal-priority jobs come out in a different order each run. What explains it?
optionA: The comparison function is not deterministic
optionB: Nothing distinguishes them, so any order is valid
optionC: The jobs are being inserted at random times
optionD: The heap is being corrupted between the runs
correctAnswerText: Nothing distinguishes them, so any order is valid
explanation: Not a bug in the heap — a missing requirement in the key. Add the tiebreak if the order matters.

prompt: A heap of numbers pops 10 before 9. What is the likely cause?
optionA: They are being compared as text, not numbers
optionB: The heap was not rebuilt after insertion
optionC: Duplicate values confused the ordering
optionD: The heap is a max heap rather than a min heap
correctAnswerText: They are being compared as text, not numbers
explanation: String comparison puts "10" before "9" because "1" precedes "9". A classic in loosely typed languages.

prompt: A heap is used to output every item in order, and is slower than sorting. Why?
optionA: The heap needed rebuilding between pops
optionB: Popping all n costs the same but with overhead
optionC: The heap was built one item at a time
optionD: Sorting uses a faster comparison method
correctAnswerText: Popping all n costs the same but with overhead
explanation: Both are O(n log n), and a library sort has far better memory behaviour. The heap wins only for partial output.

prompt: Code writes directly into the heap’s backing array and later pops the wrong item. Why?
optionA: The array needed to be sorted afterwards
optionB: The array indices no longer map to the tree
optionC: The heap property was broken without resifting
optionD: The heap size counter was not updated
correctAnswerText: The heap property was broken without resifting
explanation: Every heap operation restores the invariant. A raw write does not, and nothing checks.

prompt: When is a heap the wrong structure despite involving order?
optionA: When you need to query positions other than the extreme
optionB: When the number of items is very large
optionC: When items keep arriving continuously over time
optionD: When the priorities are all different
correctAnswerText: When you need to query positions other than the extreme
explanation: Asking for the median, a rank or a range means a balanced search tree or a sorted structure, not a heap.

prompt: For top-k where k is nearly n, what should you do?
optionA: Partition the data and heap each part
optionB: Use a heap holding the n minus k smallest
optionC: Use a heap of size k as you normally would
optionD: Sort — the heap has stopped being an advantage
correctAnswerText: Sort — the heap has stopped being an advantage
explanation: O(n log k) with k near n is O(n log n) plus overhead. The heap only pays when k is genuinely small.

prompt: You need the kth largest of an array you already hold, once. What beats a heap?
optionA: Building a balanced search tree from it
optionB: Partitioning the array around a pivot
optionC: Scanning the array k separate times
optionD: Sorting the array and indexing into it
correctAnswerText: Partitioning the array around a pivot
explanation: Quickselect averages O(n). The heap is for streams and repeated queries; for one shot on an array it loses.

prompt: Heapsort is O(n log n) and in place. Why is it rarely the library default?
optionA: It gives incorrect results on some inputs
optionB: It cannot be applied to objects, only numbers
optionC: It needs extra space despite being in place
optionD: Its memory access pattern is poor in practice
correctAnswerText: Its memory access pattern is poor in practice
explanation: It jumps around the array; merge and quicksort work locally and the cache rewards them heavily.

prompt: Should production code use a library heap or a hand-written one?
optionA: The library one, unless it cannot express the need
optionB: A hand-written one, to avoid the dependency
optionC: The library one, since sifting is hard to write
optionD: A hand-written one, for full control of it
correctAnswerText: The library one, unless it cannot express the need
explanation: Sifting is easy to write and easy to get subtly wrong. The library version has been exercised for years.

prompt: For finding the smallest of twenty items, what should you use?
optionA: A sort of the twenty items
optionB: A heap built from the twenty
optionC: A single pass over the twenty
optionD: A heap of size one, updated
correctAnswerText: A single pass over the twenty
explanation: Big-O says nothing at twenty. A linear scan is one line and beats any structure you could build.

prompt: What phrase in a problem statement most reliably suggests a heap?
optionA: Repeatedly take the best remaining one
optionB: Find all the items matching a rule
optionC: Count how many satisfy a condition
optionD: Check whether an item is present
correctAnswerText: Repeatedly take the best remaining one
explanation: Repeatedly, and best remaining. One without the other usually points somewhere else entirely.

prompt: Why is the bounded heap such a valuable pattern in real systems?
optionA: It guarantees the answer is exactly correct
optionB: Memory stays fixed however much data arrives
optionC: It processes each item more quickly than a list
optionD: It removes the need to store the input at all
correctAnswerText: Memory stays fixed however much data arrives
explanation: A log processor with a heap of 100 uses the same memory for a gigabyte as for a terabyte. That is the win.

prompt: What must a comparison function satisfy for a heap to behave?
optionA: A result computed in constant time
optionB: A different result for every pair given
optionC: A symmetric result for equal items
optionD: A consistent order with no contradictions
correctAnswerText: A consistent order with no contradictions
explanation: If a beats b and b beats c, a must beat c. An inconsistent comparator corrupts the heap without erroring.

prompt: What is the single idea behind the heap?
optionA: Store a tree without using pointers
optionB: Make insertion as fast as possible
optionC: Keep data sorted at the lowest cost
optionD: Pay only for the order you actually use
correctAnswerText: Pay only for the order you actually use
explanation: Full sorting is more order than most problems need, and the heap charges you for the part you use.

prompt: What defines a refactoring?
optionA: The design follows a recognised pattern
optionB: The change is made without any new tests
optionC: The code becomes shorter than it was before
optionD: The structure changes and the behaviour does not
correctAnswerText: The structure changes and the behaviour does not
explanation: Behaviour held constant is the whole definition. Everything else is a different kind of change.

prompt: What does extracting a function do?
optionA: Gives a block of code a name of its own
optionB: Copies a block so it can be reused later
optionC: Removes code that is no longer being used
optionD: Splits a file into two smaller files
correctAnswerText: Gives a block of code a name of its own
explanation: The name is the value. A well-named extraction can make a comment unnecessary.

prompt: What should exist before you begin refactoring?
optionA: Tests that describe the current behaviour
optionB: A written plan of the changes to make
optionC: A branch separate from the main one
optionD: Agreement from the code’s original author
correctAnswerText: Tests that describe the current behaviour
explanation: You are promising not to change behaviour. Without tests you cannot tell whether you kept that promise.

prompt: What is a code smell?
optionA: A violation of the team’s style rules
optionB: A defect that will cause a failure
optionC: A sign that something may need attention
optionD: A section of code nobody understands
correctAnswerText: A sign that something may need attention
explanation: A hint, not a verdict. A long method is sometimes exactly right, which is why it is a smell and not a rule.

prompt: How large should each refactoring step be?
optionA: Small enough to review in a few minutes
optionB: Large enough to finish the work in one go
optionC: Whatever fits into a single commit message
optionD: Small enough that the tests still pass after it
correctAnswerText: Small enough that the tests still pass after it
explanation: Green between every step. That is what makes any step safe to stop at or to undo.

prompt: Is renaming a variable a refactoring?
optionA: Only when done across a whole file
optionB: Yes, and often a valuable one
optionC: No, it changes nothing structural
optionD: Only if the name was actively wrong
correctAnswerText: Yes, and often a valuable one
explanation: The cheapest refactoring there is, and the one that most often makes the next one obvious.

prompt: What does inlining a function do?
optionA: Moves the function nearer to its callers
optionB: Replaces the calls with the body itself
optionC: Marks the function for the compiler
optionD: Makes the function run faster at runtime
correctAnswerText: Replaces the calls with the body itself
explanation: The opposite of extracting, and equally legitimate. Some abstractions are worth undoing.

prompt: How does refactoring differ from rewriting?
optionA: It keeps the system working at every point
optionB: It touches fewer files in total
optionC: It is done by the original authors
optionD: It does not require any planning
correctAnswerText: It keeps the system working at every point
explanation: A rewrite has a period where nothing runs. A refactor never does, which is why it can be abandoned safely.

prompt: Why is duplicated logic considered a smell?
optionA: It means the author did not read the code
optionB: It slows the program down when it runs
optionC: A change has to be made in several places
optionD: It makes the codebase larger than needed
correctAnswerText: A change has to be made in several places
explanation: And the cost is paid when one copy is updated and another is not, which is silent.

prompt: When is refactoring usually done?
optionA: Whenever a smell is noticed anywhere
optionB: Just before changing the code in question
optionC: Once the feature work has been completed
optionD: In a scheduled cleanup at the sprint end
correctAnswerText: Just before changing the code in question
explanation: Make the change easy, then make the easy change. Refactoring detached from a purpose rarely survives review.

prompt: Why are tests essential to refactoring specifically?
optionA: They make the refactoring go more quickly
optionB: They are required before merging a change
optionC: They document what the new design does
optionD: They are the only proof behaviour was preserved
