correctAnswerText: They are the only proof behaviour was preserved
explanation: Without them, "I did not change the behaviour" is a belief. With them, it is a checked claim.

prompt: Why take small steps rather than one large restructuring?
optionA: Large steps are harder to describe clearly
optionB: Small steps are quicker to write overall
optionC: A break is found while the cause is still obvious
optionD: Reviewers prefer smaller pull requests
correctAnswerText: A break is found while the cause is still obvious
explanation: The last green state is one step behind you. With a large step it is an hour of changes behind you.

prompt: Why keep refactoring in separate commits from feature work?
optionA: A failure can be traced to one or the other
optionB: It keeps each commit smaller in size
optionC: Reviewers can skip the refactoring parts
optionD: It makes the history easier to read later
correctAnswerText: A failure can be traced to one or the other
explanation: Mixed together, a regression could be either and reverting loses the feature. Separated, you can revert one.

prompt: Why are smells described as hints rather than rules?
optionA: Teams disagree about what counts as one
optionB: Different languages have different smells
optionC: Sometimes the smelly version is the better one
optionD: Rules would be harder for tools to check
correctAnswerText: Sometimes the smelly version is the better one
explanation: A long function of sequential steps can beat eight tiny ones. Applying smells as rules produces worse code.

prompt: What is the business case for refactoring?
optionA: Developers enjoy the work more
optionB: The software runs more efficiently
optionC: Future changes cost less to make
optionD: Defect counts fall immediately
correctAnswerText: Future changes cost less to make
explanation: It buys nothing today. It is an investment in the cost of every change after this one.

prompt: Why would you ever inline a function that already exists?
optionA: Function calls are slower than inline code
optionB: Its abstraction is in the way of a better one
optionC: Its name no longer matches what it does
optionD: It is only called from a single place
correctAnswerText: Its abstraction is in the way of a better one
explanation: Sometimes you must make it worse to make it better. Collapse the bad seam, then cut a good one.

prompt: Why is renaming considered structural work rather than cosmetic?
optionA: Renaming touches every file that uses it
optionB: Names are checked by the compiler
optionC: Tools can perform renames automatically
optionD: A name is how the next reader understands it
correctAnswerText: A name is how the next reader understands it
explanation: Code is read far more than written. A wrong name misleads every reader until somebody fixes it.

prompt: Why is untested code so hard to refactor?
optionA: It tends to be older and use outdated patterns
optionB: You must change it to test it and test it to change it
optionC: It was usually written by somebody who has left
optionD: It has more defects than tested code does
correctAnswerText: You must change it to test it and test it to change it
explanation: The circular bind of legacy work. Breaking it takes the smallest safe change that creates a seam.

prompt: Why prefer the editor’s rename over a find and replace?
optionA: It is faster than typing the replacement
optionB: It records the change in the history
optionC: It understands scope, so it misses nothing
optionD: It checks the new name is not taken
correctAnswerText: It understands scope, so it misses nothing
explanation: Find and replace hits the same word in a comment, a string and an unrelated variable. The tool does not.

prompt: How does refactoring change when a design must be settled?
optionA: It can be discovered later, from real code
optionB: It must be complete before coding starts
optionC: It stops mattering once tests exist
optionD: It becomes the reviewer’s responsibility
correctAnswerText: It can be discovered later, from real code
explanation: If the structure can be changed safely, you need not guess right up front — which is a large freedom.

prompt: A block inside a long function has a comment explaining what it does. What does that suggest?
optionA: Move the comment above the function
optionB: Expand the comment with more detail
optionC: Split the function exactly in half
optionD: Extract it and let the name say it
correctAnswerText: Extract it and let the name say it
explanation: A comment naming a block is the block asking to be a function. The comment becomes the name.

prompt: You must refactor code nobody understands and there are no tests. What comes first?
optionA: A rewrite of the worst function in it
optionB: A request for the original author’s help
optionC: Tests recording what it currently does
optionD: A document describing how it works
correctAnswerText: Tests recording what it currently does
explanation: Characterisation tests. They assert the current behaviour, bugs included, because that is what must be preserved.

prompt: Two blocks look identical. What do you check before merging them?
optionA: Whether they would change for the same reason
optionB: Whether both are covered by tests
optionC: Whether they sit in the same module
optionD: Whether they are exactly the same length
correctAnswerText: Whether they would change for the same reason
explanation: Code that looks alike but changes for different reasons is coincidence. Merging it couples two unrelated things.

prompt: A function nests five levels of conditions before doing its work. What move helps?
optionA: Return early on each failing case
optionB: Extract each level into a function
optionC: Invert the outermost condition only
optionD: Combine the conditions into one test
correctAnswerText: Return early on each failing case
explanation: Guard clauses flatten the shape. The exceptional cases leave at the top and the real work sits unindented.

prompt: The same four parameters are passed through six functions together. What does that suggest?
optionA: The call chain is one level too deep
optionB: They belong together as one thing
optionC: The functions should be combined
optionD: The parameters should be globals
correctAnswerText: They belong together as one thing
explanation: Data that always travels together is a concept without a name yet. Give it one and the signatures shrink.

prompt: You are midway through a refactor and the tests go red. What is the best move?
optionA: Push on until the restructuring is complete
optionB: Debug forward from where you are now
optionC: Return to the last green state and go smaller
optionD: Disable the failing test and continue
correctAnswerText: Return to the last green state and go smaller
explanation: Red midway means the step was too big. Going back costs minutes; debugging forward can cost an afternoon.

prompt: You find a function nothing calls. What do you do?
optionA: Delete it — the history keeps it
optionB: Mark it deprecated and leave it there
optionC: Comment it out in case it is needed
optionD: Move it into a folder of old code
correctAnswerText: Delete it — the history keeps it
explanation: Commented-out code is noise that never gets deleted. Version control already remembers everything.

prompt: A class calls the network directly, so it cannot be tested. What is the first small change?
optionA: Add a flag that disables the call
optionB: Rewrite the class to avoid the network
optionC: Write a test that uses the real network
optionD: Move the call behind something you can pass in
correctAnswerText: Move the call behind something you can pass in
explanation: One seam is enough to get a test in. Once the test exists, the rest of the refactor is safe.

prompt: The number 86400 appears in four places. What do you do?
optionA: Name it once and use the name
optionB: Replace it with a calculation
optionC: Move all four into one function
optionD: Add a comment beside each use
correctAnswerText: Name it once and use the name
explanation: SECONDS_PER_DAY. The name explains it and the single definition means one place to change.

prompt: A feature needs a messy area cleaned up first. What order do you work in?
optionA: Do both together in a single change
optionB: Add the feature and leave the mess alone
optionC: Refactor and commit, then add the feature
optionD: Add the feature, then clean up afterwards
correctAnswerText: Refactor and commit, then add the feature
explanation: Refactor first and the diff of the feature is small and readable. Afterwards, the cleanup usually never happens.

prompt: A "refactoring" pull request fixes a bug along the way. What is the problem?
optionA: Behaviour changed, so it cannot be reverted cleanly
optionB: The bug fix will not be reviewed carefully
optionC: The commit message is now inaccurate
optionD: The tests will need to be updated too
correctAnswerText: Behaviour changed, so it cannot be reverted cleanly
explanation: Revert it and you lose the fix; keep it and you keep the restructure. Two changes need two commits.

prompt: Every refactoring breaks dozens of tests even though behaviour is unchanged. What does that say?
optionA: The refactorings are larger than they should be
optionB: The tests are asserting on structure, not behaviour
optionC: The tests were written by a different team
optionD: The test suite needs to be run less often
correctAnswerText: The tests are asserting on structure, not behaviour
explanation: Tests that know about internals turn the safety net into a straitjacket. They should assert outcomes.

prompt: After a refactor, following one operation means opening eleven files. What went wrong?
optionA: Extraction was applied past the point it helped
optionB: The operation was too complex to begin with
optionC: The functions were given unhelpful names
optionD: The files were organised in the wrong folders
correctAnswerText: Extraction was applied past the point it helped
explanation: Each extraction was defensible and the total is unreadable. Smells applied as rules produce exactly this.

prompt: A shared function has grown four boolean flags since two blocks were merged. What does that tell you?
optionA: The two cases were never really the same
optionB: The flags should be replaced by an enum
optionC: The callers are using it incorrectly
optionD: The function needs splitting by parameter
correctAnswerText: The two cases were never really the same
explanation: Flags accumulating after a merge is the sign that the duplication was coincidental. Separate them again.

prompt: A refactoring branch is three weeks old and cannot be merged. What was the mistake?
optionA: The branch was not rebased often enough
optionB: It was never kept in a mergeable state
optionC: The scope was agreed with the wrong people
optionD: The team did not review it quickly enough
correctAnswerText: It was never kept in a mergeable state
explanation: Refactoring done properly is mergeable at every step. A branch that is not is a rewrite wearing the name.

prompt: A tidy refactor made a loop noticeably slower. What most likely happened?
optionA: The compiler can no longer optimise it
optionB: Work that was hoisted out got moved back in
optionC: The code now uses more memory per pass
optionD: The new functions are slower to call
correctAnswerText: Work that was hoisted out got moved back in
explanation: Extracting a function can quietly pull a setup step inside the loop. Behaviour held; cost did not.

prompt: A function called getUser also writes to the database. What is the real problem?
optionA: The function has no tests covering the write
optionB: The name promises something the code breaks
optionC: The function is doing two things at once
optionD: The database write belongs in another layer
correctAnswerText: The name promises something the code breaks
explanation: All three are true; the dangerous one is the name, because callers act on it without reading the body.

prompt: A refactor passed every test and broke production. What was the gap?
optionA: The refactor was larger than it appeared
optionB: Production uses a different configuration
optionC: The tests were run against the wrong build
optionD: The tests did not cover the path that broke
correctAnswerText: The tests did not cover the path that broke
explanation: The net only catches what it covers. Green means the covered behaviour held, not that all behaviour held.

prompt: A one-line fix arrives with 600 lines of unrelated tidying. What is the cost?
optionA: The commit history becomes harder to read
optionB: The tidying will introduce new defects
optionC: The actual fix cannot be reviewed properly
optionD: The author spent more time than needed
correctAnswerText: The actual fix cannot be reviewed properly
explanation: Reviewers skim large diffs. The one line that matters gets less attention than if it had arrived alone.

prompt: Production code now has branches that only run during tests. What went wrong?
optionA: The branches were never removed afterwards
optionB: The seam was cut inside instead of at the edge
optionC: The tests are covering too much at once
optionD: The test framework needed the extra paths
correctAnswerText: The seam was cut inside instead of at the edge
explanation: You are now shipping code the tests do not exercise and testing code you do not ship. Inject at the boundary.

prompt: When is ugly code not worth refactoring?
optionA: When nobody needs to read or change it
optionB: When the original author has left
optionC: When it was written a long time ago
optionD: When it has no tests covering it
correctAnswerText: When nobody needs to read or change it
explanation: Refactoring buys cheaper future change. Where there is no future change, there is nothing to buy.

prompt: When does a rewrite beat incremental refactoring?
optionA: When the team wants to use newer technology
optionB: When refactoring would take several months
optionC: When the code is beyond anybody’s understanding
optionD: Rarely — usually when the platform itself is gone
correctAnswerText: Rarely — usually when the platform itself is gone
explanation: Incomprehensible code is an argument for characterisation tests, not for discarding the knowledge inside it.

prompt: How do you make the case for refactoring to a sceptical manager?
optionA: By explaining the design principles involved
optionB: As a matter of engineering professionalism
optionC: By showing how poor the current code is
optionD: In terms of what the next features will cost
correctAnswerText: In terms of what the next features will cost
explanation: "This area takes three days per change and would take one." That is a sentence a manager can act on.

prompt: How do you know when to stop refactoring an area?
optionA: When the functions are all short enough
optionB: When no smells remain anywhere in it
optionC: When the code matches the team’s style
optionD: When the change you came to make is now easy
correctAnswerText: When the change you came to make is now easy
explanation: The purpose bounds the work. Without one, refactoring continues until somebody runs out of patience.

prompt: Should refactoring be planned as separate tickets?
optionA: Yes, so the time spent is visible and tracked
optionB: Mostly no — it belongs inside the work it enables
optionC: Yes, so the team can prioritise it properly
optionD: No, it should be done in developers’ own time
correctAnswerText: Mostly no — it belongs inside the work it enables
explanation: Separate tickets are the first thing dropped when a deadline looms, so the cleanup never happens.

prompt: Which area is riskiest to refactor?
optionA: One with the longest functions in it
optionB: One nobody on the team has read
optionC: One with poor tests and heavy traffic
optionD: One written in an older style
correctAnswerText: One with poor tests and heavy traffic
explanation: Risk is exposure times the chance of being wrong. Poor tests supply the second and traffic the first.

prompt: A release is tomorrow and you notice a mess. What is the right call?
optionA: Refactor only the very worst part
optionB: Raise it as a blocker for the release
optionC: Refactor it now while you can see it
optionD: Note it and refactor after the release
correctAnswerText: Note it and refactor after the release
explanation: Timing is part of the judgement. The same refactor is right on Monday and reckless the night before a release.

prompt: How much test coverage do you need before refactoring an area?
optionA: Enough to cover the behaviour you might break
optionB: At least as much as the rest of the codebase
optionC: Full coverage of every line in the area
optionD: Whatever the team’s threshold requires
correctAnswerText: Enough to cover the behaviour you might break
explanation: Coverage of the behaviour at risk, not of the file. A percentage target measures the wrong thing here.

prompt: Why do codebases that refactor continuously stay easier to work in?
optionA: The developers are more skilled on average
optionB: The code follows patterns more consistently
optionC: The mess never gets large enough to be scary
optionD: The tests are written before the code is
correctAnswerText: The mess never gets large enough to be scary
explanation: Small messes get tidied in the course of work. Large ones need permission, a plan and courage.

prompt: What separates refactoring from just changing code?
optionA: You worked in small, reviewable steps
optionB: You can prove nothing about behaviour moved
optionC: You followed a named refactoring move
optionD: You improved the design of the code
correctAnswerText: You can prove nothing about behaviour moved
explanation: The proof is what makes it a discipline. Without it, you have changed a lot of code and are hoping.

prompt: What does a unit test check?
optionA: One file of the source code
optionB: One piece of logic on its own
optionC: One requirement from the spec
optionD: One feature from end to end
correctAnswerText: One piece of logic on its own
explanation: In isolation. The isolation is what makes it fast and makes a failure point at one place.

prompt: What does an integration test check?
optionA: That each piece works on its own
optionB: That the system performs fast enough
optionC: That the whole product meets its spec
optionD: That pieces work correctly together
correctAnswerText: That pieces work correctly together
explanation: The seams. Units can each be right while the assumptions between them disagree.

prompt: What does an end-to-end test exercise?
optionA: The API layer with stubbed storage
optionB: Every function the feature calls
optionC: The user interface components alone
optionD: The real system as a user would
correctAnswerText: The real system as a user would
explanation: Through the real interface against a real stack. The most realistic and the most expensive kind.

prompt: What shape should a test suite usually have?
optionA: Only the level the team prefers
optionB: An equal number at every level
optionC: Many fast tests, few slow ones
optionD: Many slow tests, few fast ones
correctAnswerText: Many fast tests, few slow ones
explanation: The pyramid. Cheap tests catch most mistakes; expensive ones catch what only reality can show.

prompt: What is a test double?
optionA: A test that runs twice to check stability
optionB: A stand-in for something the code depends on
optionC: A second copy of a test for another case
optionD: A duplicate of the code under test
correctAnswerText: A stand-in for something the code depends on
explanation: Mocks, stubs and fakes are all doubles. They exist so a unit can be run without its real collaborators.

prompt: What is a flaky test?
optionA: One that fails more often than it passes
optionB: One that depends on another test
optionC: One that takes too long to finish
optionD: One that passes or fails on the same code
correctAnswerText: One that passes or fails on the same code
explanation: Same input, different verdict. That inconsistency is what destroys the suite’s authority.

prompt: What does test coverage measure?
optionA: How many requirements have tests
optionB: Which lines ran while the tests ran
optionC: How much behaviour has been verified
optionD: How thorough the assertions are
correctAnswerText: Which lines ran while the tests ran
explanation: Executed, not checked. A test with no assertions at all still raises the number.

prompt: What is a regression test?
optionA: One that checks performance over time
optionB: One that runs after every release
optionC: One that tests the previous version
optionD: One that stops an old bug returning
correctAnswerText: One that stops an old bug returning
explanation: Written when the bug is fixed, kept forever. It is the cheapest test to justify, because it already happened.

prompt: What makes a test suite automated rather than manual?
optionA: It covers most of the codebase
optionB: It produces a report when it finishes
optionC: It was written in a scripting language
optionD: It runs without anybody asking it to
correctAnswerText: It runs without anybody asking it to
explanation: A suite somebody must remember to run is a suite that stops being run within about a month.

prompt: What does an assertion do in a test?
optionA: States what must be true for it to pass
optionB: Records what the code produced
optionC: Sets up the data the test will use
optionD: Describes what the test is for
correctAnswerText: States what must be true for it to pass
explanation: The only line that can fail. A test without one runs the code and reports success regardless.

prompt: Why should most tests be at the unit level?
optionA: They cover more of the code per test
optionB: They are the easiest kind of test to write
optionC: They are the only level that finds defects
optionD: They are fast, and a failure names one cause
correctAnswerText: They are fast, and a failure names one cause
explanation: Speed decides how often it runs, and precision decides how long the fix takes. Units win on both.

prompt: Why is a flaky test worse than having no test?
optionA: It runs more slowly than a reliable test
optionB: It hides the defect it was written for
optionC: It takes longer to fix than to rewrite
optionD: The team learns to ignore every red build
correctAnswerText: The team learns to ignore every red build
explanation: The damage spreads beyond that one test. Once red might mean nothing, no red means anything.

prompt: Why can high coverage coexist with a useless suite?
optionA: Some lines cannot be covered at all
optionB: Coverage counts test code as well as source
optionC: Running a line is not the same as checking it
optionD: Coverage tools miss some kinds of branch
correctAnswerText: Running a line is not the same as checking it
explanation: Call everything, assert nothing, and the report says 100%. Coverage bounds quality; it does not measure it.

prompt: Why should tests assert on behaviour rather than on internals?
optionA: Otherwise every restructuring breaks them
optionB: Internals change less often than outputs
optionC: Internals are harder to assert on
optionD: Behaviour tests run more quickly
correctAnswerText: Otherwise every restructuring breaks them
explanation: A test coupled to the implementation opposes the refactoring it was supposed to make safe.

prompt: Why keep end-to-end tests few in number?
optionA: They need a separate team to maintain
optionB: They find fewer defects than unit tests
optionC: They are slow and break for many reasons
optionD: They cannot be run automatically
correctAnswerText: They are slow and break for many reasons
explanation: A failure could be any layer, the network or a timing window. Diagnosing one costs far more than writing it.

prompt: Why replace a real dependency with a double?
optionA: To control what it does and keep it fast
optionB: To make the test cover more of the code
optionC: To avoid writing tests for that dependency
optionD: To keep the dependency from being changed
correctAnswerText: To control what it does and keep it fast
explanation: You can make it fail on demand, which is how error paths get tested at all.

prompt: Why does suite speed matter so much?
optionA: Slow suites cost more in build minutes
optionB: A slow suite gets run less and less often
optionC: Slow tests are more likely to be flaky
optionD: Fast suites find more defects per test
correctAnswerText: A slow suite gets run less and less often
explanation: A suite run once a day catches a mistake a day later. One run per save catches it while you are still there.

prompt: Why must each test be independent of the others?
optionA: Otherwise they cannot be run in parallel
optionB: Otherwise failures are harder to read
optionC: Otherwise order decides whether they pass
optionD: Otherwise the suite takes longer to run
correctAnswerText: Otherwise order decides whether they pass
explanation: Shared state means a test passes only because another ran first, and the suite fails when anything is reordered.

prompt: Why does the wording of a failure matter?
optionA: It determines whether the build stops
optionB: It is read by someone with no context
optionC: It is included in the coverage report
optionD: It is the only record of the test
correctAnswerText: It is read by someone with no context
explanation: "expected true, got false" sends somebody into the source. "expected 3 retries, got 1" fixes it in a minute.

prompt: What does writing the test first actually give you?
optionA: Fewer defects in the finished code
optionB: Higher coverage than writing it after
optionC: Proof the test can fail, and a usable design
optionD: A faster route to finishing the feature
correctAnswerText: Proof the test can fail, and a usable design
explanation: A test written after the code has never been seen to fail, so nobody knows whether it can.

prompt: You are testing a discount calculation with twelve rules. At what level?
optionA: Unit tests over the calculation alone
optionB: Integration tests against the database
optionC: End-to-end tests through the checkout
optionD: Manual tests run before each release
correctAnswerText: Unit tests over the calculation alone
explanation: Pure logic with many cases is exactly what units are for. Twelve cases through a browser is an hour per run.

prompt: Your code builds a complex database query. What test tells you most?
optionA: One that mocks the database entirely
optionB: One that runs the whole request flow
optionC: One that checks the query string matches
optionD: One that runs it against a real database
correctAnswerText: One that runs it against a real database
explanation: Asserting on the string tests your own formatting. Only the database can say whether the query is right.

prompt: Which inputs are worth testing for a function taking a list?
optionA: Empty, one item, many, and the invalid case
optionB: Several lists of different random sizes
optionC: The largest list the function allows
optionD: A representative list of about ten items
correctAnswerText: Empty, one item, many, and the invalid case
explanation: The boundaries are where the bugs are. Three typical lists exercise the same path three times.

prompt: Testing "registering a user sends a welcome email", what do you assert?
optionA: That the mail queue length increased
optionB: That the mail helper method was called
optionC: That an email was sent to that address
optionD: That no exception was raised by it
correctAnswerText: That an email was sent to that address
explanation: The outcome survives a rewrite of how mail is sent. The method call does not.

prompt: Tests share a database. How do you keep them independent?
optionA: Clean up at the end of each test
optionB: Reset to a known state before each one
optionC: Run them strictly in a fixed order
optionD: Give each test a unique record id
correctAnswerText: Reset to a known state before each one
explanation: Before, not after — a test that fails midway never reaches its cleanup and poisons the next one.

prompt: A test fails occasionally because a page has not finished loading. What is the fix?
optionA: Retry the test when it fails
optionB: Wait for the thing you need to appear
optionC: Increase the overall test timeout
optionD: Add a fixed delay before the assertion
correctAnswerText: Wait for the thing you need to appear
explanation: Wait on a condition, never on the clock. A fixed delay is slow when it works and flaky when it does not.

prompt: Logic depends on the current date. How do you test it reliably?
optionA: Pass the time in rather than reading it
optionB: Compare against a recomputed date
optionC: Allow a margin around the expected value
optionD: Run the tests only at a fixed hour
correctAnswerText: Pass the time in rather than reading it
explanation: The clock is a dependency like any other. Injected, you can test the end of February without waiting for it.

prompt: A bug is reported in production. What is the first thing to write?
optionA: A note in the defect tracker
optionB: A fix for the line that looks wrong
optionC: A failing test that reproduces it
optionD: A log line to confirm the cause
correctAnswerText: A failing test that reproduces it
explanation: The failing test proves you understand it and proves the fix worked. Both from the same few lines.

prompt: What should a test name say?
optionA: The kind of test that it is
optionB: The number of the requirement
optionC: The situation and what should happen
optionD: The function that is being tested
correctAnswerText: The situation and what should happen
explanation: "rejects a transfer that would overdraw the account." The failure output then reads as a sentence.

prompt: Tests need objects with twenty fields, of which each test cares about two. What helps?
optionA: A copy of the full object in each test
optionB: A shared fixture object used by every test
optionC: A builder giving defaults, overridden per test
optionD: A fixture file loaded before the suite
correctAnswerText: A builder giving defaults, overridden per test
explanation: The test then shows only what matters to it, and the other eighteen fields stop hiding the point.

prompt: A test has never failed in two years and covers active code. What should you check?
optionA: Whether it asserts anything at all
optionB: Whether the code is actually reached
optionC: Whether it runs in the CI pipeline
optionD: Whether the code has changed since
correctAnswerText: Whether it asserts anything at all
explanation: Break the code deliberately and see if it goes red. A test that cannot fail is a comment that costs runtime.

prompt: Every collaborator is mocked and the tests all pass, yet the feature is broken. Why?
optionA: The feature needs an end-to-end test
optionB: The mocks were configured incorrectly
optionC: The mocks assert your assumptions, not reality
optionD: The tests are running the wrong code
correctAnswerText: The mocks assert your assumptions, not reality
explanation: You tested that your code works against a world you invented. Nothing checked that world matches this one.

prompt: The suite passes in order and fails when shuffled. What is the cause?
optionA: The tests are running too quickly in parallel
optionB: State is leaking from one test to the next
optionC: The shuffle exposed a timing problem
optionD: Some tests were written for a fixed order
correctAnswerText: State is leaking from one test to the next
explanation: A test is relying on something another one set up. Shuffling is a cheap way to find it.

prompt: Renaming a private method breaks forty tests. What does that reveal?
optionA: The tests reach inside the implementation
optionB: The rename was applied incompletely
optionC: The method was more public than it seemed
optionD: The tests share too much setup code
correctAnswerText: The tests reach inside the implementation
explanation: Behaviour did not change and forty tests disagreed. They were asserting on how, not on what.

prompt: A team configures flaky tests to retry three times. What is the risk?
optionA: The results become harder to read
optionB: A real intermittent bug is now invisible
optionC: The flaky tests will never be fixed
optionD: The suite takes three times as long
correctAnswerText: A real intermittent bug is now invisible
explanation: Some flakiness is the test; some is a genuine race in the product. Retrying hides both equally well.

prompt: A team is told to reach 90% coverage. What usually happens?
optionA: Tests appear that execute code without checking it
optionB: Coverage rises and defect counts fall
optionC: The most important paths get covered first
optionD: The team writes far more integration tests
correctAnswerText: Tests appear that execute code without checking it
explanation: A number that is targeted stops measuring anything. The easiest way to reach it is the least useful one.

prompt: A suite takes forty minutes and developers push without running it. What is the root problem?
optionA: The build machines are underpowered
optionB: The team lacks discipline about testing
optionC: Too much is being tested at a high level
optionD: There are simply too many tests now
correctAnswerText: Too much is being tested at a high level
explanation: Forty minutes almost always means a pyramid standing on its head. The fix is moving tests down a level.

prompt: A test computes the expected value using the same formula as the code. What is wrong?
optionA: It will agree with the code even when wrong
optionB: It makes the test harder to understand
optionC: It will be slower than a literal value
optionD: It duplicates logic that should be shared
correctAnswerText: It will agree with the code even when wrong
explanation: The expected value must come from outside the code — worked out by hand, or from the specification.

prompt: The suite has sixty skipped tests. What does that represent?
optionA: Tests that will be re-enabled later
optionB: A suite that runs faster than it should
optionC: Features that were never completed
optionD: Coverage the team believes it still has
correctAnswerText: Coverage the team believes it still has
explanation: Everybody counts them as covered and none of them run. Skipped tests should be fixed or deleted.

prompt: A failing test prints two 400-line objects that differ somewhere. What went wrong in its design?
optionA: The test was checking too many cases at once
optionB: The test framework formats output poorly
optionC: The objects should have been serialised first
optionD: It asserts on everything instead of what matters
correctAnswerText: It asserts on everything instead of what matters
explanation: Assert on the fields the test is about. Whole-object comparison fails loudly and says nothing.

prompt: What deserves a test least?
optionA: A calculation with several branches
optionB: A bug that reached production once
optionC: A boundary between two services
optionD: A getter that returns a stored field
correctAnswerText: A getter that returns a stored field
explanation: Tests cost maintenance. Spend them where the code could plausibly be wrong.

prompt: What is a test suite ultimately for?
optionA: Finding as many defects as possible
optionB: Meeting the quality standards required
optionC: Letting people change the code without fear
optionD: Documenting how the system behaves
correctAnswerText: Letting people change the code without fear
explanation: It does the others too. But a suite nobody trusts enough to change code behind has failed at its job.

prompt: When does writing tests first work least well?
optionA: When the feature is large and complicated
optionB: When the team has not used it before
optionC: When the deadline is uncomfortably close
optionD: When you do not yet know what you are building
correctAnswerText: When you do not yet know what you are building
explanation: Exploration needs to be thrown away cheaply. Tests on code you will discard are wasted effort.

prompt: Is it ever right to delete a passing test?
optionA: No, a passing test is always worth keeping
optionB: Only with the original author’s agreement
optionC: Yes, when it costs more than it protects
optionD: Only when the code it tested is removed
correctAnswerText: Yes, when it costs more than it protects
explanation: Tests are code and carry maintenance. A brittle test asserting what three others do is a net loss.

prompt: What is the central trade-off in choosing a test level?
optionA: How easy it is to write against to maintain
optionB: How much it covers against how long it takes
optionC: How many defects it finds against its cost
optionD: How real it is against how fast and precise
correctAnswerText: How real it is against how fast and precise
explanation: Realism rises and both speed and precision fall. Every level decision is a position on that line.

prompt: Two services must agree on a message format. What testing approach fits?
optionA: End-to-end tests exercising both together
optionB: Each mocks the other in its own tests
optionC: Both check against one shared definition
optionD: Manual checks before each deployment
correctAnswerText: Both check against one shared definition
explanation: Contract testing. Each side mocking the other is how two suites stay green while the integration is broken.

prompt: Should test code be held to the same standard as production code?
optionA: Yes, but only the integration level ones
optionB: No, duplication in tests is always fine
optionC: Yes — it is read and changed just as often
optionD: No, tests are throwaway by their nature
correctAnswerText: Yes — it is read and changed just as often
explanation: With one exception: a little duplication in tests is often better than a shared helper nobody can follow.

prompt: You inherit a large system with no tests. Where do you start?
optionA: By measuring the current coverage first
optionB: With end-to-end tests of the main flows
optionC: At the lowest level, function by function
optionD: Around the part you are about to change
correctAnswerText: Around the part you are about to change
explanation: Testing everything will not be finished. Testing what you are about to touch pays for itself this week.

prompt: What does a green build actually tell you?
optionA: The code behaves as it is supposed to
optionB: The coverage was sufficient this time
optionC: The change is safe to release to users
optionD: Nothing you checked for has gone wrong
correctAnswerText: Nothing you checked for has gone wrong
explanation: Green is bounded by the suite. Reading it as "safe" is how tested systems still break on release day.

prompt: How do you tell whether a suite is any good?
optionA: By how quickly the whole suite runs
optionB: By the number of tests it contains
optionC: By the percentage of the lines that it covers
optionD: By whether the team trusts it to catch mistakes
correctAnswerText: By whether the team trusts it to catch mistakes
explanation: Trust is the measurable outcome. Everything else in this file is a way of earning or losing it.

prompt: What is an API, from the designer’s point of view?
optionA: A promise about how the system behaves
optionB: A document describing the available calls
optionC: The layer between client and database
optionD: A set of endpoints the server exposes
correctAnswerText: A promise about how the system behaves
explanation: A promise, which is why breaking it is a different kind of act from changing your own internals.

prompt: How are REST endpoints conventionally named?
optionA: After the things, with the verb in the method
optionB: After the action the endpoint performs
optionC: After the function that handles them
optionD: After the screen that calls them
correctAnswerText: After the things, with the verb in the method
explanation: GET /orders, not /getOrders. The method already carries the verb, so repeating it adds nothing.

prompt: What does it mean for an operation to be idempotent?
optionA: Repeating it leaves the same result
optionB: It can be run by several callers
optionC: It never changes any stored data
optionD: It always returns the same response
correctAnswerText: Repeating it leaves the same result
explanation: Same end state, however many times it arrives. That is what makes a retry safe.

prompt: What is an API version for?
optionA: Separating the internal and public APIs
optionB: Tracking which release the code was built from
optionC: Letting the contract change without breaking callers
optionD: Showing how mature the interface is
correctAnswerText: Letting the contract change without breaking callers
explanation: Two promises live side by side while callers move. Without that, a change is a coordinated outage.

prompt: Which change breaks existing callers?
optionA: Adding an optional query parameter
optionB: Removing a field from the response
optionC: Adding a new endpoint alongside
optionD: Adding a field to the response
correctAnswerText: Removing a field from the response
explanation: Additions are safe; removals and renames are not. That asymmetry shapes almost every API decision.

prompt: Are error responses part of the API contract?
optionA: Only the status codes are part of it
optionB: No, they are implementation details
optionC: Only for errors the caller can fix
optionD: Yes — callers write code against them
correctAnswerText: Yes — callers write code against them
explanation: Changing an error shape breaks the handling code as surely as changing a success shape breaks the parsing.

prompt: Why does a list endpoint need pagination?
optionA: It keeps the response format simple
optionB: It reduces the load on the database
optionC: Clients prefer to read data in pages
optionD: The collection will grow past what fits
correctAnswerText: The collection will grow past what fits
explanation: Every unpaginated list endpoint is a future outage waiting for the collection to get large enough.

prompt: Why does an API need internal consistency?
optionA: It makes the documentation shorter
optionB: It reduces the amount of server code
optionC: It is required by the REST standard
optionD: A caller can then guess the next endpoint
correctAnswerText: A caller can then guess the next endpoint
explanation: A consistent API is partly learnable without documentation, which is the strongest thing usability can buy.

prompt: Should an API response mirror the database table?
optionA: No — it should suit the caller
optionB: Yes, if the table is well designed
optionC: Yes, it keeps the mapping simple
optionD: Only for internal APIs, not public ones
correctAnswerText: No — it should suit the caller
explanation: Mirror the table and every schema change becomes a breaking API change you did not intend.

prompt: What is the most important thing API documentation provides?
optionA: A complete list of every field
optionB: A record of the version history
optionC: A worked example the caller can copy
optionD: A description of the architecture
correctAnswerText: A worked example the caller can copy
explanation: People start from an example and read the reference when it fails. Reference-only documentation is a wall.

prompt: Why does idempotence matter over a network?
optionA: Servers may process requests concurrently
optionB: A caller cannot tell a lost reply from a failure
optionC: Retries are faster than reporting an error
optionD: Networks deliver some requests out of order
correctAnswerText: A caller cannot tell a lost reply from a failure
explanation: The request may have succeeded and the response been lost. Retrying is the only option, so it must be safe.

prompt: Why is adding a response field usually safe?
optionA: Extra fields are stripped in transit
optionB: Callers request the fields they need
optionC: Callers ignore fields they do not know
optionD: Callers validate against a schema first
correctAnswerText: Callers ignore fields they do not know
explanation: Usually. A caller that rejects unknown fields makes even additions breaking, which is worth knowing about.

prompt: What does exposing your database shape actually cost you?
optionA: Callers can infer your table structure
optionB: Responses become larger than needed
optionC: You can no longer change it freely
optionD: Queries have to be written differently
correctAnswerText: You can no longer change it freely
explanation: Your schema stops being yours. Renaming a column is now a negotiation with every integrator.

prompt: Why should an error carry a stable code as well as a message?
optionA: Codes are shorter to send than messages
optionB: Callers branch on the code, not the words
optionC: Messages cannot be translated reliably
optionD: Codes can be logged more efficiently
correctAnswerText: Callers branch on the code, not the words
explanation: Without a code, integrators match on your message text, and your next copy edit breaks their code.

prompt: Why is an API that needs twenty calls per screen a problem?
optionA: The client code becomes longer
optionB: Latency adds up, especially on mobile
optionC: Each call needs its own documentation
optionD: The server does more work per screen
correctAnswerText: Latency adds up, especially on mobile
explanation: Twenty round trips on a slow connection is seconds of blank screen. The design leaked onto the user.

prompt: Why return a proper status code rather than 200 with an error inside?
optionA: It is shorter than a body field
optionB: Everything in between reads the code too
optionC: Clients cannot parse bodies reliably
optionD: The standard forbids the alternative
correctAnswerText: Everything in between reads the code too
explanation: Proxies, load balancers, monitoring and retry logic all act on the code. 200 tells all of them it worked.

prompt: Why can page-number pagination miss or repeat records?
optionA: Items shift position as data is added
optionB: The client may request pages twice
optionC: The sort order is not guaranteed
optionD: Page sizes may vary between requests
correctAnswerText: Items shift position as data is added
explanation: An insert before your position pushes one item from page two onto page three, unseen. Cursors avoid that.

prompt: Why does the default behaviour of an endpoint matter so much?
optionA: Defaults affect the server’s load
optionB: Defaults cannot be changed later
optionC: Defaults are hardest to document
optionD: Most callers will never change it
correctAnswerText: Most callers will never change it
explanation: The default is the design for almost everybody. An unpaginated default means most callers fetch everything.

prompt: Why can you not simply delete an endpoint nobody should be using?
optionA: Old clients cannot be updated at all
optionB: Someone is using it and you cannot see them
optionC: The documentation would become wrong
optionD: Deletion requires a new version number
correctAnswerText: Someone is using it and you cannot see them
explanation: Usage data tells you who called yesterday, not who calls monthly. Retirement is measured, announced, then done.

prompt: Why design the API before building the implementation?
optionA: It lets the front end start work sooner
optionB: It produces better documentation
optionC: The interface is the hardest part to change
optionD: It reveals the data model earlier
correctAnswerText: The interface is the hardest part to change
explanation: Internals can be rewritten on a Tuesday. The interface needs everybody who depends on it to agree.

prompt: A payment call may be retried after a timeout. How do you avoid double charges?
optionA: Reject any request that arrives twice quickly
optionB: Ask the caller to confirm before retrying
optionC: Compare the amount against recent payments
optionD: Have the caller send a key you check against
correctAnswerText: Have the caller send a key you check against
explanation: The key makes the retry a repeat of the same operation rather than a second one. You return the first result.

prompt: A submitted form has four invalid fields. What should the response contain?
optionA: A single message listing them
optionB: All four problems, named by field
optionC: A count of the invalid fields
optionD: The first problem encountered
correctAnswerText: All four problems, named by field
explanation: One at a time means four round trips and a user fixing one box per attempt. Report them together.

prompt: A response field is badly named and you want to fix it. What do you do?
optionA: Rename it in the next major version only
optionB: Add the new name, keep the old, retire it later
optionC: Leave it, since the name is only cosmetic
optionD: Rename it and announce the change clearly
correctAnswerText: Add the new name, keep the old, retire it later
explanation: Both for a while, then measure who still reads the old one. Expand, migrate, contract.

prompt: A dashboard needs data from five resources. What is a reasonable approach?
optionA: Five calls the client makes in parallel
optionB: One endpoint returning what the dashboard needs
optionC: A stream the client subscribes to
optionD: One endpoint returning everything available
correctAnswerText: One endpoint returning what the dashboard needs
explanation: Purpose-built endpoints are not impure REST so much as an admission that screens are real.

prompt: A feed has constant insertions at the top. Which pagination fits?
optionA: A timestamp range chosen by the client
optionB: A page number the client increments
optionC: An offset counted from the beginning
optionD: A cursor pointing at the last item seen
correctAnswerText: A cursor pointing at the last item seen
explanation: The cursor is anchored to an item, so inserts elsewhere cannot shift what comes next.

prompt: An operation takes four minutes. How should the API handle it?
optionA: Run it faster so it fits in a request
optionB: Hold the connection open until it finishes
optionC: Accept it, return a job the caller can poll
optionD: Split it into four separate endpoints
correctAnswerText: Accept it, return a job the caller can poll
explanation: 202 with a job resource. Anything holding a connection for minutes will be cut by something in between.

prompt: Which fields should a new resource expose?
optionA: Every field the record holds
optionB: The ones callers need, and no more
optionC: The ones cheapest to compute
optionD: The ones the first caller asked for
correctAnswerText: The ones callers need, and no more
explanation: Every exposed field is a promise. Adding one later is easy; withdrawing one you should not have shown is not.

prompt: You must version a public API. What is the most common approach?
optionA: A version segment at the front of the path
optionB: A version field inside the request body
optionC: A separate domain for each version
optionD: A version chosen per endpoint as needed
correctAnswerText: A version segment at the front of the path
explanation: /v1/orders. Visible in a log, a browser and a bug report, which headers are not.

prompt: A client wants to change one field of a large resource. What should the API accept?
optionA: The complete resource, as stored
optionB: Just the fields being changed
optionC: The old and the new values both
optionD: A list of the operations to apply
correctAnswerText: Just the fields being changed
explanation: Requiring the whole resource means a client that read it a moment ago overwrites somebody else’s change.

prompt: A caller exceeds their rate limit. What should the response tell them?
optionA: That they should reduce their usage
optionB: That they are limited, and when to retry
optionC: That the request could not be processed
optionD: That their account may be suspended
correctAnswerText: That they are limited, and when to retry
explanation: 429 plus a retry-after. Without the second part, a well-meaning client can only guess, usually badly.

prompt: An API returns 200 for everything with a success flag in the body. What breaks?
optionA: The responses become larger than needed
optionB: Monitoring and retries see only successes
optionC: Clients cannot read the flag reliably
optionD: Errors cannot carry enough detail
correctAnswerText: Monitoring and retries see only successes
explanation: Your error rate dashboard reads zero during an outage, because every failure was reported as a success.

prompt: A database refactor cannot proceed because clients read the column names. What was the error?
optionA: The refactor was planned without consultation
optionB: The database was designed for the API
optionC: The storage shape became the public contract
optionD: The clients were written against the wrong docs
correctAnswerText: The storage shape became the public contract
explanation: Made years ago, paid now. A translation layer at the edge would have cost an hour then.

prompt: Customers occasionally get two identical orders. What is the likely cause?
optionA: Two servers processed the request at once
optionB: A retry after a timeout created a second one
optionC: The client submitted the form too quickly
optionD: The database wrote the same record twice
correctAnswerText: A retry after a timeout created a second one
explanation: The first request succeeded and its response was lost. Without an idempotency key the retry is a new order.

prompt: Fixing a typo in an error message broke a customer’s integration. What was missing?
optionA: A test covering that error path
optionB: A version bump for the change
optionC: A stable code they could branch on
optionD: A notice period before the change
correctAnswerText: A stable code they could branch on
explanation: They matched on the text because you gave them nothing else. The typo was the symptom, not the cause.

prompt: An endpoint that was fine for two years now times out. What most likely changed?
optionA: The database queries became less efficient
optionB: The collection grew past a workable size
optionC: More clients are calling it concurrently
optionD: The response format grew more complex
correctAnswerText: The collection grew past a workable size
explanation: Unpaginated endpoints do not fail on release day. They fail on the day the data gets big enough.

prompt: Three endpoints return dates in three different formats. What does that cost the caller?
optionA: The responses are larger than needed
optionB: Dates may be parsed with lost precision
optionC: Nothing can be reused between endpoints
optionD: The documentation becomes longer
correctAnswerText: Nothing can be reused between endpoints
explanation: Every inconsistency is a special case in the client. The API stops being learnable and becomes memorisable.

prompt: A mobile list screen downloads two megabytes to show ten names. What is wrong?
optionA: The client is caching the data poorly
optionB: The list is not being paginated by the server
optionC: The response carries far more than the screen uses
optionD: The images are not being compressed
correctAnswerText: The response carries far more than the screen uses
explanation: A summary representation for lists and a full one for detail. One shape for both always fails one of them.

prompt: An endpoint with no traffic for a month was deleted, and a customer broke. What was missed?
optionA: Some integrations run only occasionally
optionB: The traffic data was being measured wrongly
optionC: The endpoint had an internal caller too
optionD: The deletion was not properly announced
correctAnswerText: Some integrations run only occasionally
explanation: A quarterly reconciliation job shows no traffic for eleven weeks and then matters enormously.

prompt: Two users edit different fields of one record and one change disappears. Why?
optionA: The record was cached on the client
optionB: Each sent the whole record as they had read it
optionC: The two requests arrived at the same time
optionD: The database rejected the second write
correctAnswerText: Each sent the whole record as they had read it
explanation: The second full write carried a stale copy of the first user’s field. Partial updates avoid the whole class.

prompt: An API has grown to 200 endpoints like /updateUserEmail and /updateUserPhone. What happened?
optionA: The resources were modelled too finely
optionB: Each new need became its own endpoint
optionC: The team added endpoints without review
optionD: The naming convention was never agreed
correctAnswerText: Each new need became its own endpoint
explanation: Verb-shaped APIs grow one endpoint per need forever. Resource-shaped ones absorb new fields into what exists.

prompt: What changes most between an internal API and a public one?
optionA: How the errors should be reported
optionB: How carefully it should be documented
optionC: How the endpoints should be named
optionD: How expensive it is to change later
correctAnswerText: How expensive it is to change later
explanation: Internal, you can update every caller yourself in an afternoon. Public, you cannot, and that changes everything.

prompt: An operation does not fit the resource model cleanly. What should you do?
optionA: Move the operation to another service
optionB: Rework the model until it fits
optionC: Design what is clearest and move on
optionD: Force it into a resource anyway
correctAnswerText: Design what is clearest and move on
explanation: REST is a style that usually helps. Contorting a genuine action into a fake noun helps nobody.

prompt: What does keeping three API versions alive actually cost?
optionA: Every change must be made three times over
optionB: The documentation becomes three times longer
optionC: Three times the server resources are needed
optionD: Callers are confused about which to use
correctAnswerText: Every change must be made three times over
explanation: Including security fixes. Versions are a promise to maintain, which is why fewer and shorter is better.

prompt: Should clients be able to specify exactly which fields they want?
optionA: Yes, it always reduces the data transferred
optionB: No, it makes caching impossible to do
optionC: Only if the flexibility is genuinely needed
optionD: Yes, it is the modern approach to APIs
correctAnswerText: Only if the flexibility is genuinely needed
explanation: It costs caching, predictable performance and a simple contract. Worth it for some APIs, not most.

prompt: What most reliably improves an API’s design?
optionA: Writing thorough documentation for it
optionB: Building a real client against it yourself
optionC: Reviewing it against a style guide
optionD: Having another team read the spec
correctAnswerText: Building a real client against it yourself
explanation: Awkwardness is invisible from the server side and obvious after twenty minutes of calling it.

prompt: How do you design an API that can change later?
optionA: Add extension points wherever possible
optionB: Promise as little as you can get away with
optionC: Document which parts may change
optionD: Version every endpoint from the start
correctAnswerText: Promise as little as you can get away with
explanation: Every field, code and behaviour you expose is frozen by somebody. The smallest honest surface stays flexible.

prompt: Whose mental model should the API reflect?
optionA: The caller’s, expressed in their terms
optionB: The database’s, for a clean mapping
optionC: The domain expert’s, for accuracy
optionD: The team’s, since they maintain it
correctAnswerText: The caller’s, expressed in their terms
explanation: An API is a user interface for programmers. Organised around your internals, it is organised around nobody.

prompt: You discover a design flaw in an API thousands depend on. What is usually right?
optionA: Add the better way and leave the old working
optionB: Fix it now and notify every caller
optionC: Document the flaw and leave it alone
optionD: Fix it properly in the next major version
correctAnswerText: Add the better way and leave the old working
explanation: Two ways to do it is ugly and cheap. A break is elegant and expensive, and the bill goes to other people.

prompt: How do you keep API documentation from going stale?
optionA: Review it as part of every release
optionB: Keep it short enough to maintain
optionC: Assign an owner responsible for it
optionD: Generate or verify it from the code itself
correctAnswerText: Generate or verify it from the code itself
explanation: Hand-maintained docs drift within months, and wrong documentation is worse than none.

prompt: What makes API design harder than designing internal code?
optionA: You cannot change it by yourself afterwards
optionB: It has to handle far more traffic
optionC: It is written in a different style
optionD: It must be documented thoroughly
correctAnswerText: You cannot change it by yourself afterwards
explanation: Internal code answers to you. An API answers to everyone who built on it, which is why you think first.

prompt: What is a database index?
optionA: A second structure for finding rows quickly
optionB: A copy of the table kept sorted by key
optionC: A cache of the rows queried most often
optionD: A constraint ensuring values stay unique
correctAnswerText: A second structure for finding rows quickly
explanation: A lookup structure held beside the table. It is extra data, which is where all its costs come from.

prompt: What does adding an index cost?
optionA: More memory while queries are running
optionB: Slower reads on the other columns
optionC: A longer time to open a connection
optionD: Slower writes and more storage used
correctAnswerText: Slower writes and more storage used
explanation: Every insert, update and delete must maintain it. That is the bet you are making on every index.

prompt: What is a full table scan?
optionA: Reading every row to find the matches
optionB: Reading the table into memory at once
optionC: Reading every column of each row
optionD: Reading the index from start to end
correctAnswerText: Reading every row to find the matches
explanation: What the database does with no usable index. Fine on a small table, ruinous on a large one.

prompt: What is a composite index?
optionA: An index shared between two tables
optionB: An index built from a computed value
optionC: One index covering several columns in order
optionD: Two separate indexes used in one query
correctAnswerText: One index covering several columns in order
explanation: In order. The order is the whole design decision, and it is where most indexing mistakes live.

prompt: Does a primary key need an index created for it?
optionA: Yes, it must be added separately
optionB: Only if the key is not an integer
optionC: No, the database makes one already
optionD: Only on tables above a certain size
correctAnswerText: No, the database makes one already
explanation: Uniqueness has to be checked on every insert, and checking it without an index would mean a scan.

prompt: What does EXPLAIN tell you?
optionA: How long the query took when it last ran
optionB: How the database intends to run the query
optionC: Whether the query returns correct results
optionD: Which indexes exist on the tables used
correctAnswerText: How the database intends to run the query
explanation: The plan. It is the only way to know whether an index you added is actually being used.

prompt: What does it mean for a column to be highly selective?
optionA: The column holds no empty values
optionB: The column is used in many queries
optionC: A value matches very few rows
optionD: The values are stored in sorted order
correctAnswerText: A value matches very few rows
explanation: An email address is selective; a yes-or-no flag is not. Selectivity decides whether an index helps at all.

prompt: What is a covering index?
optionA: One replacing all the other indexes
optionB: One holding every column the query needs
optionC: One built across two joined tables
optionD: One that covers every row in the table
correctAnswerText: One holding every column the query needs
explanation: The database answers from the index alone and never opens the table. The fastest read there is.

prompt: What does a unique index do beyond speeding lookups?
optionA: It reduces the storage the table needs
optionB: It keeps the rows in a sorted order
optionC: It refuses duplicate values on insert
optionD: It removes duplicates already present
correctAnswerText: It refuses duplicate values on insert
explanation: It is a constraint as much as an index, which is why it is the right way to enforce "one per customer".

prompt: Which columns are the usual candidates for an index?
optionA: Ones holding the largest values
optionB: Ones returned in the select list
optionC: Ones filtered, joined or sorted on
optionD: Ones updated least frequently
correctAnswerText: Ones filtered, joined or sorted on
explanation: WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY. A column only ever selected is along for the ride, not searched by.

prompt: Why does an index make a lookup so much faster?
optionA: It stores the rows in a smaller format
optionB: It runs the search on several threads
optionC: It narrows the search instead of reading all
optionD: It keeps the rows entirely in memory
correctAnswerText: It narrows the search instead of reading all
explanation: A million rows becomes about twenty steps. That is the difference between a scan and a tree descent.

prompt: Why does a table with six indexes write slowly?
optionA: The database checks each one for conflicts
optionB: The indexes compete for the same lock
optionC: Each write must update all six as well
optionD: The row has to be written six times over
correctAnswerText: Each write must update all six as well
explanation: One logical insert is seven physical writes. Indexes are read speed bought with write speed.

prompt: Why does the column order in a composite index matter?
optionA: The database reads it left to right
optionB: It can only be entered from the left
optionC: Later columns are compressed more
optionD: The first column is stored separately
correctAnswerText: It can only be entered from the left
explanation: Like a phone book sorted by surname then forename. Knowing only the forename does not help you.

prompt: Why might the database ignore an index on a true-or-false column?
optionA: Boolean columns cannot be indexed usefully
optionB: Reading half the rows is cheaper that way
optionC: The index would be too large to load
optionD: The optimiser cannot read such indexes
correctAnswerText: Reading half the rows is cheaper that way
explanation: Matching half the table, an index means random jumps to every second row. A straight scan beats that.

prompt: Why is a covering index faster than an ordinary one?
optionA: The index is smaller on the disk
optionB: The table itself is never touched
optionC: The index is held fully in memory
optionD: Fewer columns have to be compared
correctAnswerText: The table itself is never touched
explanation: A normal index finds the row and then fetches it. Covering skips that second, random-access half.

prompt: Why can an index remove the cost of ORDER BY?
optionA: Sorting an index is faster than a table
optionB: The index already holds them in that order
optionC: The index caches the sorted result set
optionD: The index tells the sorter where to start
correctAnswerText: The index already holds them in that order
explanation: Read it in order and the sort disappears entirely — which matters enormously on a large result.

prompt: What does an index nobody queries actually cost?
optionA: Only the disk space it occupies
optionB: Time when the optimiser considers it
optionC: Nothing, since it is never read from
optionD: Write time and space, forever, for nothing
correctAnswerText: Write time and space, forever, for nothing
explanation: Which is why "add one just in case" is not free, and why unused indexes are worth hunting down.

prompt: Why does WHERE LOWER(email) = ? not use an index on email?
optionA: The optimiser skips text comparisons
optionB: The index holds the original values
optionC: Functions are not allowed in WHERE
optionD: The index cannot compare text values
correctAnswerText: The index holds the original values
explanation: The index is sorted by the raw column. The database cannot know where the lowercased ones would sit.

prompt: How does the database decide whether to use an index?
optionA: It estimates the cost from stored statistics
optionB: It follows the order the indexes were made
optionC: It tries both ways and keeps the faster
optionD: It always uses one when a column matches
correctAnswerText: It estimates the cost from stored statistics
explanation: An estimate from sampled statistics. Stale statistics therefore produce confidently wrong plans.

prompt: Why does indexing a two-hundred-row table rarely help?
optionA: The optimiser ignores small tables
optionB: The index would be larger than the table
optionC: Small tables cannot hold an index
optionD: Reading all of it is already cheap
correctAnswerText: Reading all of it is already cheap
explanation: The whole table is likely one or two pages in memory. There is no scan cost left to remove.

prompt: Queries filter on tenant_id always and on status sometimes. What index do you build?
optionA: One on tenant_id first, then status
optionB: One on status first, then tenant_id
optionC: One on status alone, since it varies
optionD: Two separate single-column indexes
correctAnswerText: One on tenant_id first, then status
explanation: The always-present column leads. That one index then serves both the tenant-only and the combined query.

prompt: Your lookups all use LOWER(email). How do you make them indexed?
optionA: Index the expression, or store it lowercased
optionB: Add a second index on the raw column
optionC: Sort the table by the email column
optionD: Remove the function from the query
correctAnswerText: Index the expression, or store it lowercased
explanation: Index what you actually search by. Either a functional index, or a column holding the normalised form.

prompt: A hot query filters on user_id and returns only created_at. How do you make it covering?
optionA: Index every column in the table
optionB: Index user_id and include created_at
optionC: Index user_id and cache the results
optionD: Index created_at and user_id equally
correctAnswerText: Index user_id and include created_at
explanation: Filter column first, returned column carried along. The table is then never opened at all.

prompt: A join between orders and customers is slow. What is usually missing?
optionA: A covering index on both tables
optionB: An index on the sorted column
optionC: A unique constraint on the join
optionD: An index on the joining column
correctAnswerText: An index on the joining column
explanation: Foreign keys are not automatically indexed in every database, and an unindexed one scans per row.

prompt: A feed filters by author and sorts by date descending. What index serves it?
optionA: One on date only
optionB: One on author, then date
optionC: One on author only
optionD: One on date, then author
correctAnswerText: One on author, then date
explanation: Equality column first, then the sort column. The rows arrive filtered and already in order.

prompt: You added an index. How do you confirm it is being used?
optionA: Look at the size of the index file
optionB: Check the index appears in the schema
optionC: Read the query plan for that query
optionD: Time the query before and after
correctAnswerText: Read the query plan for that query
explanation: Timing can improve for unrelated reasons, like a warm cache. The plan states what actually happened.

prompt: Only the 2% of orders that are pending are ever queried by status. What fits?
optionA: An index covering just those rows
optionB: An index on the status column
optionC: A separate table for pending orders
optionD: An index on status and created date
correctAnswerText: An index covering just those rows
explanation: A partial index. Tiny, cheap to maintain, and it serves the only query that asks the question.

prompt: How do you decide which indexes to drop?
optionA: Read the usage counters the database keeps
optionB: Drop any index on a small table
optionC: Remove all but the primary key
optionD: Drop the ones added most recently
correctAnswerText: Read the usage counters the database keeps
explanation: Most databases count scans per index. Zero over a full business cycle is the evidence you want.

prompt: You must add an index to a large live table. What matters?
optionA: Building it without blocking the writes
optionB: Building it before the table grows
optionC: Building two and dropping the slower
optionD: Building it during the busiest period
correctAnswerText: Building it without blocking the writes
explanation: A plain CREATE INDEX can lock the table for minutes. Most databases offer a concurrent form for this.

prompt: You have an index on (a, b) and want one on (a). What should you do?
optionA: Nothing — the first one already serves it
optionB: Add it and drop the composite index
optionC: Add it, since single columns are faster
optionD: Replace the composite with two singles
correctAnswerText: Nothing — the first one already serves it
explanation: A composite serves any leftmost prefix of itself. The extra index is pure write cost.

prompt: An index exists on created_at but WHERE DATE(created_at) = ? still scans. Why?
optionA: The statistics have not been refreshed
optionB: Date columns cannot be indexed usefully
optionC: The index was built on the wrong column
optionD: The function hides the column from the index
correctAnswerText: The function hides the column from the index
explanation: Compare against a range of raw timestamps instead, and the same index starts working immediately.

prompt: An index on (status, tenant_id) is unused by a query filtering only on tenant_id. Why?
optionA: The two columns are of different types
optionB: The index was created after the query
optionC: tenant_id is not selective enough
optionD: The query does not constrain the first column
correctAnswerText: The query does not constrain the first column
explanation: There is no way in without the leading column. Reversing the order would serve both queries.

prompt: A query that was fast for months suddenly picks a scan after a bulk import. What happened?
optionA: The import rebuilt the index incorrectly
optionB: The index was dropped during the import
optionC: The table exceeded its maximum size
optionD: The statistics no longer match the data
correctAnswerText: The statistics no longer match the data
explanation: The optimiser is costing against a picture of yesterday’s table. Refresh the statistics after bulk loads.

prompt: Inserts into a reporting table have become very slow. What would you check first?
optionA: How many indexes the table carries
optionB: How many columns the table has
optionC: How large each individual row is
optionD: How often the table is queried
correctAnswerText: How many indexes the table carries
explanation: Reporting tables collect indexes, one per ad-hoc report, and every one of them taxes every insert.

prompt: An indexed integer column is queried with a string value and the index is skipped. Why?
optionA: The query is rejected and retried as a scan
optionB: The database must convert before comparing
optionC: The index stores integers in another form
optionD: String comparisons cannot use an index
correctAnswerText: The database must convert before comparing
explanation: The conversion is applied to the column, which is the same failure as wrapping it in a function.

prompt: LIKE 'smith%' uses the index but LIKE '%smith' does not. Why the difference?
optionA: The index stores text in reverse order
optionB: The second form matches too many rows
optionC: Only a known beginning locates a position
optionD: Trailing wildcards are more expensive
correctAnswerText: Only a known beginning locates a position
explanation: An index is sorted from the left. Not knowing the start is like searching a dictionary by last letter.

prompt: A query with WHERE a = ? OR b = ? ignores both single-column indexes. Why might that be?
optionA: The indexes conflict with each other
optionB: The optimiser only reads one index
optionC: Combining two index scans can cost more
optionD: OR conditions are never indexable
correctAnswerText: Combining two index scans can cost more
explanation: It must scan both and merge the results. Sometimes rewriting as a union of two queries is faster.

prompt: An index on is_active, where 95% of rows are active, is never used. Why?
optionA: Boolean values are stored without an index
optionB: The optimiser cannot estimate its cost
optionC: Matching almost everything, a scan is cheaper
optionD: The column changes too often to index
correctAnswerText: Matching almost everything, a scan is cheaper
explanation: Worth noting the mirror image: an index on the rare 5% would be used, which is what partial indexes are for.

prompt: An index on a heavily updated table has grown far larger than its data. What is happening?
optionA: The index is storing duplicate values
optionB: The index was built with wrong options
optionC: The column values have grown longer
optionD: Deleted entries are still occupying space
correctAnswerText: Deleted entries are still occupying space
explanation: Bloat. Churn leaves dead entries behind, and a periodic rebuild is what reclaims the space.

prompt: Each query is fast and indexed, yet the page takes four seconds. What should you suspect?
optionA: The rows returned are too large to send
optionB: The database connection is the bottleneck
optionC: The indexes are not actually being used
optionD: The page is issuing far too many queries
correctAnswerText: The page is issuing far too many queries
explanation: A thousand fast queries is slow. Indexing cannot fix a problem whose cause is the number of round trips.

prompt: When should you add an index?
optionA: When the schema is first designed
optionB: When a column appears in any WHERE
optionC: When the table passes a certain size
optionD: When a real query is measurably slow
correctAnswerText: When a real query is measurably slow
explanation: Indexes are answers to measured questions. Added speculatively, most of them are permanent write tax.

prompt: What most changes how aggressively you should index?
optionA: The total size of the database
optionB: The number of tables involved
optionC: The database product being used
optionD: The ratio of reads to writes
correctAnswerText: The ratio of reads to writes
explanation: A reporting store can carry many; an event ingest table can barely afford one. Same rules, opposite answers.

prompt: When is adding an index the wrong response to a slow query?
optionA: When the table is updated several times a day
optionB: When the query already has one index on it
optionC: When the query asks for far more than it needs
optionD: When the database is under heavy load
correctAnswerText: When the query asks for far more than it needs
explanation: Indexing a query that pulls a million rows to count them speeds up the wrong thing. Fix the question.

prompt: Should every slow query get its own tailored index?
optionA: No, only the slowest should get one
optionB: No — one index often serves several
optionC: Yes, tailored indexes are always fastest
optionD: Yes, provided the table is read-heavy
correctAnswerText: No — one index often serves several
explanation: Composite indexes serve every leftmost prefix. Designing across the query set beats one per query.

prompt: Why can an index that helped on your laptop fail to help in production?
optionA: The data volume and distribution differ
optionB: The query is written differently there
optionC: Production uses a different database
optionD: Production has more indexes competing
correctAnswerText: The data volume and distribution differ
explanation: A thousand rows fits in memory, so everything is fast. Plans are chosen against the data that is there.

prompt: Why review a table’s indexes periodically?
optionA: The table grows beyond their capacity
optionB: Indexes degrade in accuracy over time
optionC: The queries they were built for may be gone
