optionD: The build machines are unreliable
correctAnswerText: The pipeline has stopped being believed
explanation: It has become a coin toss to be repeated until it agrees with them, which is no signal at all.

prompt: Tests pass locally and fail in CI. What is the usual reason?
optionA: The CI configuration is out of date
optionB: Something exists locally that CI does not have
optionC: The tests run in a different order in CI
optionD: The CI machines are slower than laptops
correctAnswerText: Something exists locally that CI does not have
explanation: A file, a variable, an installed tool, a running service. CI is the honest environment; your laptop is not.

prompt: Builds started failing only after they were parallelised. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The test suite is too large to split
optionB: The parallel stages run out of order
optionC: The machines have too little memory
optionD: They share a database or another resource
correctAnswerText: They share a database or another resource
explanation: Sequentially, sharing one database was invisible. In parallel, two runs truncate each other’s tables.

prompt: A release passed staging and failed in production with a dependency error. What would you check?
optionA: Whether the deployment order differed
optionB: Whether production has less memory
optionC: Whether staging skipped some tests
optionD: Whether production got a rebuilt artefact
correctAnswerText: Whether production got a rebuilt artefact
explanation: A rebuild an hour later can resolve a dependency differently. Promotion of one artefact removes the question.

prompt: Merges routinely take a day to resolve. What is the underlying cause?
optionA: People are editing the same files
optionB: The merge tool is configured badly
optionC: Branches are living far too long
optionD: The team is too large for one repository
correctAnswerText: Branches are living far too long
explanation: A day of conflicts is weeks of divergence presenting its bill. The fix is upstream of the merge.

prompt: The pipeline is green but a broken change reached production. What should you check first?
optionA: Whether the deployment used that build
optionB: Whether the tests actually ran at all
optionC: Whether the tests cover that code
optionD: Whether production differs from staging
correctAnswerText: Whether the tests actually ran at all
explanation: All four are candidates. A stage that exits 0 because it found no tests is the one people never suspect.

prompt: A token appeared in a public build log. What is the necessary response?
optionA: Rotate it — it must be treated as public
optionB: Make the build logs private in future
optionC: Add the token to the masking list
optionD: Delete the log and keep using the token
correctAnswerText: Rotate it — it must be treated as public
explanation: The last two are worth doing afterwards. Neither of them un-publishes a credential that was already shown.

prompt: Builds now wait 20 minutes before they even start. What is happening?
optionA: Demand has outgrown the available runners
optionB: The repository has become too large
optionC: The triggers are configured incorrectly
optionD: The pipeline has too many stages now
correctAnswerText: Demand has outgrown the available runners
explanation: Queue time is invisible in the build duration and is felt exactly the same by the person waiting.

prompt: Errors appear during a rolling deployment and stop once it completes. Why?
optionA: The schema change broke the older version
optionB: The load balancer was misconfigured
optionC: The old instances ran out of memory
optionD: The new version needs a warm cache
correctAnswerText: The schema change broke the older version
explanation: Both versions run at once during a rollout, and a column dropped for the new one breaks the old one.

prompt: Deployments work when one particular engineer does them. What does that indicate?
optionA: They have permissions others lack
optionB: They deploy at a quieter time of day
optionC: They check more carefully than others
optionD: A step is in their head, not the pipeline
correctAnswerText: A step is in their head, not the pipeline
explanation: The pipeline is incomplete and a person is silently filling the gap, until the week they are on leave.

prompt: What is worth automating in a pipeline first?
optionA: Whatever the tooling makes easiest
optionB: Whatever takes the longest to do by hand
optionC: Whatever the team finds most tedious
optionD: Whatever is done often and gets done wrong
correctAnswerText: Whatever is done often and gets done wrong
explanation: Frequency times error rate. A fiddly step done twice a year may be cheaper as a written checklist.

prompt: When is a manual approval before production genuinely useful?
optionA: On every deployment, as a safety net
optionB: When a person adds judgement a check cannot
optionC: When the release is larger than usual
optionD: When the team is new to deploying
correctAnswerText: When a person adds judgement a check cannot
explanation: An approval that is always given is a delay pretending to be a control, and it trains people to click through.

prompt: Where is continuous deployment a poor fit?
optionA: Where the team is smaller than five people
optionB: Where the system has many dependencies
optionC: Where the codebase is more than a decade old
optionD: Where a release must be certified before use
correctAnswerText: Where a release must be certified before use
explanation: Medical devices, aviation, some financial systems. Continuous delivery still applies; the last step does not.

prompt: Which pair best describes a delivery process’s health?
optionA: How often you ship and how fast you recover
optionB: How many releases and how many rollbacks
optionC: How long a build takes and how many tests
optionD: How many builds run and how many pass
correctAnswerText: How often you ship and how fast you recover
explanation: Frequency and recovery time together resist gaming. Either alone can be improved by doing less.

prompt: How do you resolve wanting both a fast pipeline and thorough checks?
optionA: Remove the checks that rarely catch anything
optionB: Run everything but allow merges meanwhile
optionC: Run the fast ones per push, the rest less often
optionD: Accept a slower pipeline for the coverage
correctAnswerText: Run the fast ones per push, the rest less often
explanation: Split by feedback need. Quick checks gate the merge; long suites run nightly or before a release.

prompt: What is the cost of feature toggles?
optionA: They slow the application down at runtime
optionB: Each one doubles the paths to reason about
optionC: They must be configured per environment
optionD: They cannot be tested before release
correctAnswerText: Each one doubles the paths to reason about
explanation: Ten toggles is a thousand combinations, most never tested. They are debt with a removal date.

prompt: A team installs a CI server and nothing improves. What was missed?
optionA: The configuration of the pipeline stages
optionB: The habits the tool was meant to support
optionC: The training needed to use the tool
optionD: The budget for enough build machines
correctAnswerText: The habits the tool was meant to support
explanation: Buying the tool is the easy half. Merging daily and stopping to fix a red build is where the value is.

prompt: What do teams most often underestimate about pipelines?
optionA: That they need a specialist to build
optionB: That they must be documented fully
optionC: That they require dedicated hardware
optionD: That they need maintaining like any code
correctAnswerText: That they need maintaining like any code
explanation: It rots like anything else, and a pipeline nobody maintains becomes a pipeline nobody trusts.

prompt: Who should be able to deploy to production?
optionA: Only a release manager or lead
optionB: Anyone on the team, through the pipeline
optionC: Only the operations team on request
optionD: Only the engineer who owns the service
correctAnswerText: Anyone on the team, through the pipeline
explanation: Bottlenecking on one person makes deployment rare, which makes each one bigger and more dangerous.

prompt: What is the point of all of this?
optionA: Catching every defect before release
optionB: Deploying as many times as possible
optionC: Removing manual work from the team
optionD: Making a change safe enough to be routine
correctAnswerText: Making a change safe enough to be routine
explanation: Not zero defects and not maximum deployments. A release that is boring is the actual goal.

prompt: What does deploying actually mean?
optionA: Building the code ready for release
optionB: Merging a change into the main branch
optionC: Putting a built version into an environment
optionD: Making a new feature visible to users
correctAnswerText: Putting a built version into an environment
explanation: Deploying and releasing are different acts, and separating them is what lets teams ship unfinished work safely.

prompt: What is a rolling deployment?
optionA: Deploying to each environment in turn
optionB: Releasing to users in stages by region
optionC: Replacing instances a few at a time
optionD: Restarting all instances together
correctAnswerText: Replacing instances a few at a time
explanation: The service stays up throughout, which is also why both versions are running during it.

prompt: What is a blue-green deployment?
optionA: Two regions receiving the release in turn
optionB: Two full environments, with traffic switched over
optionC: Two versions running side by side permanently
optionD: Two stages of a release, tested separately
correctAnswerText: Two full environments, with traffic switched over
explanation: Switch the traffic, and switch it back if it goes wrong. Rollback becomes a routing change.

prompt: What is a canary release?
optionA: Releasing to internal staff before customers
optionB: Deploying at a time when traffic is lowest
optionC: Testing the new version before any traffic
optionD: Sending a small share of traffic to the new version
correctAnswerText: Sending a small share of traffic to the new version
explanation: A live experiment with a bounded blast radius. You are buying evidence with a small number of users.

prompt: What does a zero-downtime deployment require?
optionA: A deployment that completes very quickly
optionB: A maintenance page during the switch
optionC: Old instances serving until new ones are ready
optionD: All instances restarting at the same moment
correctAnswerText: Old instances serving until new ones are ready
explanation: Overlap. Something must be answering at every instant, which means two versions coexist by design.

prompt: What is the fastest way to recover from a bad release?
optionA: Disable the affected feature
optionB: Restart the running instances
optionC: Put the previous version back
optionD: Fix the fault and deploy again
correctAnswerText: Put the previous version back
explanation: Roll back first, diagnose afterwards. Fixing forward under pressure is how one incident becomes two.

prompt: Why are database changes harder to deploy than code changes?
optionA: They need a different set of tools
optionB: They take much longer to apply
optionC: They cannot simply be rolled back
optionD: They require the service to stop
correctAnswerText: They cannot simply be rolled back
explanation: Code is replaceable; data is not. A dropped column does not come back when you redeploy yesterday’s build.

prompt: Why must a new instance report when it is ready?
optionA: So the deployment can be timed accurately
optionB: So the logs record the startup order
optionC: So traffic is not sent before it can serve
optionD: So the old instance knows when to stop
correctAnswerText: So traffic is not sent before it can serve
explanation: Started is not ready. Without a readiness signal, a rollout sends real users to a warming instance.

prompt: What should differ between environments?
optionA: The configuration, not the build
optionB: The build, compiled for each one
optionC: Neither, they should be identical
optionD: Both, since the needs differ
correctAnswerText: The configuration, not the build
explanation: One artefact everywhere. The moment the build differs, staging stops being evidence about production.

prompt: What should an instance do when told to stop during a deployment?
optionA: Hand its connections to another instance
optionB: Finish its current work, then exit
optionC: Refuse until the work is complete
optionD: Exit at once to free the slot
correctAnswerText: Finish its current work, then exit
explanation: Stop accepting new requests, finish the ones in flight, then go. Otherwise every rollout drops some.

prompt: Why is "two versions are live at once" the key fact about rollouts?
optionA: It doubles the resources needed briefly
optionB: It means the logs mix two sources
optionC: It makes the deployment take longer
optionD: Everything shared between them must suit both
correctAnswerText: Everything shared between them must suit both
explanation: Database, cache, queue, session store. Anything one version changes, the other has to survive.

prompt: What does a canary tell you that staging cannot?
optionA: Whether the build deploys successfully
optionB: How it behaves under real traffic and data
optionC: How long the deployment will take
optionD: Whether the tests pass in production
correctAnswerText: How it behaves under real traffic and data
explanation: Real users do things no test author imagined, at volumes no staging environment reproduces.

prompt: Why do mature teams focus on recovery time rather than preventing all failures?
optionA: Failures cannot be eliminated, only made cheap
optionB: Users forgive outages that are brief
optionC: Recovery is easier to measure accurately
optionD: Prevention requires more testing effort
correctAnswerText: Failures cannot be eliminated, only made cheap
explanation: You can halve the cost of a bad release far more reliably than you can halve their likelihood.

prompt: Why is renaming a column a three-release job?
optionA: The old data has to be copied across
optionB: Both names must work while both versions run
optionC: The index must be rebuilt separately
optionD: The rename itself takes a long time
correctAnswerText: Both names must work while both versions run
explanation: Add, write both and backfill, then remove. Doing it in one release breaks whichever version loses the race.

prompt: What is the main cost of blue-green deployment?
optionA: Running two full environments at once
optionB: The traffic switch taking a long time
optionC: Users losing their sessions at cutover
optionD: The inability to roll back quickly
correctAnswerText: Running two full environments at once
explanation: Double the infrastructure during the switch, which is why it suits systems where an instant rollback is worth it.

prompt: Why is a small release easier to recover from?
optionA: It touches fewer parts of the system
optionB: It can be deployed more quickly
optionC: There is only one thing it could have been
optionD: It is reviewed more carefully first
correctAnswerText: There is only one thing it could have been
explanation: Diagnosis is a search. One change means no search at all; two hundred changes means an evening of bisecting.

prompt: Why are stateless services easier to deploy?
optionA: They use less memory while running
optionB: They do not need health checks
optionC: They start up more quickly than others
optionD: Any instance can be replaced at any time
correctAnswerText: Any instance can be replaced at any time
explanation: Sessions held in memory turn every rollout into a choice about whose session to destroy.

prompt: Why is a deployment not finished when the pipeline goes green?
optionA: The rollout may still be in progress
optionB: Many faults only appear under real use
optionC: The caches have not yet warmed up
optionD: The pipeline cannot verify production
correctAnswerText: Many faults only appear under real use
explanation: Green means it deployed. Whether it works is answered by the error rate over the next twenty minutes.

prompt: What does a rule against Friday deployments really tell you?
optionA: The team cannot recover quickly enough
optionB: The releases are tested insufficiently
optionC: The team deploys too often already
optionD: The system has too many dependencies
correctAnswerText: The team cannot recover quickly enough
explanation: The fear is rational given the recovery time. Fix the recovery and the day of the week stops mattering.

prompt: Why is a documented manual deployment still a problem?
optionA: A step will be skipped under pressure
optionB: It takes longer than an automated one
optionC: Documents are hard to keep updated
optionD: It requires a specific person to do it
correctAnswerText: A step will be skipped under pressure
explanation: All four are true. The first is the one that causes outages, and always at the worst moment.

prompt: You must remove a column the current code still reads. What is the order?
optionA: Drop it, then release the new code
optionB: Drop it and release at the same time
optionC: Release the new code, then drop it at once
optionD: Stop reading it, release, then drop it
correctAnswerText: Stop reading it, release, then drop it
explanation: The code change ships and settles first. Only when nothing reads it is dropping it safe.

prompt: You send 5% of traffic to a new version. What decides whether to continue?
optionA: How long it has run without alerts
optionB: Whether the instances stay healthy
optionC: Whether any errors appear at all
optionD: Its error rate and latency against the rest
correctAnswerText: Its error rate and latency against the rest
explanation: Compared against the other 95% running concurrently. An absolute error count says nothing without a baseline.

prompt: Requests fail during every rollout. What is the likely missing step?
optionA: Deploying at a time with less traffic
optionB: Removing the instance from the pool before stopping
optionC: Increasing the number of instances first
optionD: Waiting longer between each batch of instances
correctAnswerText: Removing the instance from the pool before stopping
explanation: Stop the traffic, then stop the process. Killing an instance still in the pool drops whatever it was serving.

prompt: A feature is half built but you want to keep merging. What do you do?
optionA: Deploy it only to staging for now
optionB: Keep it on a branch until finished
optionC: Ship it switched off behind a flag
optionD: Merge it and revert before release
correctAnswerText: Ship it switched off behind a flag
explanation: The branch stays short and the code is exercised in production paths long before anybody sees it.

prompt: How do you know your rollback actually works?
optionA: By having done one recently on purpose
optionB: By testing it in the staging environment
optionC: By keeping the previous artefact available
optionD: By reviewing the rollback procedure
correctAnswerText: By having done one recently on purpose
explanation: An untested rollback is a plan, not a capability, and the first attempt is always during an incident.

prompt: A release changes a queue message format. What must hold during the rollout?
optionA: The queue is drained before the release
optionB: The new consumers can read the old messages
optionC: The producers are deployed after consumers
optionD: The messages are versioned by the sender
correctAnswerText: The new consumers can read the old messages
explanation: Messages written by the old version are still in the queue when the new consumers start reading it.

prompt: What should a readiness check actually verify?
optionA: That the configuration was loaded
optionB: That the port is accepting connections
optionC: That the process has finished starting
optionD: That the instance can serve a real request
correctAnswerText: That the instance can serve a real request
explanation: A check returning OK unconditionally is how an instance with no database connection receives traffic.

prompt: During a front-end rollout, a page loads a file that no longer exists. What prevents this?
optionA: Clearing the browser cache on release
optionB: Serving the files from one server only
optionC: Keeping the old files available after release
optionD: Deploying all the files simultaneously
correctAnswerText: Keeping the old files available after release
explanation: A page loaded a minute ago asks for its own chunks. Deleting the old build strands everyone mid-session.

prompt: What makes it easy to tell whether a release caused a problem?
optionA: Marking deployments on the same graphs
optionB: Keeping a list of what each release held
optionC: Deploying only at scheduled times
optionD: Recording the release in a changelog
correctAnswerText: Marking deployments on the same graphs
explanation: A vertical line on the error graph answers in one second what log archaeology answers in an hour.

prompt: A data change will take six hours over millions of rows. How should it run?
optionA: In batches, separately from the deployment
optionB: In one transaction during a quiet period
optionC: After the deployment, in a single pass
optionD: Inside the deployment, before it completes
correctAnswerText: In batches, separately from the deployment
explanation: Decoupled and resumable. A six-hour step inside a release is a six-hour window where nothing can be rolled back.

prompt: Errors appear during every rollout and vanish once it finishes. What does that mean?
optionA: The rollout is happening too quickly
optionB: The new version starts too slowly
optionC: The two versions are not compatible
optionD: The load balancer is misconfigured
correctAnswerText: The two versions are not compatible
explanation: Errors bounded exactly by the rollout window is the signature. Something shared cannot serve both versions.

prompt: A release is bad but rolling back would lose data. What went wrong earlier?
optionA: The migration ran too slowly to interrupt
optionB: The backup was not taken before deploying
optionC: The release was larger than it should have been
optionD: The schema change was not backwards compatible
correctAnswerText: The schema change was not backwards compatible
explanation: The decision that trapped you was made when the migration was written, not when the release failed.

prompt: Users are logged out every time you deploy. What is the cause?
optionA: The session cookie expires on release
optionB: The authentication service restarts too
optionC: Sessions are held in the instance memory
optionD: The new version uses a different secret
correctAnswerText: Sessions are held in the instance memory
explanation: The last is also possible. Memory-held sessions is the common one, and it makes every rollout user-visible.

prompt: New instances return errors for their first few seconds. What is missing?
optionA: A readiness check gating the traffic
optionB: A warm-up request after starting
optionC: A longer pause between the batches
optionD: A higher memory limit at startup
correctAnswerText: A readiness check gating the traffic
explanation: The platform sent traffic as soon as the process existed, because nothing told it to wait for anything more.

prompt: A release works in staging and fails in production on a missing setting. What would prevent this?
optionA: Failing at startup when a setting is absent
optionB: Adding a default value for the setting
optionC: Documenting the settings each release needs
optionD: Copying the staging configuration across
correctAnswerText: Failing at startup when a setting is absent
explanation: Fail loudly at boot rather than at the first request that needs it, which may be hours later.

prompt: A rollout stops with half the instances on each version. What state are you in?
optionA: Effectively rolled back to the old version
optionB: Safely paused until somebody intervenes
optionC: Running the new version for all new requests
optionD: Both versions serving, which may be worse than either
correctAnswerText: Both versions serving, which may be worse than either
explanation: A stuck rollout is not a safe resting place. Decide quickly: complete it or roll it back.

prompt: After a release, some users see a page with broken styling until they refresh. Why?
optionA: The stylesheet failed to deploy correctly
optionB: The browser cached the wrong stylesheet
optionC: Their cached page references replaced files
optionD: The new styles conflict with the old ones
correctAnswerText: Their cached page references replaced files
explanation: An old page in an open tab asking for files the new release renamed. Keeping both builds available avoids it.

prompt: Service A was deployed expecting a new field from service B, which is not yet deployed. What broke?
optionA: The two services use different versions
optionB: The field was named inconsistently
optionC: The consumer shipped before the provider
optionD: The services were deployed too quickly
correctAnswerText: The consumer shipped before the provider
explanation: Provider first, consumer second, and the consumer tolerant of the field’s absence until it is everywhere.

prompt: The database load spikes for ten minutes after every deployment. What explains it?
optionA: The old connections are not closed
optionB: The new instances start with empty caches
optionC: The migration runs after the deployment
optionD: The health checks query the database
correctAnswerText: The new instances start with empty caches
explanation: Every rollout is a cold start for anything cached in process. Either warm them or move the cache out.

prompt: A codebase has sixty flags, most permanently on. What has that cost?
optionA: Confusion about which features exist
optionB: Slower evaluation on every request
optionC: Paths that exist but are never exercised
optionD: A larger configuration to maintain
correctAnswerText: Paths that exist but are never exercised
explanation: The off branches still compile and nobody tests them. Turning one off in an incident is then a gamble.

prompt: What should decide between rolling, blue-green and canary?
optionA: How many instances you are running
optionB: What a bad release would cost you here
optionC: Which one the platform supports best
optionD: How often you deploy each week
correctAnswerText: What a bad release would cost you here
explanation: An internal tool and a payment system have the same options and completely different right answers.

prompt: A small team asks whether to build canary deployments. What is the honest answer?
optionA: No, canaries only suit large systems
optionB: Yes, provided the traffic is high enough
optionC: Yes, it is the safest available approach
optionD: Get a reliable rollback working first
correctAnswerText: Get a reliable rollback working first
explanation: A canary detects a bad release. Without a fast rollback, detecting it early does not help very much.

prompt: When is the best time to deploy?
optionA: At a fixed time the team has agreed
optionB: As soon as the change has been merged
optionC: When the people who can fix it are available
optionD: When the traffic is at its lowest point
correctAnswerText: When the people who can fix it are available
explanation: Deploying into the quiet hours means fewer users affected and nobody awake to notice for six hours.

prompt: A release caused an outage. What is the most useful response afterwards?
optionA: Identifying who made the mistake
optionB: Increasing the testing before release
optionC: Asking what let it through undetected
optionD: Adding an approval step before release
correctAnswerText: Asking what let it through undetected
explanation: The person will be more careful for a fortnight. The gap in the process will be there next year.

prompt: Why does deploying more often tend to reduce risk?
optionA: There is less time for defects to appear
optionB: The team writes more careful code
optionC: Each release is smaller and better practised
optionD: Users report problems more quickly
correctAnswerText: Each release is smaller and better practised
explanation: Counterintuitive and well evidenced. Rare deployments are large, unpractised and therefore dangerous.

prompt: Which release needs the most caution?
optionA: One that changes data in a way you cannot undo
optionB: One that touches the most source files
optionC: One that includes a new dependency
optionD: One that has been waiting the longest
correctAnswerText: One that changes data in a way you cannot undo
explanation: Everything else can be rolled back. Deleted data and sent emails are the ones that do not come back.

prompt: Is a short maintenance window ever the right choice?
optionA: Yes, when it is far simpler and users accept it
optionB: No, zero downtime is always achievable
optionC: Yes, but only for internal systems
optionD: No, users never tolerate any downtime
correctAnswerText: Yes, when it is far simpler and users accept it
explanation: An internal tool at 3am on a Sunday. Zero-downtime machinery has a cost, and sometimes it is not worth paying.

prompt: What is the most dangerous kind of bad release?
optionA: One that takes the whole service down
optionB: One that affects only some users
optionC: One whose damage is not visible for days
optionD: One that requires a manual rollback
correctAnswerText: One whose damage is not visible for days
explanation: A total outage is noticed in ninety seconds. Data quietly corrupted for a week is the one that ends careers.

prompt: What does a healthy deployment process feel like?
optionA: Boring, and done without an audience
optionB: Quick, with everyone on standby
optionC: Rare, and thoroughly prepared for
optionD: Careful, with several people watching
correctAnswerText: Boring, and done without an audience
explanation: Boring is the goal. A deployment that needs the team gathered is one nobody is confident about.

prompt: What single fact prevents most deployment disasters?
optionA: Configuration belongs outside the build
optionB: Two versions will be running at the same time
optionC: Rollback must be tested before it is needed
optionD: Every release should be as small as possible
correctAnswerText: Two versions will be running at the same time
explanation: All four matter. The first is the one that explains the schema rules, the message formats and the sessions.

prompt: What is an injection attack?
optionA: Input that bypasses the login page
optionB: Input being treated as instructions
optionC: Input that is larger than expected
optionD: Input sent to the wrong endpoint
correctAnswerText: Input being treated as instructions
explanation: Data crossing into code. SQL, HTML, shell and template injection are all the same bug in different parsers.

prompt: What is cross-site scripting?
optionA: A script reading data from another site
optionB: A request sent from one site to another
optionC: A page loading content from a bad source
optionD: Attacker script running in a user’s page
correctAnswerText: Attacker script running in a user’s page
explanation: Their code, your origin, the user’s session. That is why it can do anything the user could.

prompt: What is cross-site request forgery?
optionA: A request replayed from an earlier session
optionB: An attacker stealing the session cookie
optionC: Another site making a request as the user
optionD: A forged response from a trusted server
correctAnswerText: Another site making a request as the user
explanation: The browser attaches your cookies to a request the user never intended to make.

prompt: How does SQL injection happen?
optionA: The database password was guessed
optionB: User input is built into the query text
optionC: The database allows remote connections
optionD: The query returns more rows than intended
correctAnswerText: User input is built into the query text
explanation: String concatenation. The database cannot tell your query apart from what the user appended to it.

prompt: What does HTTPS protect?
optionA: The data once it reaches the server
optionB: The application from bad user input
optionC: The traffic between browser and server
optionD: The user from visiting a fake site
correctAnswerText: The traffic between browser and server
explanation: The wire only. It says nothing about whether the site is honest or the code behind it is safe.

prompt: What does the same-origin policy prevent?
optionA: One site reading another site’s responses
optionB: One site loading images from another
optionC: One site sending requests to another
optionD: One site linking to another site
correctAnswerText: One site reading another site’s responses
explanation: Sending is allowed, reading is not — which is exactly why CSRF works and why it needs its own defence.

prompt: What does CORS do?
optionA: Blocks requests from untrusted origins
optionB: Encrypts requests between two origins
optionC: Relaxes the same-origin rule deliberately
optionD: Verifies the identity of the caller
correctAnswerText: Relaxes the same-origin rule deliberately
explanation: It is a relaxation, not a protection. Configuring it wide open removes a defence rather than adding one.

prompt: Can a secret be hidden in front-end code?
optionA: Yes, if it is stored encrypted
optionB: No — anything shipped can be read
optionC: Yes, if the code is minified
optionD: No, unless it is in a build variable
correctAnswerText: No — anything shipped can be read
explanation: Shipped to the browser means given away. Minifying and encrypting only slow down the reading.

prompt: What does a content security policy do?
optionA: Checks the content for known attacks
optionB: Encrypts the content the page returns
optionC: Limits where the page may load code from
optionD: Blocks requests from other websites
correctAnswerText: Limits where the page may load code from
explanation: A second line of defence: even if a script is injected, the browser refuses to run it.

prompt: Why are third-party packages a security concern?
optionA: Their code runs with your privileges
optionB: They increase the size of the build
optionC: They are usually written carelessly
optionD: They may stop being maintained
correctAnswerText: Their code runs with your privileges
explanation: A dependency is code you did not write running where your code runs, with everything your code can reach.

prompt: What do SQL injection, XSS and command injection have in common?
optionA: A parser reads data as instructions
optionB: They all need the user to be logged in
optionC: They all target the database layer
optionD: They all come from missing validation
correctAnswerText: A parser reads data as instructions
explanation: Seeing them as one pattern is what lets you spot the next variant in a language you have never used.

prompt: Why does a parameterised query stop SQL injection completely?
optionA: The driver rejects suspicious characters
optionB: The query is parsed before the value arrives
optionC: The database checks the value for keywords
optionD: The value is escaped before being inserted
correctAnswerText: The query is parsed before the value arrives
explanation: The structure is fixed first, so the value can never become structure. That is why it is a complete fix.

prompt: Why is blocking dangerous characters a weak defence?
optionA: It can be turned off by mistake
optionB: It rejects too much legitimate input
optionC: You cannot list every dangerous form
optionD: It has to run on every request
correctAnswerText: You cannot list every dangerous form
explanation: Encodings, unicode variants, nesting. You are guessing at the attacker’s vocabulary and they only need one word.

prompt: Why does escaping depend on where the value is being placed?
optionA: Different frameworks escape differently
optionB: Each context treats characters differently
optionC: Some contexts allow more characters
optionD: Escaping twice would corrupt the value
correctAnswerText: Each context treats characters differently
explanation: Safe in HTML text, dangerous in an attribute, useless inside a script block. One escape does not fit all.

prompt: Why does the browser help an attacker in a CSRF attack?
optionA: It sends your cookies with any request to you
optionB: It caches the authenticated response
optionC: It trusts requests from any origin
optionD: It allows scripts to read your cookies
correctAnswerText: It sends your cookies with any request to you
explanation: Cookies are attached by destination, not by who initiated it. The request looks perfectly authentic.

prompt: Why is XSS so damaging even without stealing a password?
optionA: The script can read the server’s files
optionB: The script persists after the user leaves
optionC: The script can modify the database
optionD: The script can act as the user directly
correctAnswerText: The script can act as the user directly
explanation: It does not need the session token. It is already inside the session and can just make the requests.

prompt: What is the difference between validating input and encoding output?
optionA: One rejects the request, the other changes it
optionB: One is for security, the other is for data quality
optionC: One checks it is sensible, one makes it safe there
optionD: One happens early, the other happens later
correctAnswerText: One checks it is sensible, one makes it safe there
explanation: Validation cannot know where the value will end up. Encoding is done at each place it is used.

prompt: Why does one insecure script on an HTTPS page matter?
optionA: It makes the whole page load more slowly
optionB: It prevents the certificate from validating
optionC: It stops cookies being marked as secure
optionD: It can be replaced and then controls the page
correctAnswerText: It can be replaced and then controls the page
explanation: Anything on the network can swap that file, and a script has full control of the page it loads into.

prompt: Why should a stack trace never reach the user?
optionA: It may contain the user’s own data
optionB: It makes the application look unreliable
optionC: It is too long for the response body
optionD: It maps out the system for an attacker
correctAnswerText: It maps out the system for an attacker
explanation: Paths, library versions, query fragments, internal hostnames. Reconnaissance you handed over free.

prompt: Why have a content security policy if you already escape output?
optionA: It protects against other attacks too
optionB: Escaping cannot cover every context
optionC: One missed spot is then not fatal
optionD: It is required by security standards
correctAnswerText: One missed spot is then not fatal
explanation: Defence in depth assumes you will make a mistake somewhere, because over a large codebase you will.

prompt: A query concatenates a username into its WHERE clause. What is the correct fix?
optionA: Pass the value as a bound parameter
optionB: Reject usernames containing symbols
optionC: Escape the quotes in the username
optionD: Limit the username to twenty characters
correctAnswerText: Pass the value as a bound parameter
explanation: The only complete answer. The other three are attempts to out-guess the attacker’s input.

prompt: You must display a user’s comment on a page. What do you do?
optionA: Strip the tags out of it first
optionB: Escape the angle brackets yourself
optionC: Insert it as text, not as markup
optionD: Store it already escaped in the database
correctAnswerText: Insert it as text, not as markup
explanation: Let the framework insert it as text. Storing it escaped breaks it everywhere it is not rendered as HTML.

prompt: How do you defend a form against CSRF?
optionA: Accept the form only over HTTPS
optionB: Check the referring page is your own
optionC: Require a token the other site cannot know
optionD: Require the user to confirm the action
correctAnswerText: Require a token the other site cannot know
explanation: A token they cannot read, plus SameSite cookies. The referrer can be absent and is not a control.

prompt: What is the biggest risk in accepting file uploads?
optionA: A file with an unexpected format
optionB: A file larger than the disk allows
optionC: A file containing a known virus
optionD: A file that the server will execute
correctAnswerText: A file that the server will execute
explanation: Store them outside the served directory, rename them, and never trust the name or type the client sent.

prompt: Your login redirects to a URL from the query string. What must you add?
optionA: A confirmation page before redirecting
optionB: An encoding of the URL parameter
optionC: A check that it points at your own site
optionD: A signature on the redirect value
correctAnswerText: A check that it points at your own site
explanation: Otherwise your domain becomes the credible first half of a phishing link. Allow-list the destinations.

prompt: Your API needs to serve one known front-end domain. How do you set CORS?
optionA: Reflect back whatever origin asked
optionB: Allow that one origin explicitly
optionC: Allow any origin ending in your domain
optionD: Allow all origins for simplicity
correctAnswerText: Allow that one origin explicitly
explanation: Reflecting the origin with credentials allowed is the same as allowing everybody, and it is a common mistake.

prompt: How do you keep dependency risk manageable?
optionA: Pin every version and never change them
optionB: Update everything to the latest weekly
optionC: Vendor them all into your repository
optionD: Scan them regularly and update deliberately
correctAnswerText: Scan them regularly and update deliberately
explanation: Never updating accumulates known holes; updating blindly ships whatever was published last night.

prompt: What should be set on a session cookie?
optionA: A long expiry so users stay logged in
optionB: Flags stopping scripts and cross-site sending
optionC: An encrypted value the server can read
optionD: A domain covering all your subdomains
correctAnswerText: Flags stopping scripts and cross-site sending
explanation: HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite. Three flags that remove XSS theft and most of CSRF at once.

prompt: Your server fetches a URL the user supplies. What is the danger?
optionA: It can be slow and block the request
optionB: It can return content of any type
optionC: It can return a very large response
optionD: It can be aimed at your internal network
correctAnswerText: It can be aimed at your internal network
explanation: Your server is inside the firewall. A user-supplied URL makes it a proxy into everything you do not expose.

prompt: How should a production error be reported?
optionA: The detail, but only to logged-in users
optionB: The full detail, so users can report it
optionC: A generic message out, the detail in the logs
optionD: A generic message and nothing recorded
correctAnswerText: A generic message out, the detail in the logs
explanation: With a reference id the user can quote, so support can find the detail without it ever being shown.

prompt: A framework escapes by default, yet one field renders raw HTML. Where is the bug?
optionA: Somebody opted out of escaping for that field
optionB: The framework fails on that data type
optionC: The field is rendered on the server
optionD: The field was stored without escaping
correctAnswerText: Somebody opted out of escaping for that field
explanation: Every framework has the escape hatch, and every XSS hole in a modern app is somebody using it.

prompt: A team uses an ORM and still has SQL injection. How?
optionA: The ORM version has a known flaw
optionB: The ORM does not escape all types
optionC: A raw query was written for one case
optionD: The database driver was misconfigured
correctAnswerText: A raw query was written for one case
explanation: Usually one report or a dynamic ORDER BY. The ORM protects what goes through it and nothing else.

prompt: A price field is validated in the browser and accepted as sent. What can happen?
optionA: The form can be submitted twice over
optionB: The validation message can be bypassed
optionC: The field can be left entirely empty
optionD: A crafted request sets any price at all
correctAnswerText: A crafted request sets any price at all
explanation: The browser is one client among many. Client validation is a convenience; the server check is the control.

prompt: An API key was put in the front-end build as an environment variable. Is it secret?
optionA: No, but only if someone inspects it
optionB: No — it is in the file every visitor downloads
optionC: Yes, because build variables are not exposed
optionD: Yes, provided the build is minified
correctAnswerText: No — it is in the file every visitor downloads
explanation: Build-time substitution writes the literal value into the bundle. It is as public as the page itself.

prompt: A profile endpoint saves every field of the request body. What can a user do?
optionA: Store more data than the limit allows
optionB: Send fields the form never showed them
optionC: Overwrite another user’s profile data
optionD: Cause the request to fail validation
correctAnswerText: Send fields the form never showed them
explanation: isAdmin, accountBalance, tenantId. Accept a named list of fields rather than whatever arrived.

prompt: A thumbnail service fetched an internal admin URL and returned its contents. What is this?
optionA: The server was used as a proxy inward
optionB: A caching bug returning the wrong page
optionC: A failure of the authentication layer
optionD: A misconfigured firewall rule
correctAnswerText: The server was used as a proxy inward
explanation: Server-side request forgery. The internal service trusted the network position, and the network position was yours.

prompt: A team logs the full request body to debug a problem. What have they created?
optionA: A store of passwords and tokens in plain text
optionB: A performance problem on every request
optionC: A log volume that will fill the disk
optionD: A privacy notice that is now inaccurate
correctAnswerText: A store of passwords and tokens in plain text
explanation: All four are real; the first is the one that turns a debugging aid into a breach nobody is watching.

prompt: A signup form says "that email is already registered". What has it given away?
optionA: Which addresses have accounts with you
optionB: How the passwords are being stored
optionC: How many users the system has
optionD: Which addresses are currently active
correctAnswerText: Which addresses have accounts with you
explanation: A real usability tension, not a clear bug — but for a sensitive service it is a list worth not publishing.

prompt: A content security policy allows inline scripts. What has it lost?
optionA: The ability to load external scripts
optionB: Its effect on older browser versions
optionC: Compatibility with the framework
optionD: Most of its protection against injection
correctAnswerText: Most of its protection against injection
explanation: Injected scripts are inline scripts. Allowing them permits precisely what the policy exists to block.

prompt: An old debug endpoint is still live in production. Why is that dangerous?
optionA: Nobody is maintaining or watching it
optionB: It was not written by the current team
optionC: It duplicates an existing endpoint
optionD: It uses an outdated response format
correctAnswerText: Nobody is maintaining or watching it
explanation: Unreviewed, unpatched, often unauthenticated, and absent from everyone’s mental model of the attack surface.

prompt: A scan reports forty issues. How do you order them?
optionA: By how quickly each one can be fixed
optionB: By how many places each one appears
optionC: By the severity score the tool assigned
optionD: By what an attacker could actually reach and do
correctAnswerText: By what an attacker could actually reach and do
explanation: A critical finding behind an admin login matters less than a medium one on the signup page.

prompt: A control is secure and users route around it. What is the verdict?
optionA: It is a problem for the product team
optionB: It has failed, whatever the design says
optionC: It should be kept and made easier
optionD: It is working and users need training
correctAnswerText: It has failed, whatever the design says
explanation: Behaviour is part of the system. A control people avoid gives you the appearance of security and none of it.

prompt: When should security be considered in a feature?
optionA: While it is being designed
optionB: Before the release goes out
optionC: During the code review
optionD: After the first scan reports
correctAnswerText: While it is being designed
explanation: Late-found problems are design problems, and a design problem found at review costs a rewrite.

prompt: What can an automated scanner not find?
optionA: Logic flaws in how the feature works
optionB: Known vulnerable library versions
optionC: Missing security response headers
optionD: Common injection patterns in code
correctAnswerText: Logic flaws in how the feature works
explanation: A checkout that lets you apply a discount twice is a serious flaw and looks like correct code to a scanner.

prompt: What does designing as though you will be breached change?
optionA: You test the application more often
optionB: You limit what any one failure reaches
optionC: You keep less data about your users
optionD: You spend more on perimeter defences
correctAnswerText: You limit what any one failure reaches
explanation: It moves the question from "can they get in" to "what can they do once they have", which is answerable.

prompt: What is the most reliable way to protect a piece of data?
optionA: To encrypt it at rest and in transit
optionB: To keep an audit log of every access
optionC: To restrict who is allowed to read it
optionD: Not to store it in the first place
correctAnswerText: Not to store it in the first place
explanation: Data you never collected cannot leak, cannot be subpoenaed and needs no controls. It is the strongest answer.

prompt: How much security is enough for a given system?
optionA: Enough to stop every known attack
optionB: Enough that attacking costs more than it gains
optionC: As much as the schedule allows for
optionD: Enough to pass the compliance requirements
correctAnswerText: Enough that attacking costs more than it gains
explanation: Economics, not perfection. A student forum and a bank need genuinely different amounts of effort.

prompt: A stranger emails describing a vulnerability in your site. What is the right response?
optionA: Refer the matter to your legal team
optionB: Ignore it unless they provide proof
optionC: Ask how they found it before acting
optionD: Thank them, verify it, and fix it
correctAnswerText: Thank them, verify it, and fix it
explanation: Hostility to reporters is why serious flaws end up disclosed publicly instead of quietly to you.

prompt: Why is using a mature framework a security decision?
optionA: Its code has been reviewed by more people
optionB: It comes with security documentation
optionC: It is updated more often than your own
optionD: Its defaults already close the common holes
correctAnswerText: Its defaults already close the common holes
explanation: Escaping, CSRF tokens, parameterised queries, secure cookies — free unless you deliberately turn them off.

prompt: What question catches most web vulnerabilities?
optionA: Is this connection encrypted
optionB: Where does untrusted data end up here
optionC: Are the dependencies up to date
optionD: Is this endpoint properly authenticated
correctAnswerText: Where does untrusted data end up here
explanation: Follow the untrusted value to every place it lands. Injection, XSS, SSRF and path traversal all fall out of it.

prompt: Which input should be treated as untrusted?
optionA: Anything that failed validation before
optionB: Anything typed in by a human user
optionC: Anything that came from outside your code
optionD: Anything arriving over the network
correctAnswerText: Anything that came from outside your code
explanation: Files, environment, other services, your own database if a user put it there. Not just form fields.

prompt: How should input validation be written?
optionA: Reject what is known bad, accept the rest
optionB: Accept everything and check it later
optionC: Clean the input and then accept it
optionD: Accept what is known good, reject the rest
correctAnswerText: Accept what is known good, reject the rest
explanation: You can finish a list of what is allowed. You can never finish a list of what is not.

prompt: Where should an API key live?
optionA: In the code, but clearly marked
optionB: In a constants file in the repository
optionC: In configuration supplied at run time
optionD: In a comment beside where it is used
correctAnswerText: In configuration supplied at run time
explanation: Outside the code entirely. Anything in the repository is readable by everyone who can clone it.

prompt: What kind of random should generate a password reset token?
optionA: A hash of the user’s identifier
optionB: The language’s standard random function
optionC: A cryptographically secure generator
optionD: A value derived from the current time
correctAnswerText: A cryptographically secure generator
explanation: An ordinary generator is predictable from its previous outputs, which for a token is the whole game.

prompt: What database account should an application use?
optionA: One shared with the other services
optionB: One created per developer on the team
optionC: One with full rights, for simplicity
optionD: One with only the rights it needs
correctAnswerText: One with only the rights it needs
explanation: An injection flaw then reaches only what that account could reach, which may be far less than everything.

prompt: What should a security check do if it cannot complete?
optionA: Refuse the request
optionB: Retry until it completes
optionC: Allow the request
optionD: Log it and continue
correctAnswerText: Refuse the request
explanation: Fail closed. A permission service timing out must not become a permission service saying yes.

prompt: Why keep a record of every dependency you ship?
optionA: So the licences can be checked properly
optionB: So you can tell whether an advisory affects you
optionC: So the build can be reproduced exactly
optionD: So unused packages can be removed
correctAnswerText: So you can tell whether an advisory affects you
explanation: When a serious flaw is announced, the first question is "are we affected" and it should take minutes.

prompt: How should two secret values be compared?
optionA: By checking their lengths first
optionB: With a comparison taking a fixed time
optionC: By hashing both and comparing those
optionD: With the standard equality operator
correctAnswerText: With a comparison taking a fixed time
explanation: Ordinary comparison stops at the first difference, and that timing is measurable over enough attempts.

prompt: What should the default setting of a security option be?
optionA: The safe one, with opting out explicit
optionB: Whatever most deployments will want
optionC: The permissive one, for compatibility
optionD: Unset, so it must always be chosen
correctAnswerText: The safe one, with opting out explicit
explanation: Most people never change a default, so the default is the real policy for almost every deployment.

prompt: What should never appear in an application log?
optionA: Passwords, tokens and card numbers
optionB: Error messages and stack traces
optionC: User identifiers and request paths
optionD: Timestamps and response times
correctAnswerText: Passwords, tokens and card numbers
explanation: Logs are copied, shipped and widely readable. Anything in them should be assumed to be seen.

prompt: Why does an allow-list stay correct as the system grows?
optionA: It can be generated from the schema
optionB: New unknown inputs are refused by default
optionC: It rejects fewer legitimate requests
optionD: It is shorter and easier to maintain
correctAnswerText: New unknown inputs are refused by default
explanation: The same reasoning as deny-by-default permissions: the unknown case lands on the safe side automatically.

prompt: A secret was committed and removed in the next commit. Why is it still a problem?
optionA: The removal commit draws attention to it
optionB: It remains in the repository history
optionC: It may be cached by the build system
optionD: The file may exist on other machines
correctAnswerText: It remains in the repository history
explanation: All four are real. The history is the one that keeps it available to everyone who ever clones the repository.

prompt: Why does a predictable token defeat the whole mechanism?
optionA: It will eventually repeat a value
optionB: It reveals when it was generated
optionC: It can be brute-forced more quickly
optionD: Anyone who can guess it can use it
correctAnswerText: Anyone who can guess it can use it
explanation: A token is a credential. If it can be computed rather than guessed, there is no security in it at all.

prompt: Why is a safe-by-construction function better than a coding rule?
optionA: It is faster than checking at run time
optionB: It requires less documentation
optionC: It protects people who never read the rule
optionD: It can be verified by the compiler
correctAnswerText: It protects people who never read the rule
explanation: Rules depend on memory and attention. An interface that cannot express the unsafe call depends on neither.

prompt: What does least privilege buy you when a flaw is exploited?
optionA: The exploit is harder to perform at all
optionB: The affected component can be isolated
optionC: The attacker inherits only that much reach
optionD: The flaw is detected sooner than otherwise
correctAnswerText: The attacker inherits only that much reach
explanation: It assumes exploitation rather than preventing it, and turns a total compromise into a partial one.

prompt: Why is a catch block that allows the action so dangerous?
optionA: Causing an error becomes a way through
optionB: It makes the code harder to test
optionC: It slows the request down noticeably
optionD: It hides the original fault from the logs
correctAnswerText: Causing an error becomes a way through
explanation: An attacker who can make your permission check throw has found the way past it.

prompt: Why is deserialising untrusted data dangerous in some languages?
optionA: The data may be larger than expected
optionB: The data may contain invalid characters
optionC: The types may not match what is wanted
optionD: Reconstructing objects can run their code
correctAnswerText: Reconstructing objects can run their code
explanation: Constructors and hooks fire during reconstruction, so the payload chooses what runs. Prefer plain formats.

prompt: Why is joining a user-supplied name onto a directory path risky?
optionA: The name may be longer than allowed
optionB: The name may match an existing file
optionC: The name may contain invalid characters
optionD: The name can navigate out of the directory
correctAnswerText: The name can navigate out of the directory
explanation: Path traversal. Resolve the final path and confirm it is still inside the directory you intended.

prompt: Why should you not implement your own encryption?
optionA: Broken cryptography looks exactly like working
optionB: The performance will be much worse
optionC: The algorithms are too complex to code
optionD: Standards forbid custom implementations
correctAnswerText: Broken cryptography looks exactly like working
explanation: Your test decrypts what you encrypted, and passes whether or not the scheme resists any actual attack.

prompt: Why does code review catch security bugs the author missed?
optionA: The reviewer reads it more carefully
optionB: The author wrote it under time pressure
optionC: The author assumed how it would be used
optionD: The reviewer knows more about security
correctAnswerText: The author assumed how it would be used
explanation: You test what you meant. A second reader asks what happens if the input is not what you had in mind.

prompt: A user requests a file by name from an uploads folder. How do you serve it safely?
optionA: Strip the dots and slashes from the name
optionB: Resolve the path and check it is still inside
optionC: Prefix the name with the folder path
optionD: Reject any name containing a slash
correctAnswerText: Resolve the path and check it is still inside
explanation: Check the resolved result, not the input. Filtering characters loses to encodings and symbolic links.

prompt: You must run a command with a user-supplied argument. What is safest?
optionA: Quote the argument inside the command string
optionB: Remove the shell metacharacters from it
optionC: Pass the arguments as a list, with no shell
optionD: Run the command as an unprivileged user
correctAnswerText: Pass the arguments as a list, with no shell
explanation: No shell means no shell syntax to be injected. The last is worth doing too, but it is containment, not prevention.

prompt: A key was pushed to a public repository an hour ago. What must you do?
optionA: Delete the commit that added it
optionB: Make the repository private
optionC: Rewrite the history to remove it
optionD: Rotate the key immediately
correctAnswerText: Rotate the key immediately
explanation: Public repositories are scraped within minutes. Cleaning the history afterwards is tidying, not remediation.

prompt: Your team keeps forgetting to scope queries by tenant. What is the durable fix?
optionA: A comment on each repository method
optionB: A test that checks the common queries
optionC: A data layer that cannot query without one
optionD: A rule in the code review checklist
correctAnswerText: A data layer that cannot query without one
explanation: Make the unsafe call unwritable. Reviews and tests catch what somebody remembered to look for.

prompt: You need request logging for debugging. How do you keep it safe?
optionA: Log the body and restrict who reads it
optionB: Log named fields, never the whole body
optionC: Log the body with the passwords removed
optionD: Log the body only when an error occurs
correctAnswerText: Log named fields, never the whole body
explanation: An allow-list again. Redacting by name misses the field somebody adds next month.

prompt: Why put a maximum size on an uploaded file or a request body?
optionA: Large inputs take longer to validate
optionB: The storage will otherwise fill up
optionC: Unbounded input is a way to exhaust the server
optionD: Users will send the wrong file by mistake
correctAnswerText: Unbounded input is a way to exhaust the server
explanation: Any unbounded resource a stranger controls is a denial-of-service waiting to be noticed.

prompt: You need to store passwords. Which primitive is correct?
optionA: A fast general-purpose hash
optionB: A slow password hashing function
optionC: A hash applied many times over
optionD: Symmetric encryption with a key
correctAnswerText: A slow password hashing function
explanation: bcrypt, scrypt or argon2. Encryption is reversible and a fast hash is what makes cracking cheap.

prompt: Users want to customise an email template. What is the risk to manage?
optionA: The template may be badly formatted
optionB: Template syntax can reach into the runtime
optionC: The email may fail to send correctly
optionD: The template may be very large
correctAnswerText: Template syntax can reach into the runtime
explanation: Server-side template injection. Give them a restricted syntax with a fixed set of placeholders.

prompt: What combination keeps dependencies both stable and safe?
optionA: Always installing the newest versions
optionB: Only using packages from large projects
optionC: Pinned versions plus regular advisory checks
optionD: Pinned versions reviewed once a year
correctAnswerText: Pinned versions plus regular advisory checks
explanation: Pinning stops surprise changes; scanning stops the pin becoming a known hole you are choosing to keep.

prompt: What kind of test most helps security?
optionA: One checking the dependencies are current
optionB: One running a scanner against the build
optionC: One asserting the wrong request is refused
optionD: One asserting the right request succeeds
correctAnswerText: One asserting the wrong request is refused
explanation: Abuse cases. The happy path passes whether or not the check exists, so it proves nothing about the check.

prompt: A permission check is wrapped in a try block that returns true on error. What is the effect?
optionA: The permission is cached incorrectly
optionB: Errors are silently hidden from the logs
optionC: The check runs more slowly than needed
optionD: Any error becomes a granted permission
correctAnswerText: Any error becomes a granted permission
explanation: The exception path is now the bypass, and it is usually written by somebody avoiding a flaky dependency.

prompt: Invite codes are built from a counter and a timestamp. What can an attacker do?
optionA: Work out codes that have not been issued
optionB: Cause the same code to be issued twice
optionC: Tell when each code was generated
optionD: Read the codes of other existing users
correctAnswerText: Work out codes that have not been issued
explanation: Both inputs are known or guessable, so the code is computed rather than secret. It is not a token at all.

prompt: An app connects to its database as the owner account. Why does that worsen an injection flaw?
optionA: The connection is slower to establish
optionB: The audit log records the wrong user
optionC: The queries bypass the normal indexes
optionD: The injected query can do anything at all
correctAnswerText: The injected query can do anything at all
explanation: Read-only rights would turn a catastrophic flaw into a data exposure. Owner rights leave nothing in reserve.

prompt: A mobile app enforces a spending limit and the API does not. What follows?
optionA: A modified client can exceed the limit
optionB: The API will reject the extra requests
optionC: The limit will be applied inconsistently
optionD: The limit only applies to new versions
correctAnswerText: A modified client can exceed the limit
explanation: Apps are decompiled and requests are replayed. Any rule that matters must live where you control it.

prompt: A service accepts a serialised object from a client and reconstructs it. What is the worst case?
optionA: An object with unexpected values is created
optionB: Memory is exhausted by a large payload
optionC: Code of the attacker’s choosing runs on the server
optionD: The parser throws and the request fails
correctAnswerText: Code of the attacker’s choosing runs on the server
explanation: The others are the mild outcomes. Full remote code execution is why this class is treated so seriously.

prompt: A signature check compares byte by byte and returns on the first mismatch. What leaks?
optionA: How much of the signature was correct
optionB: Whether the request was authenticated
optionC: The algorithm being used to sign
optionD: The signature that was expected
correctAnswerText: How much of the signature was correct
explanation: Measured over many attempts, that is enough to build the signature a byte at a time.

prompt: A snippet copied from an answer online disables certificate verification. Why did it "work"?
optionA: It retried the connection on failure
optionB: It cached the certificate locally
optionC: It used a more permissive protocol
optionD: It removed the check that was failing
correctAnswerText: It removed the check that was failing
explanation: The error went away because the verification did. The connection is now encrypted to whoever answered.

prompt: Debug mode is enabled in production. What does that typically expose?
optionA: Internal detail and sometimes a console
optionB: A slower response on every request
optionC: The version of the framework in use
optionD: The list of installed dependencies
correctAnswerText: Internal detail and sometimes a console
explanation: Some frameworks ship an interactive debugger on the error page, which is remote code execution by design.

prompt: An unauthenticated endpoint generates a PDF report. What is the risk?
optionA: The reports may contain private data
optionB: The endpoint will be slow for real users
optionC: The PDFs will fill the available storage
optionD: Anyone can consume your server capacity
correctAnswerText: Anyone can consume your server capacity
explanation: Any expensive operation a stranger can trigger repeatedly is a denial of service with no exploit needed.

prompt: Code checks a balance, then deducts it in a separate step. What can go wrong?
optionA: The check uses the wrong account
optionB: Two requests both pass the check first
optionC: The balance is read from a stale cache
optionD: The deduction fails and is not retried
correctAnswerText: Two requests both pass the check first
explanation: Time-of-check to time-of-use. The check and the change must happen as one atomic operation.

prompt: Your team keeps making the same security mistake. What is the best response?
optionA: Add it to the code review checklist
optionB: Add a scanner rule that detects the pattern
optionC: Run a training session on the topic
optionD: Change the code so the mistake is hard to make
correctAnswerText: Change the code so the mistake is hard to make
explanation: A recurring mistake is a design problem. The other three depend on attention, which is what already failed.

prompt: What is the honest cost of the secure option?
optionA: Usually more code and more friction
optionB: Usually a longer time to release
optionC: Usually a larger infrastructure bill
optionD: Usually worse runtime performance
correctAnswerText: Usually more code and more friction
explanation: Pretending it is free is how teams stop believing the advice. Say what it costs and why it is worth it.

prompt: What should shape how much effort a feature’s security gets?
optionA: How many users will reach the feature
optionB: How recently the framework was updated
optionC: What it would cost you if it were abused
optionD: How complex the feature is to build
correctAnswerText: What it would cost you if it were abused
explanation: A profile photo and a payment instruction deserve different amounts of paranoia. Spend where the loss is.

prompt: Reviewing a change for security, what do you look at first?
optionA: Whether the new code has enough tests
optionB: Whether the dependencies are up to date
optionC: Whether the error handling is complete
optionD: Where untrusted data enters and where it goes
correctAnswerText: Where untrusted data enters and where it goes
explanation: Trace the data. Most vulnerabilities are a value arriving somewhere its handler did not expect it.

prompt: You inherit a codebase with many security weaknesses. Where do you start?
optionA: With the parts that have the fewest tests
optionB: With the oldest code in the repository
optionC: With whatever a scanner flags as critical
optionD: Where untrusted input reaches something powerful
correctAnswerText: Where untrusted input reaches something powerful
explanation: Reachability first. A flaw nobody can trigger from outside is a lower priority than a mild one on a public route.

prompt: Is it ever right to knowingly ship a security weakness?
optionA: No, security issues must always be fixed
optionB: Yes, if it is understood, recorded and owned
optionC: No, unless the feature is disabled
optionD: Yes, if the chance of exploitation is low
correctAnswerText: Yes, if it is understood, recorded and owned
explanation: Accepted risk is a legitimate decision. Unrecorded risk is the same weakness with nobody responsible for it.

prompt: What should you assume about code you did not write yourself?
optionA: It follows the current best practice
optionB: It is correct for its example, not your case
optionC: It handles the error cases properly
optionD: It has been reviewed by somebody already
correctAnswerText: It is correct for its example, not your case
explanation: Snippets, answers and generated code optimise for demonstrating the idea, not for surviving hostile input.

prompt: Someone on the team introduces a serious vulnerability. What matters most afterwards?
optionA: That they understand what they did wrong
optionB: That it is recorded against the feature
optionC: Why nothing in the process caught it
optionD: That the fix is deployed immediately
correctAnswerText: Why nothing in the process caught it
explanation: Deploy the fix, of course. But the durable question is why review, tests and design all let it through.

prompt: A developer adds a flag that skips authentication locally. What is the danger?
optionA: It makes local testing less realistic
optionB: It will one day be enabled in production
optionC: It hides authentication bugs from tests
optionD: It adds a branch that is never covered
correctAnswerText: It will one day be enabled in production
explanation: All three of the others are true. The first is the one that becomes an incident report.

prompt: What habit does secure coding really come down to?
optionA: Keeping up with the published advisories
optionB: Asking what happens if this input is hostile
optionC: Knowing the common vulnerability classes
optionD: Using the security features of the framework
correctAnswerText: Asking what happens if this input is hostile
explanation: The classes change and the frameworks change. The question generalises to code you have never seen.

prompt: What is threat modelling?
optionA: Scanning the code for security defects
optionB: Testing a built system for vulnerabilities
optionC: Listing the known risks in the industry
optionD: Working out how a design could be attacked
correctAnswerText: Working out how a design could be attacked
explanation: A design activity. Testing and scanning find what is already built; this is about what you are about to build.

prompt: What is an asset in a threat model?
optionA: A server the system runs on
optionB: A component of the system
optionC: A dependency the system uses
optionD: Something worth protecting
correctAnswerText: Something worth protecting
explanation: Data, money, reputation, availability. Naming them is how you decide where the effort goes.

prompt: What is a threat actor?
optionA: Somebody who might attack, and why
optionB: A system component that can fail
optionC: A person who found a vulnerability
optionD: A user with elevated permissions
correctAnswerText: Somebody who might attack, and why
explanation: Motive included. A bored customer, a competitor and a criminal group want different things and try differently.

prompt: What is the attack surface?
optionA: Every component the system contains
optionB: Every known weakness in the design
optionC: Every place an outsider can reach in
optionD: Every user who can log in to it
correctAnswerText: Every place an outsider can reach in
explanation: Endpoints, forms, file uploads, queues, third-party callbacks. Reducing it is one of the cheapest defences.

prompt: What is a trust boundary?
optionA: A point where data changes who controls it
optionB: A limit on what a user is allowed to do
optionC: A firewall between two parts of a network
optionD: A separation between two deployed services
correctAnswerText: A point where data changes who controls it
explanation: Wherever data crosses one, it must be validated. Most vulnerabilities sit on a boundary nobody drew.

prompt: What is the simplest useful structure for a threat model?
optionA: Scan, triage, remediate, verify, report to the business
optionB: What are we building, what can go wrong, what now, did it work
optionC: Design, implement, test, deploy, monitor for incidents
optionD: Identify assets, rank them, assign owners, review annually
correctAnswerText: What are we building, what can go wrong, what now, did it work
explanation: Four questions any team can hold in their heads. The formal methods are refinements of these.

prompt: When is threat modelling most valuable?
optionA: After the first incident has occurred
optionB: Before the security review is booked
optionC: While the design can still be changed
optionD: Once the first version is working
correctAnswerText: While the design can still be changed
explanation: Its whole advantage is that a design problem is still a conversation rather than a rewrite.

prompt: What are the possible responses to an identified threat?
optionA: Document it, or escalate it to management
optionB: Test for it, or monitor for it in production
optionC: Reduce it, move it, remove it, or accept it
optionD: Fix it now, or schedule a fix for later
correctAnswerText: Reduce it, move it, remove it, or accept it
explanation: Mitigate, transfer, eliminate, accept. Accepting is a real answer when it is recorded and owned.

prompt: What does a data flow diagram contribute?
optionA: It documents the system for new joiners
optionB: It records the components and their owners
optionC: It proves the design meets the requirements
optionD: It shows where data goes and who touches it
correctAnswerText: It shows where data goes and who touches it
explanation: Following the data is how the boundaries become visible, and the boundaries are where the threats are.

prompt: What should a threat modelling session produce?
optionA: A report for the security team to review
optionB: A ranked list of every possible threat
optionC: Decisions and work somebody has taken on
optionD: A document describing the system design
correctAnswerText: Decisions and work somebody has taken on
explanation: If nothing changes in the plan afterwards, the session was a meeting rather than an engineering activity.

prompt: Why is a design-stage finding so much cheaper than a production one?
optionA: Nothing has been built around it yet
optionB: It does not need a formal fix
optionC: There is more time available then
optionD: Fewer people need to be involved
correctAnswerText: Nothing has been built around it yet
explanation: A whiteboard change costs a conversation. The same change six months later costs a migration.

prompt: Why is "protect the system" a useless goal?
optionA: It ignores the cost of the protection
optionB: It does not name any attacker
optionC: You cannot tell whether you achieved it
optionD: It is too large a task for one team
correctAnswerText: You cannot tell whether you achieved it
explanation: "Stop one customer reading another’s invoices" can be designed for and tested. The vague version cannot.

prompt: Why does it matter who you imagine attacking?
optionA: It decides which standards you must meet
optionB: Some attackers are outside your control
optionC: Their capability and goal change the design
optionD: It determines the budget you can request
correctAnswerText: Their capability and goal change the design
explanation: Defending against a curious user and against a funded group are different systems, not different amounts of care.

prompt: Why do vulnerabilities cluster at trust boundaries?
optionA: Each side assumes the other checked
optionB: Boundaries are written by two teams
optionC: Boundaries are harder to test properly
optionD: Data is transformed as it crosses
correctAnswerText: Each side assumes the other checked
explanation: The classic gap: the front end validated it, so the service did not, and the service is callable directly.

prompt: Why should the building team do the threat modelling rather than a specialist alone?
optionA: Specialists are too expensive to involve
optionB: They know how it really works, and will act on it
optionC: Specialists do not understand the domain
optionD: It is faster than waiting for a review
correctAnswerText: They know how it really works, and will act on it
explanation: A model handed to a team is a document. A model a team built is a set of decisions they already own.

prompt: Why is removing a feature sometimes the best security fix?
optionA: It reduces the code to be maintained
optionB: It simplifies the permission model
