optionC: What does not exist cannot be attacked
optionD: Fewer features are easier to test
correctAnswerText: What does not exist cannot be attacked
explanation: The strongest mitigation available, and the one engineers reach for last because it is not a technical fix.

prompt: Why rank threats rather than addressing them all?
optionA: Ranking is required for the audit trail
optionB: Low threats become high ones over time
optionC: Some threats cannot be mitigated at all
optionD: Effort spent everywhere is effort spent thinly
correctAnswerText: Effort spent everywhere is effort spent thinly
explanation: A model that generates forty equal threats has not helped anybody decide what to do on Monday.

prompt: Why write down the assumptions a threat model rests on?
optionA: They explain the design to reviewers
optionB: They are required by the methodology
optionC: They show what was out of scope
optionD: They may stop being true later
correctAnswerText: They may stop being true later
explanation: "Only internal staff can reach this network" is a fine assumption until the day it is not, silently.

prompt: What does asking "how would I abuse this" find that requirements do not?
optionA: Performance limits under heavy load
optionB: Defects in the feature as specified
optionC: Uses of the feature nobody intended
optionD: Gaps in the acceptance criteria
correctAnswerText: Uses of the feature nobody intended
explanation: Requirements describe the intended path. Attacks live entirely in the unintended ones.

prompt: Why is a threat model not a one-off exercise?
optionA: The system and its threats both change
optionB: The original one is usually incomplete
optionC: The team members change over time
optionD: The document becomes out of date
correctAnswerText: The system and its threats both change
explanation: A new integration, a new data type, a new customer tier. Each can invalidate what was true last year.

prompt: How do you begin threat modelling a new feature?
optionA: Draw how the data moves through it
optionB: Choose a formal methodology to follow
optionC: List the vulnerabilities it might have
optionD: Review the code that already exists
correctAnswerText: Draw how the data moves through it
explanation: The drawing is where disagreements surface. Two engineers often discover they pictured different systems.

prompt: For a student learning platform, what is a well-stated asset?
optionA: The database the platform runs against
optionB: A student’s assessment results and progress
optionC: The reputation of the organisation
optionD: The availability of the whole platform
correctAnswerText: A student’s assessment results and progress
explanation: Specific enough to design around. The last two are real concerns but too broad to produce a control.

prompt: On your diagram, where do you draw the trust boundaries?
optionA: Wherever control of the data changes hands
optionB: Between the front end and the back end
optionC: At the edge of your own network
optionD: Around each service that you deploy
correctAnswerText: Wherever control of the data changes hands
explanation: Browser to server, service to service, your code to a third party, your code to a background job.

prompt: A feature lets students share a project link. What abuse question do you ask?
optionA: What happens if the project is deleted
optionB: Who else can reach it, and what does it show
optionC: How many links can one student create
optionD: How long should the link remain valid
correctAnswerText: Who else can reach it, and what does it show
explanation: All are worth asking. The first is the threat question, because a shareable link is an access control decision.

prompt: How should you rank the threats you found?
optionA: By how recently each type was in the news
optionB: By how difficult each one is to mitigate
optionC: By how many components each one touches
optionD: By how likely they are and what they would cost
correctAnswerText: By how likely they are and what they would cost
explanation: Likelihood times impact. Difficulty belongs in planning the work, not in judging how much it matters.

prompt: A threat is real but extremely unlikely and expensive to prevent. What do you do?
optionA: Accept it explicitly, and write down who did
optionB: Leave it out of the model entirely
optionC: Escalate it to the security team
optionD: Mitigate it anyway, since it is real
correctAnswerText: Accept it explicitly, and write down who did
explanation: Acceptance is a legitimate outcome. What is not legitimate is an unrecorded risk with no owner.

prompt: What scope makes a threat modelling session actually finish?
optionA: One feature or one flow at a time
optionB: Each service the team owns, in turn
optionC: The whole system in one sitting
optionD: Everything that changed this quarter
correctAnswerText: One feature or one flow at a time
explanation: Whole-system sessions run for hours and produce a document. One flow produces three tickets.

prompt: Before designing a new control, what should you establish?
optionA: Whether the threat has occurred before
optionB: Whether the team can build it quickly
optionC: Whether something already handles this threat
optionD: Whether the control is industry standard
correctAnswerText: Whether something already handles this threat
explanation: The framework may already do it. Adding a second mechanism costs complexity and buys almost nothing.

prompt: How do you make sure a threat model changes anything?
optionA: Store the model beside the design
optionB: Schedule a follow-up review later
optionC: Circulate the notes to the team
optionD: Leave with tickets that have owners
correctAnswerText: Leave with tickets that have owners
explanation: Tracked work in the same backlog as everything else. Anything else competes with features and loses.

prompt: You mitigated a threat. How do you know it stays mitigated?
optionA: A note in the threat model document
optionB: A review before each major release
optionC: A test that fails if the control is removed
optionD: A scanner rule looking for the pattern
correctAnswerText: A test that fails if the control is removed
explanation: Otherwise a refactor removes it in eight months and nothing anywhere notices.

prompt: A team produces a 40-page threat model and ships the design unchanged. What went wrong?
optionA: It was done too late in the project
optionB: It produced a document instead of decisions
optionC: The wrong people wrote the document
optionD: The model was not detailed enough
correctAnswerText: It produced a document instead of decisions
explanation: Length is not the measure. A model that changed nothing about the plan has produced nothing.

prompt: An internal service with no authentication is breached after a network change. What failed?
optionA: The service should never have existed
optionB: The network change was made incorrectly
optionC: The breach was not detected in time
optionD: An assumption changed and nobody rechecked
correctAnswerText: An assumption changed and nobody rechecked
explanation: "Only reachable internally" was true and became false. Recorded assumptions are what make that reviewable.

prompt: A model defends thoroughly against outsiders and the damage came from a logged-in customer. What was missed?
optionA: The logging did not cover that user
optionB: The outside defences were inadequate
optionC: The authentication was too permissive
optionD: Legitimate users were not treated as actors
correctAnswerText: Legitimate users were not treated as actors
explanation: The most common gap. An authenticated user doing something they should not is the everyday case.

prompt: Data from a partner’s webhook is trusted completely. What was not drawn?
optionA: The connection between the services
optionB: The validation step in the handler
optionC: The boundary at the partner’s edge
optionD: The authentication on the endpoint
correctAnswerText: The boundary at the partner’s edge
explanation: Anything arriving from outside your control crosses a boundary, even when the sender is a partner you trust.

prompt: A session ran three hours and reached no conclusions. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The wrong people were in the room
optionB: The diagram was never completed
optionC: Nobody was chairing the discussion
optionD: The scope was the entire system
correctAnswerText: The scope was the entire system
explanation: All can contribute. Scope is the usual one, and the fix is to model one flow rather than everything.

prompt: A threat model is filled in from a template after the design is approved. What has it become?
optionA: A lightweight version of the process
optionB: A useful summary for future readers
optionC: A record of a decision already taken
optionD: A way of training the team gradually
correctAnswerText: A record of a decision already taken
explanation: Retrofitted, it can only justify what was chosen. The value was in being able to change the design.

prompt: A control identified in last year’s model is no longer in the code. How?
optionA: The control was superseded by another
optionB: The code was rewritten in a new language
optionC: Nothing tested for it, so a change removed it
optionD: The model was never actually implemented
correctAnswerText: Nothing tested for it, so a change removed it
explanation: A control with no test is a comment. Somebody refactoring had no way to know it mattered.

prompt: Every threat in a model is marked high priority. What is the effect?
optionA: The ranking gives no guidance at all
optionB: The team will fix them all eventually
optionC: The most severe ones get done first
optionD: The model is more thorough than most
correctAnswerText: The ranking gives no guidance at all
explanation: A priority everything shares is not a priority. The list is back to being unordered.

prompt: A team adopted a formal methodology and stopped threat modelling within two months. Why?
optionA: The team did not understand the notation
optionB: Security stopped requiring the exercise
optionC: The methodology produced wrong results
optionD: The process cost more than teams would pay
correctAnswerText: The process cost more than teams would pay
explanation: A lightweight version done every sprint beats a rigorous one done twice and then quietly dropped.

prompt: A two-year-old threat model no longer describes the system. What is the risk of keeping it?
optionA: It confuses new members of the team
optionB: It gives confidence that is no longer earned
optionC: It has to be reviewed by the auditors
optionD: It takes up space in the documentation
correctAnswerText: It gives confidence that is no longer earned
explanation: A stale model is worse than none, because "we threat modelled that" stops anybody looking again.

prompt: Which change most deserves a threat modelling session?
optionA: One that touches the most source files
optionB: One that uses an unfamiliar library
optionC: One that changes the database schema
optionD: One that adds a new way in from outside
correctAnswerText: One that adds a new way in from outside
explanation: New entry points, new data, new trust relationships. Internal refactors rarely change the threat picture.

prompt: How formal should a team’s threat modelling be?
optionA: As formal as they will actually keep doing
optionB: As formal as the auditors will require
optionC: As formal as the methodology specifies
optionD: As formal as the system’s risk demands
correctAnswerText: As formal as they will actually keep doing
explanation: Sustainability beats rigour, because a process that is abandoned protects nothing at all.

prompt: What can threat modelling not tell you?
optionA: Which parts of the design are risky
optionB: Whether the code implements it correctly
optionC: What is worth protecting most
optionD: Where the trust boundaries fall
correctAnswerText: Whether the code implements it correctly
explanation: It reasons about the design. The gap between a correct design and the code is what testing and review cover.

prompt: Who adds the most unexpected value in a threat modelling session?
optionA: Somebody senior enough to approve the work
optionB: Somebody who knows how users really behave
optionC: Somebody who wrote the original system
optionD: Somebody from an external security firm
correctAnswerText: Somebody who knows how users really behave
explanation: Support and operations know the workarounds people invent, and workarounds are where abuse starts.

prompt: How do you know you have mitigated enough?
optionA: When every identified threat is addressed
optionB: When attacking costs more than it would gain
optionC: When the remaining threats are unlikely
optionD: When the security team signs it off
correctAnswerText: When attacking costs more than it would gain
explanation: Security is economics. Raising the attacker’s cost above the prize is a reachable goal; perfection is not.

prompt: What is the fundamental weakness of threat modelling?
optionA: It produces too many low-value findings
optionB: It depends on the design being final
optionC: You only find what you can imagine
optionD: It takes time the team may not have
correctAnswerText: You only find what you can imagine
explanation: Which is why checklists, varied participants and outside review all help — they widen the imagination.

prompt: Is threat modelling worth it for a three-person startup?
optionA: No, until they have their first customers
optionB: Yes, in a thirty-minute form over the design
optionC: Yes, in the same detail as anyone else
optionD: No, it is a process for larger organisations
correctAnswerText: Yes, in a thirty-minute form over the design
explanation: The four questions over a whiteboard. That version costs almost nothing and catches the worst decisions.

prompt: How do you present a risk to somebody who does not write code?
optionA: As a severity rating from the framework
optionB: As a comparison to a recent news story
optionC: As what could happen, and what it would cost
optionD: As the technical mechanism of the attack
correctAnswerText: As what could happen, and what it would cost
explanation: "A customer could read another customer’s invoices" is a sentence a business owner can make a decision with.

prompt: Where does threat modelling sit relative to testing and scanning?
optionA: Alongside them, as an equivalent activity
optionB: Instead of them, for well-designed systems
optionC: After them, to explain what they found
optionD: Before them, deciding what they should cover
correctAnswerText: Before them, deciding what they should cover
explanation: It tells you what matters. Scanners then look for the known patterns and tests assert the controls you chose.

prompt: What is the durable version of this skill?
optionA: Keeping the threat documents current
optionB: Knowing the formal methodologies well
optionC: Producing a model for every project
optionD: Asking what could go wrong, while designing
correctAnswerText: Asking what could go wrong, while designing
explanation: The habit outlives the process. An engineer who asks it by reflex catches more than an annual exercise does.

prompt: What is the difference between an expected and an unexpected failure?
optionA: One happens often, the other happens rarely
optionB: One is logged, the other is shown to the user
optionC: One is part of normal use, one is a defect
optionD: One is caught, the other is allowed to crash
correctAnswerText: One is part of normal use, one is a defect
explanation: A wrong password is normal operation. A null pointer is a bug, and they deserve different treatment.

prompt: What does it mean to swallow an error?
optionA: To record it and return a default value
optionB: To catch it and carry on as if nothing happened
optionC: To catch it and convert it to another type
optionD: To let it travel up to the top of the stack
correctAnswerText: To catch it and carry on as if nothing happened
explanation: An empty catch block. The failure happened, nothing recorded it, and the program continued regardless.

prompt: Where should an error be handled?
optionA: At the outermost layer of the application
optionB: In the function that first detected it
optionC: Where there is enough context to do something
optionD: As close to where it happened as possible
correctAnswerText: Where there is enough context to do something
explanation: A low-level function knows a file is missing; only the caller knows whether that matters.

prompt: What should an error message contain?
optionA: A unique code the team can look up
optionB: What failed, and enough to act on it
optionC: The exact line of code that threw it
optionD: An apology and a support contact
correctAnswerText: What failed, and enough to act on it
explanation: Which record, which value, which operation. Enough that the reader knows what to do next.

prompt: What does failing fast mean?
optionA: Stopping as soon as something is wrong
optionB: Returning an error more quickly than usual
optionC: Retrying immediately rather than waiting
optionD: Timing out before the operation finishes
correctAnswerText: Stopping as soon as something is wrong
explanation: The alternative is continuing with bad state, which turns a clear failure into a confusing one later.

prompt: Which kind of failure is worth retrying?
optionA: One the user asked you to repeat
optionB: One that happened on the network
optionC: One that might succeed if tried again
optionD: One that returns a server error code
correctAnswerText: One that might succeed if tried again
explanation: Transient means it may pass. Retrying a rejected password is just doing the same wrong thing repeatedly.

prompt: Why give different failures different error types?
optionA: So the messages can be worded better
optionB: So a caller can react to each differently
optionC: So the errors can be counted separately
optionD: So the logs can be filtered by type
correctAnswerText: So a caller can react to each differently
explanation: One generic error forces callers to read the message text, which then cannot be changed.

prompt: What must happen to an open resource when an error occurs?
optionA: It must be closed in the catch block
optionB: It must be released on every path out
optionC: It will be released when the process ends
optionD: It should be left open for the retry
correctAnswerText: It must be released on every path out
explanation: Every path, including the ones you did not think about. That is what finally blocks and scoped resources are for.

prompt: Who are the two audiences for an error?
optionA: The caller and the function that threw it
optionB: The application and the monitoring system
optionC: The person using it and the person fixing it
optionD: The developer and the operations team
correctAnswerText: The person using it and the person fixing it
explanation: They need different things, which is why one message rarely serves both well.

prompt: What is the danger when an operation fails halfway through?
optionA: The logs will record two separate failures
optionB: The system is left in an inconsistent state
optionC: The user has to start the whole thing again
optionD: The error message will be inaccurate
correctAnswerText: The system is left in an inconsistent state
explanation: Money taken and no order placed. Half-completed work is the failure mode worth designing against.

prompt: Why is a silently swallowed error worse than a crash?
optionA: The stack trace is lost when caught
optionB: The crash would have been logged properly
optionC: The user gets no feedback either way
optionD: The damage continues with nobody knowing
correctAnswerText: The damage continues with nobody knowing
explanation: A crash is a loud event at the moment of failure. Silence turns it into corrupt data found much later.

prompt: Why is an exception a poor fit for validation failure?
optionA: Exceptions are slower than returning a value
optionB: It makes the common case read as the rare one
optionC: The caller cannot see what field failed
optionD: Exceptions cannot carry structured data
correctAnswerText: It makes the common case read as the rare one
explanation: Invalid input is the ordinary operation of a form. Modelling it as exceptional inverts the code’s emphasis.

prompt: Why stop at the first sign of a broken assumption?
optionA: The failure is nearest its cause there
optionB: It prevents the error being caught later
optionC: It saves the remaining processing time
optionD: It produces a shorter stack trace
correctAnswerText: The failure is nearest its cause there
explanation: Distance between cause and symptom is what makes debugging expensive. Failing early keeps it at zero.

prompt: Why is "something went wrong" an expensive message?
optionA: It looks unprofessional to the user
optionB: Every occurrence costs somebody an investigation
optionC: It gives no code for support to reference
optionD: It cannot be translated into other languages
correctAnswerText: Every occurrence costs somebody an investigation
explanation: Written once, paid every time it appears, by whoever has to work out what actually happened.

prompt: Why add context to an error as it travels up?
optionA: Each layer knows something the others do not
optionB: It converts the error to the right type
optionC: It lets each layer decide whether to log
optionD: It makes the stack trace shorter to read
correctAnswerText: Each layer knows something the others do not
explanation: "Connection refused" plus "loading user 42" plus "rendering the dashboard" is a story you can act on.

prompt: Why should retries wait longer each time?
optionA: Slower retries are easier to monitor
optionB: The caller may cancel in the meantime
optionC: Immediate retries make an overload worse
optionD: The failure needs time to be logged
correctAnswerText: Immediate retries make an overload worse
explanation: A struggling service hit by every client retrying at once is a service that does not recover.

prompt: Why can retrying a failed request cause duplicates?
optionA: The retry may carry different data
optionB: The retry may be sent to a different server
optionC: The request may arrive out of order
optionD: The first attempt may have succeeded quietly
correctAnswerText: The first attempt may have succeeded quietly
explanation: A lost response looks exactly like a failed request. Retrying is only safe if repeating is safe.

prompt: Why should the user see less than the log records?
optionA: Users cannot understand technical language
optionB: The log is the official record of the fault
optionC: Internal detail helps an attacker and not them
optionD: Long messages do not fit in the interface
correctAnswerText: Internal detail helps an attacker and not them
explanation: The user needs to know what to do; the log needs everything. Only one of those audiences is trusted.

prompt: Why stop calling a service that keeps failing?
optionA: It saves the cost of the network calls
optionB: It lets the service recover and you fail fast
optionC: It prevents the error spreading further
optionD: It reduces the number of errors logged
correctAnswerText: It lets the service recover and you fail fast
explanation: A circuit breaker. You stop adding load to something drowning, and stop making your users wait for a timeout.

prompt: Why might a page render without its recommendations panel?
optionA: The panel can be retried separately
optionB: One optional failure should not lose the page
optionC: The panel takes the longest to load
optionD: Recommendations are not important data
correctAnswerText: One optional failure should not lose the page
explanation: Graceful degradation. Deciding in advance which parts are optional is what makes it possible.

prompt: A lookup may legitimately find nothing. How should that be expressed?
optionA: As a null the caller should check for
optionB: As an exception the caller can catch
optionC: As a return value the caller must handle
optionD: As an empty object with a flag set
correctAnswerText: As a return value the caller must handle
explanation: Not found is an outcome, not a fault. A type the caller must unwrap makes ignoring it impossible.

prompt: You catch a database error in a service method. What should you do with it?
optionA: Log it and return a default value
optionB: Convert it into a generic service error
optionC: Re-raise it with what you were doing added
optionD: Catch it and let the caller see nothing
correctAnswerText: Re-raise it with what you were doing added
explanation: Keep the original as the cause. Replacing it loses the detail that would have identified the fault.

prompt: Three writes must all succeed or none. What do you use?
optionA: A retry of whichever one failed
optionB: A check after each of the writes
optionC: A transaction covering all three
optionD: A rollback function you call yourself
correctAnswerText: A transaction covering all three
explanation: Where a transaction is not available, compensating actions — but a hand-written rollback is the last resort.

prompt: What must every retry loop have?
optionA: A limit and an increasing delay
optionB: A check that the caller is waiting
optionC: A log line on each attempt
optionD: A different server on each try
correctAnswerText: A limit and an increasing delay
explanation: Unbounded retries turn one failing dependency into a thread pool exhausted and a service that never recovers.

prompt: How many distinct error types should a module expose?
optionA: As few as possible, ideally just one
optionB: One for the whole module, with a code
optionC: One per place an error can be raised
optionD: One per way a caller would react differently
correctAnswerText: One per way a caller would react differently
explanation: The caller’s branches decide the types. More than that is ceremony; fewer forces message-matching.

prompt: How do you serve both the user and the engineer from one failure?
optionA: A short message out, the full detail logged, linked by an id
optionB: A short message out, with the detail in a header
optionC: A detailed message shown only to signed-in users
optionD: A full message out, with the sensitive parts removed
correctAnswerText: A short message out, the full detail logged, linked by an id
explanation: The reference id is the whole trick — the user can quote it and support can find everything.

prompt: A page calls five services. How do you decide what happens when one fails?
optionA: Render whatever arrived in time
optionB: Fail the page if any of them fails
optionC: Retry each one until it succeeds
optionD: Decide in advance which are essential
correctAnswerText: Decide in advance which are essential
explanation: Essential and optional is a product decision. Made at design time it is cheap; made in an incident it is not.

prompt: Why must every outbound call have a timeout?
optionA: A hanging call holds your resources forever
optionB: The remote service may return an error
optionC: The user may navigate away meanwhile
optionD: The connection may be dropped silently
correctAnswerText: A hanging call holds your resources forever
explanation: No timeout means one slow dependency consumes every thread you have, and then you are down too.

prompt: What is the most reliable way to close a resource?
optionA: A close call at the end of the function
optionB: A periodic sweep of unclosed handles
optionC: A construct that closes it when scope ends
optionD: A close call inside the catch block
correctAnswerText: A construct that closes it when scope ends
explanation: using, with, defer, try-with-resources. Anything you must remember will be forgotten on some path.

prompt: What belongs at the top level of a web application?
optionA: A log statement for each request made
optionB: A catch block around every route handler
optionC: A handler turning any error into a response
optionD: A retry of the request that failed
correctAnswerText: A handler turning any error into a response
explanation: One boundary that guarantees no unhandled error escapes as a blank page or a stack trace.

prompt: Records are occasionally missing and nothing appears in the logs. What would you look for?
optionA: A cache serving a stale record list
optionB: A database constraint rejecting them
optionC: A network failure during the write
optionD: A catch block that does nothing at all
correctAnswerText: A catch block that does nothing at all
explanation: Failures with no trace anywhere is the signature of a swallowed error, usually added to quieten a test.

prompt: Every failure logs "service error" with no further detail. What was done wrong?
optionA: The logging happens before the detail is known
optionB: The log level was set too low to record it
optionC: The original error was replaced, not wrapped
optionD: The error type was too generic to begin with
correctAnswerText: The original error was replaced, not wrapped
explanation: Throwing a new error and discarding the cause deletes the only part that identified the fault.

prompt: A brief database blip turned into a twenty-minute outage. What likely amplified it?
optionA: The connection pool being too small
optionB: Every client retrying immediately and repeatedly
optionC: The database taking too long to restart
optionD: The error not being detected quickly enough
correctAnswerText: Every client retrying immediately and repeatedly
explanation: The retries became the load that kept it down. Backoff with jitter is what breaks that loop.

prompt: One slow downstream service brought down three services that call it. Why?
optionA: Their threads were all waiting on it
optionB: They ran out of memory buffering data
optionC: They retried until the network failed
optionD: They propagated the error incorrectly
correctAnswerText: Their threads were all waiting on it
explanation: Slow is worse than down. A missing timeout converts somebody else’s latency into your outage.

prompt: Some orders exist with no payment record. What does that suggest?
optionA: The order was created twice over
optionB: The two writes were not atomic
optionC: The payment record was deleted later
optionD: The payment service was unavailable
correctAnswerText: The two writes were not atomic
explanation: Orphaned records are the fingerprint of a multi-step operation that failed between its steps.

prompt: A catch around a whole function hides a typo in an unrelated line. How?
optionA: It converts the error into a warning level
optionB: It retries the function and masks the fault
optionC: It catches the programming error along with the rest
optionD: It prevents the function from being called
correctAnswerText: It catches the programming error along with the rest
explanation: A catch meant for a network failure also catches your own bugs, and reports them as a network failure.

prompt: Users occasionally receive two identical confirmation emails. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The queue processing the job concurrently
optionB: The user submitting the form two times
optionC: A retry after the first attempt had succeeded
optionD: The email service delivering the same message twice
correctAnswerText: A retry after the first attempt had succeeded
explanation: All are possible; the retry-after-lost-response is the one built into the code rather than the environment.

prompt: The error log has thousands of entries a day and nobody reads it. What went wrong?
optionA: The log level was configured incorrectly
optionB: The system genuinely fails that often
optionC: The log retention is set for too long
optionD: Expected outcomes are being logged as errors
correctAnswerText: Expected outcomes are being logged as errors
explanation: A failed login is not an error. Logging normal outcomes at error level is what buries the real ones.

prompt: A background job has been failing for weeks and nobody noticed. What was missing?
optionA: A schedule that runs it often enough
optionB: Anything that reports a job’s failure
optionC: A log statement inside the job
optionD: A retry when the job fails to run
correctAnswerText: Anything that reports a job’s failure
explanation: Nobody is watching a background job fail. Its failures need to reach the same place a request failure does.

prompt: A utility function catches a missing file and returns an empty string. What is the problem?
optionA: It decided for callers that this was acceptable
optionB: It failed to record the missing filename
optionC: It returned the wrong kind of default
optionD: It should have created the file instead
correctAnswerText: It decided for callers that this was acceptable
explanation: For one caller the file is optional and for another it is fatal. The utility cannot know which.

prompt: When is crashing the right response to an error?
optionA: When the error cannot be handled locally
optionB: When continuing would corrupt something
optionC: When the error has not been seen before
optionD: When the user cannot do anything about it
correctAnswerText: When continuing would corrupt something
explanation: Stopping is a legitimate design choice, and often the honest one. Corrupt data is harder to fix than downtime.

prompt: How much error handling is the right amount?
optionA: Enough for the failures that will actually occur
optionB: As much as the codebase style guide requires
optionC: Enough to satisfy the code review
optionD: Enough that no error can ever escape
correctAnswerText: Enough for the failures that will actually occur
explanation: Handling every theoretical failure buries the logic. Handling none means discovering them in production.

prompt: How do you choose between throwing and returning an error value?
optionA: By whether the error carries extra data
optionB: By how deep the call stack is at that point
optionC: By which the language community prefers
optionD: By whether the caller should be forced to decide
correctAnswerText: By whether the caller should be forced to decide
explanation: A returned value the caller must unwrap cannot be ignored. An exception can travel past everybody.

prompt: What does a good user-facing error message give them?
optionA: A code to give to the support team
optionB: Something they can actually do next
optionC: Reassurance that it is being fixed
optionD: An accurate description of the fault
correctAnswerText: Something they can actually do next
explanation: Retry, check the field, contact support with this id. A message with no next step is only bad news.

prompt: When is a circuit breaker worth the complexity?
optionA: When a dependency failing would take you with it
optionB: When the calls to it are expensive to make
optionC: When the dependency is outside your control
optionD: When a dependency fails more than occasionally
correctAnswerText: When a dependency failing would take you with it
explanation: It is a containment device. Where the dependency is optional, degrading gracefully is simpler and enough.

prompt: Why is error handling so often wrong in production?
optionA: The handling was added after the feature
optionB: The errors differ between environments
optionC: The failures are impossible to predict
optionD: The failure paths are the least tested code
correctAnswerText: The failure paths are the least tested code
explanation: The happy path runs a thousand times a day. The catch block may never have run before the night it matters.

prompt: A function is 80% error handling and 20% logic. What should you consider?
optionA: Adding comments to separate the two
optionB: Splitting it into two smaller functions
optionC: Moving the handling out to one boundary
optionD: Removing the least likely error cases
correctAnswerText: Moving the handling out to one boundary
explanation: Handling at a boundary keeps the logic readable, which is itself a correctness property.

prompt: Why is changing what errors a function raises a breaking change?
optionA: Callers have written code against them
optionB: The documentation becomes inaccurate
optionC: The tests will need to be rewritten
optionD: The error types are part of the signature
correctAnswerText: Callers have written code against them
explanation: The failure modes are as much part of the contract as the return type, and are far more often forgotten.

prompt: What should be logged at error level?
optionA: Something a person needs to look at
optionB: Any exception that was caught
optionC: Anything affecting a user request
optionD: Anything that did not go as planned
correctAnswerText: Something a person needs to look at
explanation: Severity is about the response required, not about how the code felt. Otherwise the level stops meaning anything.

prompt: What question should you ask of every call that can fail?
optionA: Which exception type will it raise
optionB: How likely is it to fail in practice
optionC: Should this be wrapped in a try block
optionD: What should happen here if it does
correctAnswerText: What should happen here if it does
explanation: Deciding rather than discovering. Every bad outage in this file began with somebody not asking it.

prompt: Who should you picture when writing a log line?
optionA: The person who reported the problem
optionB: Yourself, debugging it tomorrow morning
optionC: Somebody who has never seen this code
optionD: A tool that will parse it automatically
correctAnswerText: Somebody who has never seen this code
explanation: At three in the morning, without the source open. That picture produces almost every rule in this file.

prompt: What does a log level communicate?
optionA: How long the line should be kept
optionB: How much detail the line contains
optionC: Which component produced the line
optionD: How much attention the line deserves
correctAnswerText: How much attention the line deserves
explanation: It is a claim about the response required, which is why using them loosely destroys their value.

prompt: What is a structured log?
optionA: One with named fields, not just a sentence
optionB: One that follows a fixed message format
optionC: One written to a file rather than output
optionD: One that includes a timestamp and level
correctAnswerText: One with named fields, not just a sentence
explanation: Fields you can filter and aggregate on. A sentence can only be searched for text you happen to guess.

prompt: What is a correlation id for?
optionA: Recording which user made the request
optionB: Linking an error to its stack trace
optionC: Tying together the lines from one request
optionD: Identifying which server wrote the line
correctAnswerText: Tying together the lines from one request
explanation: Without it, one request’s lines are scattered among a hundred others arriving at the same moment.

prompt: What must never be written to a log?
optionA: The full text of the error raised
optionB: The duration the operation took
optionC: Identifiers of the records involved
optionD: Credentials, tokens and personal detail
correctAnswerText: Credentials, tokens and personal detail
explanation: Logs are copied, shipped and broadly readable. Anything in them should be treated as already disclosed.

prompt: What turns "failed to save" into a useful line?
optionA: Which record, and why it failed
optionB: The name of the function involved
optionC: The time the failure occurred
optionD: The severity level of the failure
correctAnswerText: Which record, and why it failed
explanation: Identifiers and cause. Without them the line confirms a problem exists and nothing more.

prompt: Where should an application write its logs?
optionA: To a file it manages and rotates itself
optionB: Directly to the central logging service
optionC: To its output, for the platform to collect
optionD: To a database table it can query later
correctAnswerText: To its output, for the platform to collect
explanation: The application should not know where logs end up. That is a deployment concern, not an application one.

prompt: What does logging everything cost?
optionA: Only the disk space the lines occupy
optionB: Nothing measurable in a modern system
optionC: Storage, ingestion and the reader’s attention
optionD: Only the time spent writing each line
correctAnswerText: Storage, ingestion and the reader’s attention
explanation: The attention cost is the one people forget, and it is the one that makes a log stop being read.

prompt: In what time zone should log timestamps be recorded?
optionA: A single absolute zone, everywhere
optionB: The local zone of each server
optionC: The zone of the user making the request
optionD: Whatever the platform defaults to
correctAnswerText: A single absolute zone, everywhere
explanation: UTC. Correlating servers in three countries during an incident is impossible if each uses local time.

prompt: What is generally worth a log line?
optionA: Entering and leaving each function
optionB: The value of each variable computed
optionC: Every query sent to the database
optionD: A decision taken or an outcome reached
correctAnswerText: A decision taken or an outcome reached
explanation: Decisions and outcomes reconstruct behaviour. A trace of every function call reconstructs nothing but noise.

prompt: Why are logs nearly useless without a correlation id under concurrency?
optionA: The timestamps are not precise enough
optionB: The servers write at different speeds
optionC: The lines arrive out of their true order
optionD: The lines of one request are mixed with others
correctAnswerText: The lines of one request are mixed with others
explanation: A hundred requests interleaved gives you a hundred stories in one column, with no way to separate them.

prompt: Why is a structured log more useful at scale?
optionA: You can filter and count on the fields
optionB: It is easier for a person to read
optionC: It takes up less space when stored
optionD: It can be written more quickly
correctAnswerText: You can filter and count on the fields
explanation: "Show me every failure for tenant 12 in the last hour" is a query on fields and a guess on sentences.

prompt: Why does logging expected outcomes at error level cause harm?
optionA: The level loses its technical meaning
optionB: Real errors are buried among them
optionC: The alerts become slower to fire
optionD: The log grows larger than necessary
correctAnswerText: Real errors are buried among them
explanation: A channel that is usually noise stops being read, and then the one line that mattered is not read either.

prompt: Why include the record id rather than just the operation name?
optionA: It shows how many records were affected
optionB: It proves the operation actually ran
optionC: It makes the line easier to search for
optionD: You can then reproduce and check the case
correctAnswerText: You can then reproduce and check the case
explanation: With the id you can go and look. Without it you know only that it happened to somebody.

prompt: Why can a debugger not replace logging in production?
optionA: You cannot pause a live system to inspect it
optionB: Debuggers are not installed on servers
optionC: The problem may not be reproducible
optionD: The code is compiled differently there
correctAnswerText: You cannot pause a live system to inspect it
explanation: And the failure already happened. Logs are the only record of a moment you cannot return to.

prompt: Why might a high-traffic service log only some successful requests?
optionA: The storage system cannot accept them all
optionB: The logging would slow the service down
optionC: The volume would cost more than it is worth
optionD: Successful requests contain no information
correctAnswerText: The volume would cost more than it is worth
explanation: Sample the ordinary, keep every failure. You lose little and the bill falls by an order of magnitude.

prompt: Why are logs a common source of data leaks?
optionA: They are kept for longer than the data
optionB: They are widely readable and rarely reviewed
optionC: They are stored without any encryption
optionD: They are copied to third-party services
correctAnswerText: They are widely readable and rarely reviewed
explanation: Access that would never be granted to the database is routinely granted to the logs of it.

prompt: Why log the original exception rather than a summary of it?
optionA: The detail you discard is what identifies the fault
optionB: The summary may be worded inaccurately
optionC: The original is shorter than a summary
optionD: The summary text cannot be searched reliably
correctAnswerText: The detail you discard is what identifies the fault
explanation: Whoever wrote the summary knew what they expected to go wrong. The actual failure was something else.

prompt: Why should every service use the same name for the user identifier?
optionA: It reduces the size of each log line
optionB: It makes the code easier to review
optionC: It is required by logging libraries
optionD: One query can then span all of them
correctAnswerText: One query can then span all of them
explanation: userId, user_id and uid in three services means three queries and one that you forget.

prompt: Why not keep logs indefinitely?
optionA: Cost, and the liability of holding the data
optionB: Old logs become impossible to search
optionC: The format changes between versions
optionD: They lose relevance after a few days
correctAnswerText: Cost, and the liability of holding the data
explanation: Every log line containing personal data is a record you are responsible for until you delete it.

prompt: An order fails to save. What should the log line say?
optionA: That saving an order has failed again
optionB: The stack trace from where it failed
optionC: The order id, the reason, and the operation
optionD: The full order object as it was received
correctAnswerText: The order id, the reason, and the operation
explanation: The whole object risks logging personal data and buries the point. Identify it and say what went wrong.

prompt: A user submits an invalid form. At what level does that belong?
optionA: Error, since the request failed
optionB: Information, or nothing at all
optionC: Warning, since something was wrong
optionD: Debug, since it helps development
correctAnswerText: Information, or nothing at all
explanation: Nothing is broken. A form rejecting bad input is the form doing exactly what it is for.

prompt: A request crosses three services. How do you keep the logs connected?
optionA: Have each service log the caller name
optionB: Pass the same id along with each call
optionC: Use the user id as the connecting field
optionD: Match them on the timestamp ranges
correctAnswerText: Pass the same id along with each call
explanation: Generated at the edge, passed in a header, attached to every line. The user id cannot separate two of their requests.

prompt: You want to log enough about a user to debug. What do you record?
optionA: Their identifier, not their details
optionB: Their full record, minus the password
optionC: Their email, which is easy to search
optionD: Their name, so support can find them
correctAnswerText: Their identifier, not their details
explanation: An opaque id is searchable, resolvable by anyone entitled to, and worthless to anybody who is not.

prompt: A job processes fifty thousand records. What should it log?
optionA: One line for every record processed
optionB: One line when the job starts and ends
optionC: A progress line every thousand records
optionD: A summary, plus each individual failure
correctAnswerText: A summary, plus each individual failure
explanation: Counts and durations plus the exceptions. Fifty thousand success lines cost money and tell you nothing.

prompt: What is worth logging when a service starts?
optionA: The hardware it is running on
optionB: Every dependency it has loaded
optionC: Its version and its effective settings
optionD: The time it took to start up
correctAnswerText: Its version and its effective settings
explanation: Half of all incidents begin with the wrong version or the wrong configuration. Print it, with secrets masked.

prompt: An error is logged at every layer as it travels up. What is wrong with that?
optionA: The later lines lose the original detail
optionB: The levels will be inconsistent
optionC: The log grows faster than expected
optionD: One failure appears as five separate ones
correctAnswerText: One failure appears as five separate ones
explanation: Log where it is handled. Add context on the way up; write the line once, at the place that decides.

prompt: Why record how long an external call took?
optionA: It helps estimate the server capacity
optionB: Slowness is a failure you cannot otherwise see
optionC: It proves the call was actually made
optionD: It shows which service was slowest
correctAnswerText: Slowness is a failure you cannot otherwise see
explanation: A call that succeeds in nine seconds is broken, and nothing in a success-or-failure log would say so.

prompt: You need debug detail from production for ten minutes. What is the good way?
optionA: Reproduce the issue in staging instead
optionB: Deploy a build with debug enabled
optionC: Raise the level without redeploying
optionD: Add temporary log lines and deploy
correctAnswerText: Raise the level without redeploying
explanation: A runtime switch, ideally scoped to one component. Deploying to gather evidence changes the thing you are studying.

prompt: How do you keep log fields consistent across a team?
optionA: A documented naming convention
optionB: A shared logger that supplies them
optionC: A review checklist item for logs
optionD: A linter rule on the log calls
correctAnswerText: A shared logger that supplies them
explanation: Make the consistent thing the easy thing. Conventions in a document drift within two sprints.

prompt: During an incident the only relevant line reads "error in handler". What is missing?
optionA: The name of the server that logged it
optionB: The timestamp of when it occurred
optionC: Which request, which record, and what failed
optionD: The severity level of the failure
correctAnswerText: Which request, which record, and what failed
explanation: It confirms something broke. Everything you would need to act is what was left out.

prompt: You cannot tell which log lines belong to the failing request. What was not done?
optionA: The lines were not written in order
optionB: No id was attached and carried through
optionC: The clocks were not synchronised
optionD: The level was set too high to capture
correctAnswerText: No id was attached and carried through
explanation: Under load this makes an otherwise complete log unusable, which is why it is not an optional nicety.

prompt: A team stopped looking at the error log two years ago. What probably caused that?
optionA: The logging tool became too slow
optionB: It filled with things needing no action
optionC: The errors were all already known
optionD: The team grew and nobody owned it
correctAnswerText: It filled with things needing no action
explanation: Every channel that cries wolf gets muted. The cure is making error mean error again, not asking harder.

prompt: A debugging change logged full request bodies for a month. What is the consequence?
optionA: The log retention policy was exceeded
optionB: The logging bill is higher than expected
optionC: A month of personal data now sits in the logs
optionD: The relevant lines are harder to find
correctAnswerText: A month of personal data now sits in the logs
explanation: All are true and the first is a reportable problem, not a cleanup task. It has to be purged and disclosed.

prompt: A failing dependency produced two million log lines in an hour. What went wrong in the code?
optionA: The dependency returned large errors
optionB: A retry loop logged on every attempt
optionC: The log rotation stopped working
optionD: The log level was set to debug
correctAnswerText: A retry loop logged on every attempt
explanation: Log the first, count the rest, log the summary. Logging inside a tight retry loop is its own incident.

prompt: Lines written from a background task have no request id. Why?
optionA: The logger was configured entirely separately
optionB: The request had already completed
optionC: The task runs on a different server
optionD: The context did not travel across the boundary
correctAnswerText: The context did not travel across the boundary
explanation: The id must be passed into the job explicitly, because whatever carried it implicitly does not cross that line.

prompt: A response appears to be logged before its request. How?
optionA: The lines were written out of order
optionB: The timestamp is added on ingestion
optionC: The two servers’ clocks are not in step
optionD: The log system reordered the entries
correctAnswerText: The two servers’ clocks are not in step
explanation: A few seconds of clock drift makes causality unreadable, which is why time synchronisation is an ops requirement.

prompt: A service slowed noticeably after verbose logging was enabled. What is happening?
optionA: The extra lines fill the memory buffer
optionB: The log storage is rejecting the volume
optionC: Writing and serialising the lines costs time
optionD: The logger is retrying failed writes
correctAnswerText: Writing and serialising the lines costs time
explanation: Especially synchronous writes on the request path. Logging is I/O and it is not free.

prompt: The log records "failed to process" with no stack trace. What was the coding mistake?
optionA: The logger was called at the wrong level
optionB: Only the message was passed to the logger
optionC: The stack trace was too long to store
optionD: The exception was caught too early
correctAnswerText: Only the message was passed to the logger
explanation: Logging error.message rather than the error. The one line naming the failing call is the part discarded.

prompt: Logs exist but answering a question takes half an hour of scrolling. What is the real problem?
optionA: They were never made searchable by field
optionB: They are spread across several servers
optionC: They are retained for too short a time
optionD: They contain too much detail per line
correctAnswerText: They were never made searchable by field
explanation: Unstructured text in a big pile is an archive, not a diagnostic tool. The fields are what make it one.

prompt: How do you decide how much to log?
optionA: By what the logging standard requires
optionB: By the questions you will need to answer
optionC: By how complex the component is
optionD: By how much the storage budget allows
correctAnswerText: By the questions you will need to answer
explanation: Work backwards from the incident. "Why did this user see that?" tells you exactly which fields to record.

prompt: Your logging bill exceeds your compute bill. What is the right first move?
optionA: Find what is producing the volume
optionB: Move to a cheaper provider
optionC: Reduce the retention period
optionD: Raise the minimum log level
correctAnswerText: Find what is producing the volume
explanation: It is nearly always a handful of lines in hot paths. Blanket cuts lose the lines you actually needed.

prompt: When is a metric the better answer than a log line?
optionA: When several services produce the event
optionB: When the data must be kept long term
optionC: When the event happens very frequently
optionD: When you care about the rate, not the case
correctAnswerText: When you care about the rate, not the case
explanation: "How many failed?" is a metric. "Why did this one fail?" is a log. Using either for the other is expensive.

prompt: What is the best time to improve your logging?
optionA: During a quarterly review of all the code
optionB: Before a major feature is released
optionC: When the logging budget is being set
optionD: Just after an incident, while the gaps are fresh
correctAnswerText: Just after an incident, while the gaps are fresh
explanation: "I wish I had known X" is a precise specification, and it is only available for about a day afterwards.

prompt: What should decide how long logs are kept?
optionA: How long the data itself is kept
optionB: How much storage you can afford
optionC: How far back you would realistically look
optionD: What the provider retains by default
correctAnswerText: How far back you would realistically look
explanation: Balanced against the liability of holding it. Most debugging looks back days, not months.

prompt: When should logging be thought about?
optionA: When the monitoring is being set up
optionB: During the code review of the change
optionC: After the first production problem
optionD: While writing the code, as an output of it
correctAnswerText: While writing the code, as an output of it
explanation: Logs added after an incident help the next one. Logs written with the code help the first one.

prompt: How does an audit log differ from a diagnostic log?
optionA: It is produced by a different component
optionB: It is a durable record, not a debugging aid
optionC: It contains more detail about each action
optionD: It is written at a higher severity level
correctAnswerText: It is a durable record, not a debugging aid
explanation: Different retention, different access, different tamper expectations. Mixing them serves neither purpose well.

prompt: If you sample logs, what should never be sampled away?
optionA: Requests that took a long time
optionB: Failures and anything unusual
optionC: Requests from paying customers
optionD: The first request of each session
correctAnswerText: Failures and anything unusual
explanation: Sampling the ordinary is nearly free. Sampling the rare removes exactly the cases you kept logs for.

prompt: How do you tell whether your logging is good?
optionA: By how consistent the format is
optionB: By whether every component writes some
optionC: By how many lines it produces a day
optionD: By how fast it answers a real question
correctAnswerText: By how fast it answers a real question
explanation: Time to answer. The only test that matters, and the only one you can run during a real incident.

prompt: What is the test of a single log line?
optionA: Does it record everything that happened
optionB: Does it follow the team’s log format
optionC: Could a stranger act on it without the code
optionD: Is it at the appropriate severity level
correctAnswerText: Could a stranger act on it without the code
explanation: Every other rule here is a way of passing that test, and it is worth applying as you type the line.

prompt: What is the difference between monitoring and observability?
optionA: One is automated and the other is manual
optionB: One is for servers, the other for applications
optionC: One watches known things, one answers new questions
optionD: One uses metrics and the other uses logs
correctAnswerText: One watches known things, one answers new questions
explanation: Monitoring checks what you predicted. Observability is whether you can investigate what you did not.

prompt: What is a metric?
optionA: A threshold that triggers an alert
optionB: A summary written after an incident
optionC: A record of one thing that happened
optionD: A number measured repeatedly over time
correctAnswerText: A number measured repeatedly over time
explanation: Cheap to store and aggregate because it is just numbers. That is what makes it suit rates and trends.

prompt: What does a distributed trace show?
optionA: One request’s path and timing across services
optionB: The dependencies between the services
optionC: Every request the system handled that hour
optionD: The log lines produced by one service
correctAnswerText: One request’s path and timing across services
explanation: Where the time went, service by service. It answers "which hop was slow" in one picture.

prompt: What should an alert mean?
optionA: A component has stopped responding
optionB: A person needs to do something now
optionC: Something unusual has been detected
optionD: A measurement crossed its threshold
correctAnswerText: A person needs to do something now
explanation: If nobody needs to act, it is a dashboard entry. Calling it an alert teaches people to ignore alerts.

prompt: What does the 99th percentile response time tell you?
optionA: What the slowest one in a hundred experienced
optionB: How many responses were unusually slow
optionC: The slowest response that was recorded
optionD: The average of the slowest one percent
correctAnswerText: What the slowest one in a hundred experienced
explanation: The experience at the bad end of the distribution, which is where the complaints come from.

prompt: What should you usually alert on?
optionA: An unusual pattern in the traffic
optionB: A component behaving differently
optionC: Something a user would notice
optionD: A resource nearing its limit
correctAnswerText: Something a user would notice
explanation: Symptoms, not causes. There are endless causes and only a handful of things users actually feel.

prompt: What is a dashboard best used for?
optionA: Replacing the need for alerting
optionB: Answering a specific question quickly
optionC: Displaying every metric collected
optionD: Recording the history of incidents
correctAnswerText: Answering a specific question quickly
explanation: A dashboard with forty charts answers nothing. One built around a question answers it in seconds.

prompt: What should a health check report?
optionA: Whether the whole system is working
optionB: Whether the process is still running
optionC: Whether the last request succeeded
optionD: Whether this instance can do its job
correctAnswerText: Whether this instance can do its job
explanation: Its own ability to serve. Reporting on shared dependencies makes one outage fail every instance at once.

prompt: What are the first things to measure about a service?
optionA: Its traffic, errors, latency and saturation
optionB: Its users, sessions, requests and revenue
optionC: Its memory, CPU, disk and network use
optionD: Its uptime, restarts, version and age
correctAnswerText: Its traffic, errors, latency and saturation
explanation: The four signals that describe what users experience. Resource use is a cause, and comes second.

prompt: What is a service level objective?
optionA: A limit on how much downtime is allowed
optionB: A target for how good the service should be
optionC: A measure of how the service performed
optionD: A promise made to the paying customers
correctAnswerText: A target for how good the service should be
explanation: A chosen target, such as 99.9% of requests under 300ms. It makes "good enough" a number you can check.

prompt: Why is the average response time a poor health measure?
optionA: It is calculated over too long a period
optionB: A small group can be suffering invisibly
optionC: It does not include the failed requests
optionD: It changes too slowly to be useful
correctAnswerText: A small group can be suffering invisibly
explanation: Ninety-nine fast responses and one of thirty seconds averages well and has one very unhappy user.

prompt: Why is alerting on high CPU usually a mistake?
optionA: CPU limits differ between machines
optionB: It changes too quickly to alert on
optionC: It may be fine, and low CPU may not be
optionD: CPU is difficult to measure accurately
correctAnswerText: It may be fine, and low CPU may not be
explanation: A busy server doing its job is healthy. The question is whether requests are being served, not how hard it works.

prompt: Why is a noisy alert worse than no alert?
optionA: It wakes people who then work poorly
optionB: It costs money on every notification
optionC: The real one is dismissed along with the rest
optionD: It hides the metric it was watching
correctAnswerText: The real one is dismissed along with the rest
explanation: Same shape as a flaky test or a red build that means nothing. Trust is the resource being spent.

prompt: Why is predicting what to monitor not enough?
optionA: Monitoring every case would cost too much
optionB: There are too many things to monitor them all
optionC: The worst outages are the ones nobody predicted
optionD: Predictions become outdated as code changes
correctAnswerText: The worst outages are the ones nobody predicted
explanation: Every serious incident begins with a question nobody thought to prepare a dashboard for.

prompt: Why is putting a user id on a metric a problem?
optionA: It makes the metric less accurate
optionB: It creates one series per user
optionC: It exposes personal data in charts
optionD: It slows down each measurement
correctAnswerText: It creates one series per user
explanation: High cardinality. A million users becomes a million time series, and the metrics system falls over.

prompt: Why do traces matter more once a system is split into services?
optionA: The services may be owned by other teams
optionB: The time is spread across places you cannot see
optionC: There are more log lines to read through
optionD: Each service has its own monitoring set up
correctAnswerText: The time is spread across places you cannot see
explanation: Every service reports itself as fast and the request takes four seconds. The trace shows where they went.

prompt: Why is a 100% availability target a bad objective?
optionA: It is impossible to measure precisely
optionB: It cannot account for planned maintenance
optionC: It costs more than the last fraction is worth
optionD: It would prevent all deployments
correctAnswerText: It costs more than the last fraction is worth
explanation: Each nine costs several times the last. Choosing the target is choosing what to spend, deliberately.

prompt: Why is a number useless without knowing what is normal?
optionA: Different services use different scales
optionB: The number changes throughout the day
optionC: The number may be measured incorrectly
optionD: You cannot tell whether it is a problem
correctAnswerText: You cannot tell whether it is a problem
explanation: Four hundred errors an hour is catastrophic for one service and a quiet Tuesday for another.

prompt: Why check a service from outside your own network?
optionA: It confirms the service is genuinely running
optionB: External checks are more accurate than internal ones
optionC: Everything inside can be fine while users cannot reach it
optionD: It measures the true response time better
correctAnswerText: Everything inside can be fine while users cannot reach it
explanation: DNS, certificates, load balancers, the CDN. All invisible from inside and all capable of taking you offline.

prompt: Why is instrumentation part of writing a feature?
optionA: The monitoring team cannot add it later
optionB: It is easier to write while the code is fresh
optionC: It is required before a feature can ship
optionD: You cannot add it once the incident starts
correctAnswerText: You cannot add it once the incident starts
explanation: Deploying instrumentation during an outage is slow and changes the system you are trying to observe.

prompt: For a checkout service, what is the best single alert?
optionA: The database connection count rising
optionB: The rate of failed checkouts rising
optionC: The CPU usage passing eighty percent
optionD: The number of running instances falling
correctAnswerText: The rate of failed checkouts rising
explanation: The others are sometimes causes of it. Only the first is guaranteed to matter when it fires.

prompt: Which latency figures are worth putting on a dashboard?
optionA: A middle one and a tail one together
optionB: The average over the last five minutes
optionC: The fastest and slowest recorded
optionD: The slowest request in the period
correctAnswerText: A middle one and a tail one together
explanation: The median says what it is normally like; the 99th says whether anybody is having a terrible time.

prompt: What makes a good label on a metric?
optionA: A small, fixed set of possible values
optionB: A value copied from the request body
optionC: A value that identifies each request
optionD: A value that changes over time
correctAnswerText: A small, fixed set of possible values
explanation: Endpoint, status class, region. Anything unbounded belongs in a log or a trace, never on a metric.

prompt: What should every alert link to?
optionA: The dashboard showing the metric
optionB: The list of recent deployments
optionC: A note saying what to check and do
optionD: The service’s source repository
correctAnswerText: A note saying what to check and do
explanation: The person woken at 3am may never have seen this service. A runbook is the difference between minutes and hours.

prompt: Should a health check test the shared database?
optionA: Yes, but only on every tenth check
optionB: Yes, the service cannot work without it
optionC: No — one outage would then remove every instance
optionD: No, health checks should be very fast
correctAnswerText: No — one outage would then remove every instance
explanation: Every instance fails the check, the platform removes them all, and a degraded system becomes a dead one.

prompt: Your objective allows 0.1% failures and you are using half of it. What does that mean?
optionA: You have room to keep shipping changes
optionB: You should stop deploying immediately
optionC: The objective was set too loosely
optionD: The service is behaving abnormally
correctAnswerText: You have room to keep shipping changes
explanation: That is the point of a budget: it converts reliability into a resource you can choose to spend on speed.

prompt: What makes it fastest to tell whether a release caused a problem?
optionA: Deployments marked on the metric graphs
optionB: A notification sent on each deploy
optionC: A list of who deployed and when
optionD: A changelog kept for each release
correctAnswerText: Deployments marked on the metric graphs
explanation: A vertical line where the error rate turns upward answers in a second what log archaeology answers in an hour.

prompt: Every technical metric is green and orders have stopped. What should have been watched?
optionA: The latency of the payment provider
optionB: The number of orders being placed
optionC: The queue depth in the order service
optionD: The error rate on the checkout page
correctAnswerText: The number of orders being placed
explanation: A business outcome catches failures no technical metric predicted, including the ones caused by a config change.

prompt: How should an alert threshold be chosen?
optionA: From a round number that sounds safe
optionB: From what other teams use for theirs
optionC: From what the service normally does
optionD: From the limits of the hardware
correctAnswerText: From what the service normally does
explanation: Look at a month of data first. Thresholds invented at a whiteboard fire constantly or never.

prompt: An alert fires and clears every few minutes. What is the usual fix?
optionA: Raise the threshold until it stops firing
optionB: Send the alert to a quieter channel
optionC: Require the condition to hold for a period
optionD: Check the metric less frequently
correctAnswerText: Require the condition to hold for a period
explanation: A brief spike is not an incident. Requiring five minutes of sustained breach removes most flapping.

prompt: A team receives sixty alerts a day and missed a real outage. What is the cause?
optionA: The team is too small for the number of services
optionB: The outage alert was sent to the wrong channel
optionC: Alerts that needed no action trained them to ignore
optionD: The alerting system delivered them too slowly
correctAnswerText: Alerts that needed no action trained them to ignore
explanation: Sixty a day is not sixty problems. The fix is deleting alerts, which teams find surprisingly hard.

prompt: Users complain of slowness and the average latency chart is flat. What would you check?
optionA: The high percentiles, and whether one group is affected
optionB: Whether the measurements are being recorded
optionC: Whether the complaints are about something else
optionD: Whether the chart is showing the right service
correctAnswerText: The high percentiles, and whether one group is affected
explanation: The mean absorbs a suffering minority. Break it down by percentile, and by tenant or region.

prompt: A slow database made the platform terminate every instance of a service. Why?
optionA: The platform scaled down on low traffic
optionB: The check timed out before responding
optionC: The health check tested the database too
optionD: The instances ran out of memory waiting
correctAnswerText: The health check tested the database too
explanation: A shared dependency inside a per-instance check turns degradation into total loss, automatically.

prompt: The metrics backend became unusable after a release. What was likely added?
optionA: A label with an unbounded set of values
optionB: A metric recorded far too frequently
optionC: A dashboard querying too much history
optionD: A new service reporting its own metrics
correctAnswerText: A label with an unbounded set of values
explanation: A request id or a URL with ids in it. One line of code can create millions of series.

prompt: A background job silently stopped running for a week. What was missing?
optionA: A log line each time it ran
optionB: A retry when the job failed
optionC: A dashboard showing the job
optionD: An alert on the job not completing
correctAnswerText: An alert on the job not completing
explanation: Absence is the hardest thing to notice. Alerting on "this should have happened by now" is what catches it.

prompt: Every internal dashboard is green and customers cannot load the site. What would you suspect?
optionA: The internal metrics being misconfigured
optionB: The dashboards showing stale data
optionC: A problem affecting only some customers
optionD: Something between the users and your servers
correctAnswerText: Something between the users and your servers
explanation: An expired certificate, a DNS change, a CDN fault. All invisible to anything measuring from inside.

prompt: One of twenty instances is failing every request and the overall error rate looks acceptable. What is wrong with the view?
optionA: The error rate is measured over too long
optionB: The traffic is not evenly distributed
optionC: The instances are aggregated into one number
optionD: The failing instance stopped reporting
correctAnswerText: The instances are aggregated into one number
explanation: Five percent of users are completely broken and the summary reads 5%. Break down by instance.

prompt: A 30-second outage does not appear on a chart averaged over five minutes. Why?
optionA: The metric was not collected then
optionB: The chart only shows completed periods
optionC: The outage was shorter than the timeout
optionD: The averaging smoothed it away entirely
correctAnswerText: The averaging smoothed it away entirely
explanation: Resolution decides what you can see. Brief, repeated outages are invisible at coarse granularity.

prompt: No alerts fired for three days. What is the reassuring reading and the worrying one?
optionA: Either the system is stable, or it is unused
optionB: Either traffic is low, or the thresholds are high
optionC: Either nothing broke, or the alerting is broken
optionD: Either the team fixed things, or nobody looked
correctAnswerText: Either nothing broke, or the alerting is broken
explanation: Silence is ambiguous, which is why a heartbeat alert that fires if nothing is heard is worth having.

prompt: A dashboard has sixty charts and nobody uses it during incidents. Why?
optionA: It covers too many services at once
optionB: It answers no question in particular
optionC: The charts are too small to read
optionD: It takes too long to load the data
correctAnswerText: It answers no question in particular
explanation: Built by adding every available metric rather than by asking what somebody would need to know.

prompt: A service has no monitoring at all. What do you add first?
optionA: Dashboards for each internal component
optionB: Whether users are being served successfully
optionC: Resource usage across all the machines
optionD: Detailed traces of every request path
correctAnswerText: Whether users are being served successfully
explanation: One number that says whether the product works. Everything else is for explaining why it does not.

prompt: Who should decide the reliability target for a service?
optionA: The largest customers who depend on it
optionB: The engineering team that operates it
optionC: Whatever the industry standard suggests
optionD: The business, once told what each level costs
correctAnswerText: The business, once told what each level costs
explanation: It is a spending decision. Engineering’s job is pricing the options, not choosing among them alone.

prompt: Observability tooling now costs more than the infrastructure. What is the right reaction?
optionA: Move to a cheaper observability vendor
optionB: Work out which data actually gets used
optionC: Reduce retention across the board
optionD: Accept it as the cost of reliability
correctAnswerText: Work out which data actually gets used
explanation: Most of the spend is usually on data nobody has queried. Find that before cutting indiscriminately.

prompt: What justifies waking somebody at three in the morning?
optionA: Anything the on-call rota was set up for
optionB: Anything affecting the production system
optionC: Something that will get worse if left until morning
optionD: Any breach at all of the service level objective
correctAnswerText: Something that will get worse if left until morning
explanation: The test is whether waiting costs more than the sleep. Most things can wait, and a page should be rare.

prompt: How do you tell whether a system is genuinely observable?
optionA: It has dashboards for every component
optionB: Its alerts cover all the known failures
optionC: You can answer a new question without deploying
optionD: It produces metrics, logs and traces
correctAnswerText: You can answer a new question without deploying
explanation: Having the three kinds of data is not the property. Being able to interrogate them is.

prompt: What is the most valuable monitoring question after an incident?
optionA: Who was responsible for the change
optionB: What would have told us sooner
optionC: How long did it take to recover
optionD: What caused the failure to happen
correctAnswerText: What would have told us sooner
explanation: Detection time is the part monitoring can improve, and the answer is available only right afterwards.

prompt: Why is one business metric worth many technical ones?
optionA: It requires no instrumentation to collect
optionB: It catches failures nobody predicted
optionC: It is easier for the business to read
optionD: It changes less often than technical ones
correctAnswerText: It catches failures nobody predicted
explanation: Signups falling to zero is a real alert whatever the cause, including causes no technical metric covers.

prompt: How do you know your alerting actually works?
optionA: By checking that alerts fired during incidents
optionB: By counting how many alerts fire each week
optionC: By reviewing the alert definitions regularly
optionD: By deliberately triggering it from time to time
correctAnswerText: By deliberately triggering it from time to time
explanation: An untested alert path is a hope. The first time you find out it was misconfigured should not be an outage.

prompt: How much monitoring is enough?
optionA: Enough to detect and explain what happens
optionB: Enough to cover every component in use
optionC: Enough to satisfy the reliability target
optionD: As much as the tooling budget permits
correctAnswerText: Enough to detect and explain what happens
explanation: Two jobs: know something is wrong, and find out why. Data serving neither is data you are paying to ignore.

prompt: What one rule prevents most monitoring mistakes?
optionA: Keep the dashboards up to date always
optionB: Set thresholds below the known limits
optionC: Alert on what users feel, investigate the causes
optionD: Measure everything that the system exposes
correctAnswerText: Alert on what users feel, investigate the causes
