explanation: The queue did what it promised. The consumer assumed exactly-once delivery, which it never had.

prompt: A small team runs twelve services and every feature touches five. What happened?
optionA: The services were not documented properly
optionB: The team grew more slowly than planned
optionC: The boundaries were drawn before they were known
optionD: The services should share more libraries
correctAnswerText: The boundaries were drawn before they were known
explanation: A wrong boundary inside one codebase is a refactor. Across a network it is a coordinated multi-repo change.

prompt: The database collapses each time the cache is cleared. Why?
optionA: The database restarts when the cache does
optionB: The cache clearing locks the database
optionC: Every request misses and queries at once
optionD: The cache rebuild is a heavy operation
correctAnswerText: Every request misses and queries at once
explanation: The database was sized for a high hit rate. An empty cache presents it with the full, unabsorbed load.

prompt: Two events on different servers are recorded in the wrong order. Why is this hard to fix?
optionA: The database stores times imprecisely
optionB: The events were written too quickly
optionC: The servers are in different regions
optionD: There is no single clock they both share
correctAnswerText: There is no single clock they both share
explanation: Ordering across machines needs a logical scheme, not a timestamp. Clocks drift and cannot be trusted for this.

prompt: A system sized exactly for its peak load fell over during a normal day. Why?
optionA: The traffic pattern changed over time
optionB: The peak load had been underestimated
optionC: The measurements were taken incorrectly
optionD: There was no room for a failure or a spike
correctAnswerText: There was no room for a failure or a spike
explanation: Lose one instance of four and the other three must carry 133% of their share. Headroom is not waste.

prompt: A request depends on five services each 99.9% available. What is its availability?
optionA: Roughly 99.5%, since the odds multiply
optionB: Unknowable without their failure patterns
optionC: Still 99.9%, as they are independent
optionD: Roughly 99.98%, since they back each other
correctAnswerText: Roughly 99.5%, since the odds multiply
explanation: Dependencies in series multiply their failure probabilities. Five nines of dependencies is not five nines.

prompt: A new product expects ten thousand users. What should it be built as?
optionA: Several services from the beginning
optionB: A design that can shard when needed
optionC: Whatever the team knows best
optionD: One application and one database
correctAnswerText: One application and one database
explanation: Ten thousand users is nothing. Distributing early buys complexity now against a scale that may never come.

prompt: Which data can safely be eventually consistent?
optionA: The stock level at the point of sale
optionB: The balance shown before a transfer
optionC: A follower count on a profile page
optionD: The permissions on a shared document
correctAnswerText: A follower count on a profile page
explanation: Consistency requirements are per-field, not per-system. Most data tolerates a few seconds; some does not.

prompt: What makes a system design answer convincing?
optionA: Using the well-known standard patterns
optionB: Naming the trade-off each choice makes
optionC: Handling the largest plausible scale
optionD: Covering every component in the system
correctAnswerText: Naming the trade-off each choice makes
explanation: Every choice costs something. An answer with no cost named has not been thought about properly.

prompt: What question should be asked of every component in a design?
optionA: What happens to everything else when it fails
optionB: How many requests per second it handles
optionC: Which team is responsible for running it
optionD: How it will be deployed and updated
correctAnswerText: What happens to everything else when it fails
explanation: At scale something is always failing. A design that assumes everything is up describes a system you will not have.

prompt: Why does cost belong in a system design discussion?
optionA: Cheaper systems are simpler to operate
optionB: A design nobody can afford is not a design
optionC: Cost correlates with the complexity
optionD: Budgets are set before the design starts
correctAnswerText: A design nobody can afford is not a design
explanation: Multi-region active-active is technically superior and sometimes twenty times the bill for a marginal gain.

prompt: Is a single deployable application an outdated design?
optionA: No — it is correct for most systems
optionB: Yes, services are the modern approach
optionC: Yes, unless the team is very small
optionD: No, but only for internal tools
correctAnswerText: No — it is correct for most systems
explanation: A well-organised single application avoids every distributed problem in this file, and most products never outgrow it.

prompt: How do you design for a scale you may never reach?
optionA: Choose technologies that scale automatically
optionB: Document the plan for when scale arrives
optionC: Keep the boundaries clean, not the machinery ready
optionD: Build the distributed version from the start
correctAnswerText: Keep the boundaries clean, not the machinery ready
explanation: Clean seams make the future split cheap. Building the split now pays for it whether or not it is needed.

prompt: A design is built for a million requests per second. What should you ask?
optionA: How long it took to design
optionB: Which technologies it uses
optionC: Whether the budget allows it
optionD: Where that number came from
correctAnswerText: Where that number came from
explanation: Very often it came from nowhere. An unexamined number can justify years of unnecessary complexity.

prompt: What is often left out of a system design?
optionA: How the data will be modelled
optionB: How the load will be distributed
optionC: How it will be operated and debugged
optionD: How the services will communicate
correctAnswerText: How it will be operated and debugged
explanation: Deployment, monitoring, on-call, recovery. A design that cannot be run is not finished, only drawn.

prompt: What is the question underneath most system design decisions?
optionA: How the components ought to be separated out
optionB: Which technology best fits this problem
optionC: How many machines will be needed here
optionD: Where does the state live, and what if it is lost
correctAnswerText: Where does the state live, and what if it is lost
explanation: Stateless parts are easy. Every hard problem in this file — replication, sharding, consistency — is about state.

prompt: What does NoSQL describe?
optionA: Databases that do not enforce a schema
optionB: Databases that cannot be queried with SQL
optionC: Several kinds of store that are not relational
optionD: A single alternative to relational databases
correctAnswerText: Several kinds of store that are not relational
explanation: A category rather than a technology. A document store and a graph store have almost nothing in common.

prompt: What does a document store hold?
optionA: Rows and columns without a fixed schema
optionB: Self-contained records with nested structure
optionC: Files uploaded by the application users
optionD: Text indexed for searching by keyword
correctAnswerText: Self-contained records with nested structure
explanation: The nesting is the point. An order with its lines inside it is one read rather than a join.

prompt: What can a key-value store do?
optionA: Search the values by their contents
optionB: Join two collections on a shared field
optionC: Filter records by any of their fields
optionD: Fetch a value when given its exact key
correctAnswerText: Fetch a value when given its exact key
explanation: One operation, extremely fast. Everything it cannot do is why it is not a general-purpose database.

prompt: What is a graph database good at?
optionA: Following relationships many steps deep
optionB: Storing very large volumes of records
optionC: Aggregating numbers across a dataset
optionD: Serving reads with very low latency
correctAnswerText: Following relationships many steps deep
explanation: "Friends of friends of friends" is one traversal here and three increasingly painful joins in SQL.

prompt: What is a wide-column store designed for?
optionA: Very large volumes written at high rates
optionB: Records with deeply nested structures
optionC: Data that changes shape frequently
optionD: Queries that join several collections
correctAnswerText: Very large volumes written at high rates
explanation: Time series, event logs, sensor data. Enormous write throughput, with the query flexibility given away.

prompt: What does "schemaless" actually mean?
optionA: The structure can never be changed
optionB: The application holds the schema instead
optionC: The records have no structure at all
optionD: The database infers the schema itself
correctAnswerText: The application holds the schema instead
explanation: Somebody still assumes a shape. The question is only whether anything checks it before the data is written.

prompt: Why is duplicated data often deliberate in a document store?
optionA: It makes the records easier to read
optionB: It reduces the total storage needed
optionC: It lets one read answer the whole query
optionD: It keeps the collections independent
correctAnswerText: It lets one read answer the whole query
explanation: Storage is cheap and joins are expensive or unavailable. The cost is keeping the copies in step.

prompt: What should you know before designing a NoSQL data model?
optionA: The relationships between the records
optionB: The queries the application will make
optionC: The volume of data to be stored
optionD: The entities the business deals with
correctAnswerText: The queries the application will make
explanation: The reversal from relational thinking. You shape the data around the access pattern, not the domain.

prompt: What is often weaker in a NoSQL store than a relational one?
optionA: The speed of writing a single record
optionB: The number of records it can hold
optionC: The ability to store nested data
optionD: Transactions spanning several records
correctAnswerText: Transactions spanning several records
explanation: Many guarantee atomicity within one document and nothing across two, which shapes the whole model.

prompt: What should the default data store usually be?
optionA: A document database
optionB: A relational database
optionC: Whatever the team knows
optionD: Whichever scales furthest
correctAnswerText: A relational database
explanation: Flexible queries, real transactions, decades of tooling. Moving away from it should be a decision with evidence.

prompt: Why does NoSQL modelling start from the queries?
optionA: The store cannot index arbitrary fields
optionB: A wrong shape cannot be rescued by a join
optionC: The queries are simpler to write down
optionD: The entities change more often than queries
correctAnswerText: A wrong shape cannot be rescued by a join
explanation: In SQL a new question is a new query. Here it may be a new collection and a migration of everything.

prompt: What is the hidden cost of a database that accepts any shape?
optionA: The records take up more storage space
optionB: The database cannot index the fields
optionC: The queries run more slowly over time
optionD: Every reader must handle every past shape
correctAnswerText: Every reader must handle every past shape
explanation: Three years of format changes all still present. The migration you skipped is paid in every read path.

prompt: What is the price of embedding a copy of a user’s name in every order?
optionA: The orders cannot be queried by name
optionB: Renaming means updating every copy
optionC: The user record becomes redundant
optionD: The orders take longer to write
correctAnswerText: Renaming means updating every copy
explanation: Sometimes correct — the name on a past order arguably should not change. That has to be a decision.

prompt: Why is a key-value store so fast?
optionA: It keeps all of the data in memory
optionB: It uses a more efficient storage format
optionC: It only supports the one cheap operation
optionD: It does not need to check the data
correctAnswerText: It only supports the one cheap operation
explanation: Speed bought by refusing to do anything else. Each capability a database adds costs some of it.

prompt: Why does the lack of multi-record transactions shape the data model?
optionA: Things that change together must live together
optionB: Each write must be retried until it succeeds
optionC: Records must be written in a fixed order
optionD: The application must lock records itself
correctAnswerText: Things that change together must live together
explanation: It is the strongest argument for embedding. If two things must change atomically, they need to be one document.

prompt: Why do many NoSQL stores shard more easily than relational ones?
optionA: They gave up the joins that span machines
optionB: They were designed more recently
optionC: They store less data in each record
optionD: They do not need to be consistent
correctAnswerText: They gave up the joins that span machines
explanation: The ease is the consequence of the restriction. Nothing about being newer makes distribution easy.

prompt: Why do distributed NoSQL stores often offer eventual consistency?
optionA: Strong consistency is impossible to implement
optionB: Waiting for every copy would cost availability
optionC: It reduces the storage each copy needs
optionD: Applications rarely need accurate data
correctAnswerText: Waiting for every copy would cost availability
explanation: Acknowledging a write only when every replica has it makes any replica’s failure your outage.

prompt: Why is joining in application code worse than in the database?
optionA: It is slower and you wrote the optimiser
optionB: It uses more memory in the application
optionC: It requires more lines of code to write
optionD: It cannot handle very large result sets
correctAnswerText: It is slower and you wrote the optimiser
explanation: Data crosses the network to be discarded, and decades of query optimisation are replaced by your loop.

prompt: Why might a system use both a relational and a search store?
optionA: Each answers a question the other cannot
optionB: It spreads the load across two systems
optionC: It reduces the cost of each of them
optionD: It provides a backup if one fails
correctAnswerText: Each answers a question the other cannot
explanation: The price is keeping them in step, which is a real, permanent engineering cost rather than a configuration.

prompt: What does a relational database give you that is easy to undervalue?
optionA: The ability to store nested structures
optionB: The capacity to hold very large datasets
optionC: The ability to ask a question you had not planned
optionD: The speed of reading a single record
correctAnswerText: The ability to ask a question you had not planned
explanation: Every product gets asked an unforeseen question. SQL answers it; a model shaped for known queries may not.

prompt: When should a child record be embedded rather than referenced?
optionA: When there are only a few of them
optionB: When it changes less often than the parent
optionC: When it has no identity of its own
optionD: When it is always read with its parent
correctAnswerText: When it is always read with its parent
explanation: Read together, stored together. Order lines qualify; a product catalogue referenced by every order does not.

prompt: You need to cache computed values by an exact key. What fits?
optionA: A relational database
optionB: A graph database
optionC: A document database
optionD: A key-value store
correctAnswerText: A key-value store
explanation: One access pattern, extreme speed needed, no queries. That is precisely what key-value is for.

prompt: You must find how two people are connected through any number of intermediaries. What suits?
optionA: A key-value store
optionB: A document database
optionC: A wide-column store
optionD: A graph database
correctAnswerText: A graph database
explanation: Unbounded traversal depth is the one thing SQL genuinely struggles with and graph stores exist for.

prompt: Your document store enforces nothing. What should the application do?
optionA: Validate the shape when reading
optionB: Accept whatever shape is provided
optionC: Record the version in each document
optionD: Validate the shape before writing
correctAnswerText: Validate the shape before writing
explanation: Validating on write keeps the bad data out. Validating on read means it is already in there.

prompt: You change a document’s structure. What must you decide?
optionA: Whether to version the whole collection
optionB: Whether to migrate the old ones or read both
optionC: Which index to rebuild afterwards
optionD: How to lock the collection while changing
correctAnswerText: Whether to migrate the old ones or read both
explanation: Skipping the decision is how a collection ends up with four shapes and a reader that handles three.

prompt: In a store that only fetches by key, how do you support a second access pattern?
optionA: Scan the store filtering on the field
optionB: Write a second record under a different key
optionC: Add an index on the field you need
optionD: Fetch everything and filter in code
correctAnswerText: Write a second record under a different key
explanation: Duplicate the data under the key you need. Writing twice is the cost of reading fast both ways.

prompt: Two values must always change together and the store has no cross-document transactions. What do you do?
optionA: Write them in a fixed order
optionB: Retry the second write on failure
optionC: Check them with a background job
optionD: Keep them in the same document
correctAnswerText: Keep them in the same document
explanation: The document becomes the transaction boundary, so atomicity requirements decide the document boundaries.

prompt: Should a user document embed every comment they have ever written?
optionA: Yes, provided the comments are short
optionB: Yes, it keeps the comments easy to find
optionC: No — an unbounded array will outgrow the limit
optionD: No, because comments belong to posts
correctAnswerText: No — an unbounded array will outgrow the limit
explanation: Embed bounded collections. Anything that grows without limit needs its own collection and a reference.

prompt: A document store query is slow. What applies just as it would in SQL?
optionA: It probably needs a larger instance
optionB: It probably needs the data denormalised
optionC: It probably needs the results cached
optionD: It probably needs an index on that field
correctAnswerText: It probably needs an index on that field
explanation: Being non-relational does not repeal the need for indexes. Unindexed queries scan the collection.

prompt: Your store lets you choose consistency per read. How should you decide?
optionA: By which replica is nearest to you
optionB: By how often that read is performed
optionC: By what a stale answer would cost there
optionD: By how large the returned data is
correctAnswerText: By what a stale answer would cost there
explanation: A profile picture tolerates staleness; a balance check before a withdrawal does not. It is per-operation.

prompt: An application reads four collections and joins them in code for every page. What does that indicate?
optionA: The collections should be indexed better
optionB: The data is relational and the store is not
optionC: The queries should be run in parallel
optionD: The results should be cached for reuse
correctAnswerText: The data is relational and the store is not
explanation: Reimplementing joins by hand is the clearest sign that the store choice was wrong for this data.

prompt: A collection contains documents in five different shapes. How did that happen?
optionA: The validation rules were removed
optionB: The documents were imported badly
optionC: The format changed and nothing migrated
optionD: Several applications write to it
correctAnswerText: The format changed and nothing migrated
explanation: Flexibility used as a substitute for migration. Every reader now carries the history of the format.

prompt: Writes to some user documents began failing after two years. What is the likely cause?
optionA: The documents were never being indexed
optionB: The users have too many active sessions
optionC: An embedded array grew past the size limit
optionD: The collection exceeded its record count
correctAnswerText: An embedded array grew past the size limit
explanation: It works for every user until it does not, and only for the most active ones. A slow-motion design error.

prompt: A user’s name appears differently in two places. What went wrong?
optionA: One embedded copy was not updated
optionB: The name was written in two formats
optionC: The read went to two different replicas
optionD: The user changed it between the reads
correctAnswerText: One embedded copy was not updated
explanation: The permanent cost of denormalisation: somebody must update every copy, and one path always gets missed.

prompt: The business asks a new question and answering it needs a full scan. What does that reveal?
optionA: The store cannot answer analytical questions
optionB: The collection has grown larger than planned
optionC: The indexes were never properly maintained
optionD: The model was shaped for the old queries only
correctAnswerText: The model was shaped for the old queries only
explanation: The cost of query-first modelling. It is a real trade, and it arrives as a surprise about eighteen months in.

prompt: Two related documents are sometimes inconsistent after a failure. Why?
optionA: The two writes were not atomic together
optionB: The application retried only one of them
optionC: The replication lagged between them
optionD: The writes were applied out of order
correctAnswerText: The two writes were not atomic together
explanation: Without a cross-document transaction, a crash between the two writes leaves exactly this state.

prompt: One partition of a distributed store is overwhelmed and the rest are idle. What caused it?
optionA: The other partitions have failed
optionB: The partitions were sized differently
optionC: The routing layer is not balancing
optionD: The key sends related writes to one place
correctAnswerText: The key sends related writes to one place
explanation: Keying by date sends every write today to one partition. The key must spread the traffic, not just the data.

prompt: A team chose a document store for data that is highly relational. What will they experience?
optionA: Slower writes than a relational store
optionB: Manual joins and consistency problems
optionC: A hard limit on how much they can store
optionD: An inability to index their fields
correctAnswerText: Manual joins and consistency problems
explanation: They will rebuild the parts of a relational database they threw away, more slowly and with more bugs.

prompt: A write succeeds and an immediate read does not see it. Is this a bug?
optionA: Not necessarily, since the read itself may have failed
optionB: Not necessarily — it may be the documented behaviour
optionC: Yes, a successful write must be readable
optionD: Yes, the write was not actually committed
correctAnswerText: Not necessarily — it may be the documented behaviour
explanation: Eventual consistency behaving as promised. The bug is the code that assumed otherwise.

prompt: Search results include products that were deleted weeks ago. What has failed?
optionA: The process keeping the two stores in step
optionB: The search store ran out of capacity
optionC: The search index needs to be rebuilt
optionD: The deletion did not save correctly
correctAnswerText: The process keeping the two stores in step
explanation: Two stores means a synchronisation pipeline, and that pipeline is a component that can fail silently.

prompt: What question should be answered before choosing a non-relational store?
optionA: Which store scales the furthest
optionB: What can a relational one not do here
optionC: Which store the team has used before
optionD: Which store is most popular right now
correctAnswerText: What can a relational one not do here
explanation: A specific limitation you have hit or will hit. Without one, the answer is the boring, capable default.

prompt: Why does the data store choice deserve more care than most?
optionA: It decides which language you can use
optionB: It is among the hardest things to change later
optionC: It determines the cost of the infrastructure
optionD: It affects how the team writes their code
correctAnswerText: It is among the hardest things to change later
explanation: A framework can be replaced over a quarter. A store holding years of production data usually cannot.

prompt: What is the real cost of adding a second data store?
optionA: The team having to learn a new system
optionB: The licensing and hosting of the second
optionC: The extra latency of two round trips
optionD: A permanent job keeping them consistent
correctAnswerText: A permanent job keeping them consistent
explanation: All four are real; the synchronisation is the one that produces incidents for as long as the system exists.

prompt: A store is chosen because it scales to billions of records. What should you check?
optionA: Whether the cost scales proportionally
optionB: Whether it also scales reads that far
optionC: Whether the benchmark was independent
optionD: Whether you will ever have that many
correctAnswerText: Whether you will ever have that many
explanation: Most systems have millions of rows and are choosing a store designed for a problem they will never have.

prompt: How should you think about schema flexibility?
optionA: As a way to move faster permanently
optionB: As a benefit with no real downside
optionC: As a cost deferred rather than removed
optionD: As a reason to skip data modelling
correctAnswerText: As a cost deferred rather than removed
explanation: The migration you did not write becomes a condition in every reader, and it is there for as long as the data is.

prompt: Why is "use NoSQL for nested data" weaker advice than it was?
optionA: Relational stores now handle documents well
optionB: Applications now flatten their data
optionC: Nested data has become less common
optionD: Document stores have got slower
correctAnswerText: Relational stores now handle documents well
explanation: JSON columns with indexing let you keep transactions and joins and still store a document where one fits.

prompt: What should drive the choice between store families?
optionA: The scale the system may one day reach
optionB: The operational cost of running each
optionC: The shape of the data and how it is read
optionD: The familiarity of the engineering team
correctAnswerText: The shape of the data and how it is read
explanation: All four matter. Shape and access pattern are the ones that make a store either effortless or a fight.

prompt: Who should decide whether eventual consistency is acceptable?
optionA: Whoever operates the database cluster
optionB: Whoever understands what a stale answer costs
optionC: The engineers building the data layer
optionD: Whichever the chosen store makes easiest
correctAnswerText: Whoever understands what a stale answer costs
explanation: It is a product decision presented as a technical one, and the cost differs enormously per field.

prompt: You realise the store was the wrong choice. What is the honest assessment?
optionA: Moving is straightforward with good tooling
optionB: Staying is better than any migration
optionC: Moving should wait until it fails outright
optionD: Moving is expensive and may still be right
correctAnswerText: Moving is expensive and may still be right
explanation: Data migrations are among the most expensive projects there are, and sometimes the cheaper option anyway.

prompt: What is the biggest mental shift when moving from relational modelling?
optionA: You stop needing to think about indexes
optionB: You can store much more data cheaply
optionC: You design for the reads, not the entities
optionD: You no longer have to plan the schema
correctAnswerText: You design for the reads, not the entities
explanation: Normalise then query becomes list the queries then shape the data. Everything else in this file follows from it.

prompt: What is technical debt?
optionA: Old code using outdated techniques
optionB: Any code that is poorly written
optionC: Work that was left unfinished
optionD: A shortcut taken now that costs more later
correctAnswerText: A shortcut taken now that costs more later
explanation: Borrowing time. Like a loan, it can be a sensible decision and it accrues interest either way.

prompt: What is the difference between deliberate and accidental debt?
optionA: One is recorded, the other is forgotten
optionB: One is in the code, the other in the design
optionC: One was a decision, the other was not noticed
optionD: One is repaid quickly, the other never is
correctAnswerText: One was a decision, the other was not noticed
explanation: Deliberate debt is engineering. Accidental debt is just a mistake nobody has found yet.

prompt: What is the interest on technical debt?
optionA: The extra effort every future change costs
optionB: The time it would take to fix it now
optionC: The number of defects it has caused
optionD: The amount of code that must change
correctAnswerText: The extra effort every future change costs
explanation: Paid on every change, forever, until the principal is repaid. That recurrence is the whole metaphor.

prompt: Is all badly written code technical debt?
optionA: Yes, if it slows future development
optionB: No, only untested code counts
optionC: Yes, any poor code counts as debt
optionD: No — some of it is simply careless work
correctAnswerText: No — some of it is simply careless work
explanation: Debt implies something was bought with it. Calling incompetence debt makes it sound like a strategy.

prompt: Where can technical debt exist besides the code?
optionA: Only in the parts nobody maintains
optionB: Only in the oldest parts of the system
optionC: Only in the code and its documentation
optionD: In the tests, the data and the infrastructure
correctAnswerText: In the tests, the data and the infrastructure
explanation: A schema nobody can change and a deployment only one person understands are both debt.

prompt: What should happen when a shortcut is taken deliberately?
optionA: It gets approved by a senior engineer
optionB: It gets marked with a comment in code
optionC: It gets written down with the reason
optionD: It gets fixed in the following sprint
correctAnswerText: It gets written down with the reason
explanation: Unrecorded debt becomes invisible, and invisible debt looks to the next reader like a deliberate design.

prompt: How does technical debt usually make itself felt?
optionA: The team writes fewer new features
optionB: The application runs more slowly
optionC: Small changes take longer than they should
optionD: The code fails its quality checks
correctAnswerText: Small changes take longer than they should
explanation: Delivery slowing without anybody being able to point at a cause is the classic presentation.

prompt: How is technical debt usually repaid?
optionA: By a dedicated project to clean it up
optionB: By improving the area you are working in
optionC: By documenting how it currently works
optionD: By rewriting the affected component
correctAnswerText: By improving the area you are working in
explanation: Attached to the work that needs it. Standalone cleanup projects are the first thing cut under pressure.

prompt: How should debt be described to somebody outside engineering?
optionA: In terms of the code quality problems
optionB: In terms of how long it has existed
optionC: In terms of the principles being violated
optionD: In terms of what future work will cost
correctAnswerText: In terms of what future work will cost
explanation: They can act on delivery time. They cannot act on "the coupling is too high".

prompt: Should a team aim for zero technical debt?
optionA: No, but only in the early stages
optionB: Yes, debt always costs more than it saves
optionC: Yes, if the team has the time available
optionD: No — some is the price of shipping
correctAnswerText: No — some is the price of shipping
explanation: A company with no debt has probably shipped too slowly. The goal is knowing what you owe.

prompt: Why is the interest more important than the size of the mess?
optionA: Interest grows faster than the principal
optionB: The principal cannot usually be repaid
optionC: Interest is easier to measure precisely
optionD: A mess nobody touches costs nothing
correctAnswerText: A mess nobody touches costs nothing
explanation: Awful code in a file untouched for four years is not urgent. A small tangle in a hot file is.

prompt: Why does it matter whether debt was taken on deliberately?
optionA: Only the deliberate kind can be planned for
optionB: The accidental kind costs more interest
optionC: The deliberate kind is less serious
optionD: The deliberate kind is easier to repair
correctAnswerText: Only the deliberate kind can be planned for
explanation: You know it exists, why, and roughly what repaying costs. Accidental debt is discovered, usually late.

prompt: Why does debt tend to get worse rather than stay level?
optionA: The language and tools move on
optionB: New work is built on top of the shortcut
optionC: Nobody remembers why it was taken
optionD: The original authors leave the team
correctAnswerText: New work is built on top of the shortcut
explanation: Each thing built on a bad foundation makes the foundation more expensive to change. That is compounding.

prompt: Why does "the code is bad" fail as an argument for cleanup time?
optionA: It cannot be verified by anybody outside
optionB: It gives nobody a reason to choose it over features
optionC: It suggests the team wrote the code badly
optionD: It is usually an exaggeration of the problem
correctAnswerText: It gives nobody a reason to choose it over features
explanation: A business decision needs a comparison. "Three days becomes one" competes with a feature; "bad code" does not.

prompt: Why do dedicated cleanup sprints rarely happen?
optionA: They require the whole team to be free
optionB: They are harder to estimate accurately
optionC: They produce nothing users can see
optionD: They are the easiest thing to postpone
correctAnswerText: They are the easiest thing to postpone
explanation: Both the first and last are true, and together they mean it is postponed every quarter, indefinitely.

prompt: What cost of technical debt is often left out of the argument?
optionA: The tests take longer to run each month
optionB: Good engineers leave codebases they dread
optionC: The documentation becomes inaccurate
optionD: The infrastructure bill grows over time
correctAnswerText: Good engineers leave codebases they dread
explanation: Recruitment and onboarding cost more than most cleanups, and nobody attributes it to the codebase.

prompt: Where does the debt metaphor break down?
optionA: The debt can never actually be repaid
optionB: The debt was not borrowed from anybody
optionC: The interest is charged only occasionally
optionD: You cannot see the balance or the rate
correctAnswerText: You cannot see the balance or the rate
explanation: A bank sends a statement. Technical debt has no balance, no rate and no due date, which is why it is ignored.

prompt: Why is taking on debt genuinely tempting?
optionA: The shortcut is usually the simpler design
optionB: The proper solution is often unclear
optionC: The saving is immediate and the cost is later
optionD: The saving is larger than the eventual cost
correctAnswerText: The saving is immediate and the cost is later
explanation: Timing, not size. Everything about debt follows from the benefit arriving before the bill.

prompt: What does it look like when debt becomes unmanageable?
optionA: Every change risks breaking something unrelated
optionB: The team spends time discussing quality
optionC: New engineers take longer to onboard
optionD: The codebase grows past a certain size
correctAnswerText: Every change risks breaking something unrelated
explanation: When the team cannot predict the effect of a change, feature work has effectively stopped.

prompt: Why is missing test coverage a particularly expensive kind of debt?
optionA: It makes repaying every other debt riskier
optionB: It slows down the release process
optionC: It makes the code harder to read
optionD: It allows more defects to reach production
correctAnswerText: It makes repaying every other debt riskier
explanation: It is the debt that blocks repayment of the others, which is why it compounds faster than it looks.

prompt: Which debt should be repaid first?
optionA: The one the team dislikes most
optionB: The one in the area you change most
optionC: The one that has existed the longest
optionD: The one that is largest in size
correctAnswerText: The one in the area you change most
explanation: Interest, not principal. Repayment pays back only where you keep paying the interest.

prompt: How do you ask for time to fix a slow area of the code?
optionA: Show how long the debt has existed
optionB: Explain the design problems in detail
optionC: Quantify what changes there cost today
optionD: Describe what good code would look like
correctAnswerText: Quantify what changes there cost today
explanation: "Every change here takes three days; two weeks of work makes it one." That is an investment case.

prompt: You must take a shortcut to meet a launch date. What makes it responsible?
optionA: Adding a comment beside the affected code
optionB: Getting the whole team to agree to it
optionC: Recording what it is and what it will cost
optionD: Choosing the smallest possible shortcut
correctAnswerText: Recording what it is and what it will cost
explanation: A ticket with the reason and the estimate. The comment helps whoever finds it; the ticket is visible before.

prompt: What is the most sustainable way to reduce debt?
optionA: Allocate a fixed share of each sprint
optionB: Fix whatever the tooling reports
optionC: Run a cleanup project each quarter
optionD: Improve each area as you work in it
correctAnswerText: Improve each area as you work in it
explanation: The work is justified by the feature that needed it, so it is never the thing that gets cut.

prompt: What is the most useful evidence that debt is hurting you?
optionA: How long similar changes take over time
optionB: How many warnings the linter produces
optionC: How much of the code lacks tests
optionD: How old the average file is
correctAnswerText: How long similar changes take over time
explanation: Delivery time is the thing debt actually damages. The static measures correlate weakly at best.

prompt: You cannot fix a bad component now. What can you do cheaply?
optionA: Document how it currently behaves
optionB: Put a clean interface in front of it
optionC: Add tests covering its behaviour
optionD: Mark it as deprecated in the code
correctAnswerText: Put a clean interface in front of it
explanation: Containment. New code depends on the interface, so the mess stops spreading and can be replaced later.

prompt: You want to repay debt in an untested area. What comes first?
optionA: A rewrite of the worst function
optionB: A plan for the new structure
optionC: Tests describing what it does now
optionD: Agreement from the code owner
correctAnswerText: Tests describing what it does now
explanation: Without them you cannot tell repayment from breakage, and the repayment becomes the riskier option.

prompt: A component is badly written and is being retired in three months. What do you do?
optionA: Add tests around it
optionB: Repay the worst of it
optionC: Leave it alone
optionD: Refactor it while you can
correctAnswerText: Leave it alone
explanation: The interest stops in three months. Repaying a loan that is about to be written off is wasted effort.

prompt: How should known debt be tracked?
optionA: In a separate register the team keeps
optionB: In comments where the debt lives
optionC: In the architecture documentation
optionD: In the same backlog as everything else
correctAnswerText: In the same backlog as everything else
explanation: A separate list is a list nobody prioritises against. In the backlog it competes and sometimes wins.

prompt: Who is best placed to notice debt the team has stopped seeing?
optionA: Whoever reviews the most pull requests
optionB: The engineer who has been there longest
optionC: The person who wrote the original code
optionD: Somebody who joined in the last month
correctAnswerText: Somebody who joined in the last month
explanation: Their confusion is data, and it expires within about six weeks as they normalise to it like everybody else.

prompt: The same kind of feature takes three times longer than it did two years ago. What does that suggest?
optionA: Accumulated interest on unrepaid debt
optionB: The features have become more complex
optionC: The team has become less productive
optionD: The estimates were too low before
correctAnswerText: Accumulated interest on unrepaid debt
explanation: Comparable work taking longer over time is the clearest measurable signal debt produces.

prompt: A team calls every piece of poor code "technical debt". What does that obscure?
optionA: That some of it is in old code
optionB: That some of it bought nothing at all
optionC: That some of it is more urgent
optionD: That some of it cannot be fixed
correctAnswerText: That some of it bought nothing at all
explanation: Debt implies a trade was made. Where none was, the conversation should be about how the work is done.

prompt: A shortcut from two years ago is now treated as the intended design. How?
optionA: The shortcut turned out to work well
optionB: The original author has left the team
optionC: The code was never reviewed properly
optionD: Nobody recorded that it was temporary
correctAnswerText: Nobody recorded that it was temporary
explanation: Undocumented debt becomes architecture. The next engineer copies the pattern because it looks deliberate.

prompt: A team has planned a cleanup sprint for six quarters running. What is the real problem?
optionA: Detached cleanup always loses to features
optionB: The cleanup is too large to schedule
optionC: The team is not disciplined enough
optionD: Management does not value quality
correctAnswerText: Detached cleanup always loses to features
explanation: Structural rather than a failure of will. Work with no user-visible outcome loses every prioritisation.

prompt: Engineers avoid touching one module even when it needs changing. What has happened?
optionA: The module is owned by another team
optionB: The module has no documentation
optionC: The module is written in an old style
optionD: The risk of changing it exceeds the benefit
correctAnswerText: The risk of changing it exceeds the benefit
explanation: Fear is the most reliable indicator of severe debt, and it is usually absent from any dashboard.

prompt: A bad pattern now appears in eleven places. How did that happen?
optionA: The linter did not detect the pattern
optionB: Each author copied the existing example
optionC: The pattern was recommended by a lead
optionD: The reviewers were not paying attention
correctAnswerText: Each author copied the existing example
explanation: Existing code is the strongest documentation there is. Debt propagates by being the nearest example.

prompt: A team proposes rewriting rather than repaying. What is the usual outcome?
optionA: It succeeds but costs more than planned
optionB: It removes the debt and delivers faster
optionC: It takes far longer and rediscovers old bugs
optionD: It fails because the team lacks skill
correctAnswerText: It takes far longer and rediscovers old bugs
explanation: Every odd branch in the old code was a bug somebody hit. A rewrite discards the record and meets them again.

prompt: A team is measured on a code quality score and delivery has not improved. Why?
optionA: The tool reports too many false results
optionB: The score was set at the wrong level
optionC: The team is working around the score
optionD: The score does not measure what slows them
correctAnswerText: The score does not measure what slows them
explanation: Complexity scores and coverage percentages correlate weakly with the thing that actually costs time.

prompt: A framework is four major versions behind and upgrading is now a project. How did it get here?
optionA: The team lacked the required skills
optionB: Each upgrade was deferred as not urgent
optionC: The framework changed too quickly
optionD: The upgrades were always breaking
correctAnswerText: Each upgrade was deferred as not urgent
explanation: Four cheap upgrades became one expensive one. Staying current is a form of continuous repayment.

prompt: A team consistently takes shortcuts despite knowing better. What should you examine?
optionA: Whether the deadlines are realistic
optionB: Whether the reviews are rigorous enough
optionC: Whether the team understands the risks
optionD: What the team is actually rewarded for
correctAnswerText: What the team is actually rewarded for
explanation: If only shipped features are recognised, debt is the rational response. Behaviour follows the incentive.

prompt: How much technical debt should a team carry?
optionA: As little as the schedule permits
optionB: As much as they can see and manage
optionC: Whatever the previous team left them
optionD: None, if quality is taken seriously
correctAnswerText: As much as they can see and manage
explanation: Visibility is the constraint. Debt you know about is a decision; debt you do not is an ambush.

prompt: Why might a startup rationally take on more debt than a bank?
optionA: Startups have less code to maintain
optionB: Startup engineers work more quickly
optionC: Banks have stricter quality standards
optionD: The product may not exist in a year
correctAnswerText: The product may not exist in a year
explanation: Interest on code that gets deleted is never paid. The right level of debt depends on the product’s odds.

prompt: When is a rewrite genuinely the better option?
optionA: When the code is beyond understanding
optionB: When the platform underneath is going away
optionC: When the team wants newer technology
optionD: When repayment would take many months
correctAnswerText: When the platform underneath is going away
explanation: Incomprehensible code argues for characterisation tests. A dead platform argues for a rewrite.

prompt: Who should decide whether to take on debt for a deadline?
optionA: The product manager who owns the deadline
optionB: The engineers, since they carry the cost
optionC: Whoever is most senior in the room
optionD: The business, once told what it will cost
correctAnswerText: The business, once told what it will cost
explanation: Engineering’s job is making the price visible. Making the trade in silence is what removes the choice.

prompt: Is it acceptable never to repay some debt?
optionA: Yes, where the interest is effectively zero
optionB: No, all debt should eventually be repaid
optionC: No, unless the code is being deleted
optionD: Yes, if the team has agreed to ignore it
correctAnswerText: Yes, where the interest is effectively zero
explanation: A stable component nobody touches costs nothing to hold. Repaying it is spending for no return.

prompt: Why should the human cost be part of the debt argument?
optionA: Losing and replacing engineers is expensive
optionB: Engineers deserve to enjoy their work
optionC: Unhappy teams produce more defects
optionD: Morale affects the quality of the code
correctAnswerText: Losing and replacing engineers is expensive
explanation: All four are true and the first is the one that converts into a number a business will weigh.

prompt: When is containing debt better than repaying it?
optionA: When the code has no test coverage
optionB: When it belongs to another team
optionC: When it is stable and the spread is the risk
optionD: When the team lacks time to repay it
correctAnswerText: When it is stable and the spread is the risk
explanation: An interface in front costs a day and stops it propagating, which is often the whole problem.

prompt: What is the single most useful thing a team can do about debt?
optionA: Make it visible enough to be decided about
optionB: Repay a fixed proportion every sprint
optionC: Measure it with an automated tool
optionD: Prevent any new debt from being added
correctAnswerText: Make it visible enough to be decided about
explanation: Invisible debt cannot be traded against anything. Visible debt is an ordinary prioritisation problem.

prompt: A team keeps accumulating debt despite agreeing not to. What actually changes it?
optionA: Changing what the team is measured on
optionB: Repeating the agreement more firmly
optionC: Training the team on code quality
optionD: Adding more checks to the review
correctAnswerText: Changing what the team is measured on
explanation: People optimise for what is counted. If only delivered features are counted, that is what you will get.

prompt: What is the actual skill in managing technical debt?
optionA: Writing code that never needs changing
optionB: Repaying debt as quickly as possible
optionC: Knowing what you owe and choosing when to pay
optionD: Avoiding taking on any debt at all
correctAnswerText: Knowing what you owe and choosing when to pay
explanation: The same skill as any borrowing. Teams get into trouble by not knowing the balance, not by having one.

prompt: What is a process?
optionA: A running program with its own resources
optionB: A service managed by the system
optionC: A program stored on the filesystem
optionD: A task scheduled to run at a time
correctAnswerText: A running program with its own resources
explanation: Its own memory, its own file handles, its own identifier. One program can be many processes.

prompt: Who do a file’s permission bits apply to?
optionA: Its owner, its group, and everybody else
optionB: The user who created it and the root user
optionC: The user running the current process
optionD: Each user who has been granted access
correctAnswerText: Its owner, its group, and everybody else
explanation: Three sets of three. Almost every permission problem is the process running as the wrong one of the three.

prompt: What are the three standard streams a process has?
optionA: Console, file and network
optionB: Read, write and append
optionC: Input, output and errors
optionD: Request, response and log
correctAnswerText: Input, output and errors
explanation: Output and errors being separate is what lets you keep the results and discard the noise, or the reverse.

prompt: What does a pipe between two commands do?
optionA: Runs the second only if the first succeeds
optionB: Feeds the first one’s output into the second
optionC: Saves the output of the first to a file
optionD: Runs both of the commands at the same time
correctAnswerText: Feeds the first one’s output into the second
explanation: Small tools composed into a larger one. It is the idea the whole command line is built around.

prompt: What is a signal?
optionA: A message telling a process something happened
optionB: A record written when a process exits
optionC: A flag set on a file being watched
optionD: A message a process sends to the kernel
correctAnswerText: A message telling a process something happened
explanation: Some can be handled and one cannot. That distinction is the whole of graceful versus forced shutdown.

prompt: What does "everything is a file" mean in Linux?
optionA: All data is stored on the filesystem
optionB: Every process has a file on disk
optionC: Configuration is always in text files
optionD: Devices and sockets are read like files
correctAnswerText: Devices and sockets are read like files
explanation: One interface for disks, terminals, network sockets and kernel state, which is why the tools compose so well.

prompt: What does a service manager do for a long-running program?
optionA: Collects the logs it writes to disk
optionB: Limits how much memory it may use
optionC: Starts it at boot and restarts it on failure
optionD: Schedules it to run at set times
correctAnswerText: Starts it at boot and restarts it on failure
explanation: Lifecycle. A program started from a terminal dies with the terminal; a managed service does not.

prompt: Where does a process get its environment variables?
optionA: From the system configuration files
optionB: From whatever started it
optionC: From the service manager only
optionD: From the user’s login profile
correctAnswerText: From whatever started it
explanation: Inherited from the parent. That is why a variable set in your shell is invisible to a systemd service.

prompt: Which resources should you check when a server is unwell?
optionA: Processes, users, files and sockets
optionB: Services, logs, cron jobs and mounts
optionC: Load, uptime, swap and temperature
optionD: Processor, memory, disk and network
correctAnswerText: Processor, memory, disk and network
explanation: Four questions, in that order. Almost every server problem is one of them being exhausted.

prompt: Where do system and service logs normally go?
optionA: To the directory the service runs from
optionB: To the system journal or a log directory
optionC: To a database the system maintains
optionD: To the home directory of the service user
correctAnswerText: To the system journal or a log directory
explanation: Knowing the two usual places is most of being able to investigate a server you have never seen.

prompt: You delete a large log file and the disk is still full. Why?
optionA: The filesystem needs to be remounted
optionB: The deletion has not yet been flushed
optionC: The file was moved rather than removed
optionD: A process still has the file open
correctAnswerText: A process still has the file open
explanation: The space is freed when the last handle closes. Restarting or truncating the file is what releases it.

prompt: Your application cannot read a file you can read yourself. Why?
optionA: The path is relative to another directory
optionB: The file is locked by another process
optionC: It runs as a different user than you
optionD: The file is on a read-only filesystem
correctAnswerText: It runs as a different user than you
explanation: The commonest deployment surprise. Your shell is you; the service is whatever user it was configured with.

prompt: A healthy Linux server shows almost no free memory. Is that a problem?
optionA: No — unused memory is used for caching
optionB: Yes, a process is leaking memory
optionC: Yes, it will start swapping shortly
optionD: No, but only if swap is available
correctAnswerText: No — unused memory is used for caching
explanation: Free memory is wasted memory. The figure to watch is available, which includes reclaimable cache.

prompt: Why is there a polite kill and a forceful one?
optionA: One is faster than the other to deliver
optionB: One requires higher privileges to send
optionC: One can be handled, the other cannot
optionD: One applies to services, one to processes
correctAnswerText: One can be handled, the other cannot
explanation: The polite one lets a process finish its work and close its files. The forceful one gives it no chance.

prompt: What does the load average actually measure?
optionA: The amount of memory being consumed
optionB: The number of requests being served
optionC: Processes running or waiting to run
optionD: The percentage of processor in use
correctAnswerText: Processes running or waiting to run
explanation: And it includes processes waiting on disk, so high load with idle processors usually means I/O.

prompt: A command works in your shell and fails as a scheduled job. What usually differs?
optionA: The user the command runs as
optionB: The directory the command starts in
optionC: The environment, including the search path
optionD: The permissions on the files involved
correctAnswerText: The environment, including the search path
explanation: Cron runs with a minimal environment. All four can differ, and the path is the one that catches everybody.

prompt: Why can a server fail with "too many open files" while the disk is fine?
optionA: The directory has reached its capacity
optionB: Each process may hold a limited number
optionC: The filesystem has run out of entries
optionD: The system has run out of memory
correctAnswerText: Each process may hold a limited number
explanation: Sockets count too, so a busy network service hits it long before anything to do with actual files.

prompt: A process disappears with nothing in its own logs. What should you suspect?
optionA: The service manager stopped it on purpose
optionB: The process exited normally and quietly
optionC: The disk filled and it could not write
optionD: The kernel killed it to reclaim memory
correctAnswerText: The kernel killed it to reclaim memory
explanation: The out-of-memory killer leaves nothing in the application log, because the application was not consulted.

prompt: Why do relative paths often break in a deployed service?
optionA: The service user has a different home
optionB: The filesystem layout differs on the server
optionC: It starts in a different directory than you do
optionD: Relative paths are not allowed for services
correctAnswerText: It starts in a different directory than you do
explanation: The working directory of a managed service is whatever its unit says, which is usually not where the code is.

prompt: Why is log rotation an operational necessity?
optionA: Large files are slower to write to
optionB: An unbounded log will eventually fill the disk
optionC: Old log entries stop being accurate
optionD: Log tools cannot read very large files
correctAnswerText: An unbounded log will eventually fill the disk
explanation: And a full disk takes down everything on the box, not just the thing that was writing the log.

prompt: A server is slow and you have shell access. What do you establish first?
optionA: What the logs are reporting
optionB: Which service is misbehaving
optionC: What changed most recently
optionD: Which resource is saturated
correctAnswerText: Which resource is saturated
explanation: Resource first, then owner, then cause. Reading logs before knowing what is exhausted is a slower route.

prompt: The disk is full. How do you find what is using it?
optionA: Check the logs for large writes
optionB: List the largest files in the system
optionC: Look at what each service stores
optionD: Work down the tree by directory size
correctAnswerText: Work down the tree by directory size
explanation: Top-down by directory converges in three or four steps. Searching for large files misses many small ones.

prompt: A deleted file is still held open by a running service. How do you get the space back?
optionA: Delete the file a second time
optionB: Wait for the kernel to reclaim it
optionC: Remount the filesystem it was on
optionD: Restart the service, or truncate the file
correctAnswerText: Restart the service, or truncate the file
explanation: Truncating through the process’s own handle frees it without a restart, which matters during an incident.

prompt: A service will not start because its port is in use. What do you do?
optionA: Find which process is listening on it
optionB: Wait for the port to be released
optionC: Restart the machine to clear it
optionD: Change the service to another port
correctAnswerText: Find which process is listening on it
explanation: Usually an old instance that did not stop. Identify it before changing anything else.

prompt: A service cannot write to its data directory. What is the right fix?
optionA: Run the service as the root user
optionB: Make the directory writable by everybody
optionC: Give the directory to the service’s user
optionD: Move the directory somewhere writable
correctAnswerText: Give the directory to the service’s user
explanation: Ownership, not 777 and not root. Both of those work and both remove a boundary you wanted.

prompt: A managed service is not running. What tells you most, fastest?
optionA: Whether the binary exists on disk
optionB: Its status and its recent log output
optionC: Whether the machine has been restarted
optionD: Whether the port is accepting traffic
correctAnswerText: Its status and its recent log output
explanation: Status gives the exit code and whether it is crash-looping; the log usually gives the reason.

prompt: You want to see what a service logs as you reproduce a problem. What do you do?
optionA: Read the log after reproducing it
optionB: Copy the log to your own machine
optionC: Follow the log while you trigger it
optionD: Increase the log level and restart
correctAnswerText: Follow the log while you trigger it
explanation: Following it live ties cause to effect. Reading afterwards means finding your event among everybody else’s.

prompt: What user should an application service run as?
optionA: The account of whoever deployed it
optionB: The root user, so nothing is blocked
optionC: A shared account used by all services
optionD: A dedicated account with only its own access
correctAnswerText: A dedicated account with only its own access
explanation: A compromise of the application then reaches only what that account can reach, which should be very little.

prompt: What must a scheduled job always do?
optionA: Log every step that it performs
optionB: Retry itself if it does not succeed
optionC: Report its failures somewhere a person sees
optionD: Run at a time when load is low
correctAnswerText: Report its failures somewhere a person sees
explanation: A job failing silently for weeks is the classic operational blind spot, and nobody is watching for it.

prompt: You fix a server by hand during an incident. What must follow?
optionA: Documenting the command you ran
optionB: Getting the change into the configuration
optionC: Telling the team what you changed
optionD: Verifying that the fix still works
correctAnswerText: Getting the change into the configuration
explanation: Otherwise the next rebuild silently undoes it, and the incident recurs with nobody knowing why.

prompt: Load average is 40 and the processors are mostly idle. What does that mean?
optionA: Processes are waiting on disk or network
optionB: The processors are being throttled
optionC: The load figure is being misreported
optionD: Too many processes have been started
correctAnswerText: Processes are waiting on disk or network
explanation: Linux counts uninterruptible waits in the load figure, so high load with idle processors points at I/O.

prompt: A service dies nightly with no error and no stack trace. Where do you look?
optionA: The service manager’s restart policy
optionB: The application log, at a higher level
optionC: The scheduled jobs running at that time
optionD: The kernel log, for an out-of-memory kill
correctAnswerText: The kernel log, for an out-of-memory kill
explanation: No trace because the process was not asked. The kernel log names what it killed and why.

prompt: Writes fail with "no space left" and the disk shows plenty free. What else can run out?
optionA: The open file handles available
optionB: The memory used to buffer writes
optionC: The entries that track individual files
optionD: The permissions on the directory
correctAnswerText: The entries that track individual files
explanation: Inodes. Millions of tiny files exhaust them while using barely any of the actual space.

prompt: A service works after a restart and fails after a few days with file errors. What is likely?
optionA: It opens handles and never closes them
optionB: The network connections are timing out
optionC: The disk gradually fills with its data
optionD: The memory it uses grows over time
correctAnswerText: It opens handles and never closes them
explanation: Works-then-degrades-then-restart-fixes-it is the signature of a leak, and handles is a common one.

prompt: Somebody fixed a permission error by making everything world-writable. What is the problem?
optionA: The service will still not be able to read
optionB: The files will be owned by the wrong user
optionC: The change will be undone on reboot
optionD: Any account on the box can now alter it
correctAnswerText: Any account on the box can now alter it
explanation: It works, which is why it happens. It also removes exactly the boundary that was doing its job.

prompt: Authentication against another system began failing on one server only. What is worth checking?
optionA: Whether its clock has drifted
optionB: Whether its packages were updated
optionC: Whether its certificates expired
optionD: Whether its network route changed
correctAnswerText: Whether its clock has drifted
explanation: Token and certificate validation are time-sensitive. A few minutes of drift breaks them on that box alone.

prompt: A deployed service behaves as though a configuration value is missing. What would you check?
optionA: Whether the service was restarted after
optionB: The file the value was supposed to be in
optionC: Whether the value was spelled correctly
optionD: The environment the service manager gives it
correctAnswerText: The environment the service manager gives it
explanation: All are worth checking. The service’s own environment is the one people assume matches their shell.

prompt: The process count climbs steadily until the system stops accepting new ones. What is happening?
optionA: The processes are waiting on a shared lock
optionB: Something spawns processes and never reaps them
optionC: Each request is being handled by a process
optionD: The service manager restarts them too often
correctAnswerText: Something spawns processes and never reaps them
explanation: A parent that never collects its children leaves entries behind, and the table is a finite resource.

prompt: Logs are rotated nightly and the disk still filled up. What is a likely cause?
optionA: The rotation schedule did not run at all
optionB: The compressed archives were never removed
optionC: The service kept writing to the rotated file
optionD: The log volume grew faster than expected
correctAnswerText: The service kept writing to the rotated file
explanation: All four happen. The first is the subtle one: without a signal to reopen, it writes to the renamed handle.

prompt: A problem fixed last month has returned after the server was rebuilt. Why?
optionA: The underlying cause was never addressed
optionB: The fix was reverted by another engineer
optionC: The rebuild used an older configuration
optionD: The fix was made by hand and never captured
correctAnswerText: The fix was made by hand and never captured
explanation: Manual changes are invisible to the rebuild. Every hand fix has to make its way into the configuration.

prompt: When should a manual server task become configuration?
optionA: When more than one person must do it
optionB: When the task becomes part of a process
optionC: When it takes longer than an hour by hand
optionD: As soon as it has to be done more than once
correctAnswerText: As soon as it has to be done more than once
explanation: The second time is where drift begins. After that no two servers are quite the same and nobody knows why.

prompt: What separates effective server debugging from ineffective?
optionA: Measuring before changing anything
optionB: Knowing more commands by heart
optionC: Reading every log from the beginning
optionD: Restarting things in the right order
correctAnswerText: Measuring before changing anything
explanation: Restart-and-hope sometimes works and teaches nothing. The commands can be looked up; the sequence cannot.

prompt: A server has drifted from its intended state. What is usually best?
optionA: Document the differences and keep it
optionB: Compare it against a working server
optionC: Find each difference and correct it
optionD: Rebuild it from the known configuration
correctAnswerText: Rebuild it from the known configuration
explanation: Replacement is faster and leaves a server you can reason about. Repair leaves one you merely hope about.

prompt: Why is running everything as root a poor default?
optionA: Root is blocked by most systems now
optionB: Root cannot be audited properly
optionC: Any mistake or compromise is unbounded
optionD: Root is slower for most operations
correctAnswerText: Any mistake or compromise is unbounded
explanation: Both a typo and an exploit go as far as they possibly can. Limiting the account bounds both.

prompt: Does using containers remove the need to understand Linux?
optionA: No, but only for the people who deploy
optionB: No — a container is Linux processes and permissions
optionC: Yes, except when building the base images
optionD: Yes, the platform handles the operating system
correctAnswerText: No — a container is Linux processes and permissions
explanation: Every container question in this bank — signals, users, file handles — is a Linux question underneath.

prompt: During an outage, is restarting the service before investigating acceptable?
optionA: Yes, if you capture the state first
optionB: Yes, restarting is always the priority
optionC: No, unless the restart is automated
optionD: No, the cause must be found first
correctAnswerText: Yes, if you capture the state first
explanation: Restore service, but take the logs and a snapshot of the state, or the cause goes with the restart.

prompt: How should an operations script be treated?
optionA: As a convenience nobody else will run
optionB: As production code, reviewed and versioned
optionC: As a temporary tool to be discarded
optionD: As documentation of a manual process
correctAnswerText: As production code, reviewed and versioned
explanation: A script that deletes the wrong directory does it faster than a person. It deserves the same care as any code.

prompt: What is more useful than knowing the disk is 60% full?
optionA: Knowing when it was last cleaned up
optionB: Knowing the total size of the disk
optionC: Knowing which files occupy the space
optionD: Knowing how fast that figure is rising
correctAnswerText: Knowing how fast that figure is rising
explanation: A rate gives you a date. A percentage only tells you where you are on a journey of unknown speed.

prompt: You solved an obscure server problem after two hours. What is worth ten more minutes?
optionA: Testing that it cannot recur
optionB: Adding an alert for that condition
optionC: Writing down how you found it
optionD: Explaining it to the whole team
correctAnswerText: Writing down how you found it
explanation: All four help. The write-up is what makes the next occurrence ten minutes instead of two hours.

prompt: What is worth learning here that outlasts any particular command?
optionA: The configuration of the service manager
optionB: The layout of the standard directories
optionC: The syntax of the most useful commands
optionD: The model of processes, files and resources
correctAnswerText: The model of processes, files and resources
explanation: Commands change between distributions and decades. The model explains every one of them.

prompt: What are you taking on when you add a package?
optionA: Its code, for as long as you use it
optionB: Its code, its bugs and its future changes
optionC: A tested solution to a known problem
optionD: A reduction in the code you maintain
correctAnswerText: Its code, its bugs and its future changes
explanation: Adoption, not borrowing. Its advisories become your advisories on the day they are published.

prompt: What does a lock file record?
optionA: The versions the project will accept
optionB: The exact versions that were installed
optionC: The packages the project depends on
optionD: The order the packages are loaded in
correctAnswerText: The exact versions that were installed
explanation: Exact, including everything pulled in indirectly. The manifest says what you want; this says what you got.

prompt: What is a transitive dependency?
optionA: One your dependencies brought with them
optionB: One that changes between installs
optionC: One that is optional to install
optionD: One used only during development
correctAnswerText: One your dependencies brought with them
explanation: Adding one package often installs eighty. You are responsible for all of them and chose only the first.

prompt: In semantic versioning, what does a change to the first number mean?
optionA: A change to the supported platforms
optionB: A significant new set of features
optionC: Something that may break your code
optionD: A rewrite of the whole package
correctAnswerText: Something that may break your code
explanation: Major means breaking. It is a promise the maintainer makes, and one they sometimes get wrong.

prompt: What does pinning a version achieve?
optionA: The package is checked for security
optionB: The same version installs every time
optionC: The package cannot be updated at all
optionD: The package is downloaded more quickly
correctAnswerText: The same version installs every time
explanation: Predictability. Without it, two installs a week apart can produce two different applications.

prompt: Why separate development dependencies from runtime ones?
optionA: Development ones change more frequently
optionB: Development ones are less trustworthy
optionC: Only the runtime ones ship to production
optionD: Runtime ones must be pinned exactly
correctAnswerText: Only the runtime ones ship to production
explanation: A smaller shipped set is a smaller attack surface and a smaller image. Test tools do not belong in production.

prompt: What is a security advisory for a package?
optionA: A published flaw, with versions affected
optionB: A warning that the package is outdated
optionC: A notice that the package is unmaintained
optionD: A recommendation to use an alternative
correctAnswerText: A published flaw, with versions affected
explanation: Published means attackers have it too. The clock starts when it is announced, not when you read it.

prompt: Why keep a list of everything your application includes?
optionA: To know how large the application will be
optionB: To check the licences are all compatible
optionC: To answer quickly whether an advisory affects you
optionD: To reduce the number of packages used
correctAnswerText: To answer quickly whether an advisory affects you
explanation: When a serious flaw is announced, "are we affected" should take minutes rather than an afternoon.

prompt: Why does a package’s licence matter?
optionA: It determines whether it can be modified
optionB: It affects how the package is supported
optionC: It can place obligations on your own code
optionD: It decides whether it can be redistributed
correctAnswerText: It can place obligations on your own code
explanation: Some require you to publish your source if you distribute. That is a business constraint, not a detail.

prompt: What are you comparing when deciding whether to add a package?
optionA: The size of the package against your code
optionB: Writing it once against maintaining it forever
optionC: The quality of its code against your own
optionD: The time to install against the time to write
correctAnswerText: Writing it once against maintaining it forever
explanation: A twenty-line utility is usually cheaper to write than to adopt, upgrade and audit for five years.

prompt: Why is the lock file committed to the repository?
optionA: So the install runs more quickly
optionB: So the versions can be reviewed
optionC: So the manifest can stay flexible
optionD: So every machine builds the same thing
correctAnswerText: So every machine builds the same thing
explanation: Without it, your laptop, the build server and production can each resolve a different set of versions.

prompt: Why is never updating dependencies a costly choice?
optionA: Known flaws accumulate and upgrades get harder
optionB: Old versions stop being downloadable
optionC: The team falls behind on new features
optionD: Newer versions run faster than old ones
correctAnswerText: Known flaws accumulate and upgrades get harder
explanation: Both halves compound. Four deferred upgrades become one project nobody can schedule.

prompt: Why is always taking the newest version also risky?
optionA: You ship whatever was published last night
optionB: Updates take time away from features
optionC: Newer versions have more dependencies
optionD: The newest version is the least tested
correctAnswerText: You ship whatever was published last night
explanation: Including a compromised release. Several real supply-chain attacks worked exactly this way.

prompt: Why do indirect dependencies deserve the same attention as direct ones?
optionA: They are chosen by somebody else entirely
optionB: They are usually smaller and less tested
optionC: They are updated less often than direct ones
optionD: Their code runs with the same privileges
correctAnswerText: Their code runs with the same privileges
explanation: The runtime does not distinguish. A flaw eight levels deep runs in your process just the same.

prompt: Why can a patch release still break your build?
optionA: The versioning is a convention, not a guarantee
optionB: Your code may depend on the old bug
optionC: Patch releases may add new features
optionD: The package manager resolves it differently
correctAnswerText: The versioning is a convention, not a guarantee
explanation: Both the first and third happen. The version number is the maintainer’s opinion about their own change.

prompt: Why are package registries an attractive target?
optionA: One package reaches thousands of applications
optionB: Registries have weaker security than companies
optionC: Package code is rarely reviewed by anybody
optionD: Packages are installed with full privileges
correctAnswerText: One package reaches thousands of applications
explanation: Leverage. Compromising one popular package is worth more than compromising any single company.

prompt: Why does it matter whether a package is still maintained?
optionA: It will become slower over time
optionB: Nobody will fix its next security flaw
optionC: It will stop working with new versions
optionD: It will be removed from the registry
correctAnswerText: Nobody will fix its next security flaw
explanation: An unmaintained package with an advisory leaves you forking it, replacing it, or shipping the flaw.

prompt: Why is a package containing five lines of code not free?
optionA: It is more likely to be unmaintained
optionB: It will be larger once installed than expected
optionC: It carries the same ongoing overhead as a large one
optionD: It cannot be audited as easily as your own
correctAnswerText: It carries the same ongoing overhead as a large one
explanation: Advisories, upgrades, licence checks, an entry in the tree. The overhead is per package, not per line.

prompt: Why can two packages be impossible to install together?
optionA: They provide the same functionality twice
optionB: They need incompatible versions of a third
optionC: They were built for different platforms
optionD: They use incompatible licence terms
correctAnswerText: They need incompatible versions of a third
explanation: The diamond problem. Some ecosystems allow two copies to coexist and some cannot, which decides how bad it is.

prompt: Why should a build install strictly from the lock file?
optionA: Otherwise the cache cannot be reused
optionB: Otherwise the manifest becomes inaccurate
optionC: Otherwise the install takes much longer
optionD: Otherwise it is not testing what you will ship
correctAnswerText: Otherwise it is not testing what you will ship
explanation: A build that resolves fresh versions has tested a different application from the one being deployed.

prompt: What combination keeps dependencies stable and safe?
