explanation: The story stops at "and then I built it". The result is the part that says whether it worked.

prompt: What should a "tell me about a failure" answer describe?
optionA: A failure caused by somebody else’s decision
optionB: A strength that occasionally causes problems
optionC: A small mistake with no real consequence
optionD: A real failure, and what you changed after
correctAnswerText: A real failure, and what you changed after
explanation: A disguised success is the most transparent answer in interviewing, and it wastes the question.

prompt: How should you prepare for behavioural questions?
optionA: Read about the company and its products
optionB: Memorise answers to the common questions
optionC: Practise speaking clearly and confidently
optionD: Have several real stories you know well
correctAnswerText: Have several real stories you know well
explanation: Six good stories cover most questions between them. Memorised answers break the moment you are probed.

prompt: What is a question about disagreeing with a colleague really assessing?
optionA: Whether you avoid conflict in a team
optionB: Whether you defer to more senior people
optionC: Whether you can disagree and still work together
optionD: Whether you usually turn out to be right
correctAnswerText: Whether you can disagree and still work together
explanation: They are hiring somebody who will disagree with them. How you do it is the entire question.

prompt: You are asked about something you have never done. What is the best response?
optionA: Describe how you would handle it
optionB: Say so, and offer the nearest real thing
optionC: Ask for a different question instead
optionD: Find a way to answer with what you have
correctAnswerText: Say so, and offer the nearest real thing
explanation: A student project or a group assignment is a real occasion. Inventing one fails the first follow-up question.

prompt: How long should a behavioural answer be?
optionA: A couple of minutes, then let them probe
optionB: Under a minute, to respect their time
optionC: Long enough to cover every detail
optionD: As long as it takes to tell it fully
correctAnswerText: A couple of minutes, then let them probe
explanation: Interviews are conversations. A six-minute monologue prevents the follow-up questions you want.

prompt: Why ask what you did rather than what you would do?
optionA: Hypothetical answers are easy to give well
optionB: Past behaviour is easier to verify
optionC: Past situations are easier to describe
optionD: Hypotheticals take longer to answer
correctAnswerText: Hypothetical answers are easy to give well
explanation: Anybody can describe the ideal response. Only somebody who did it can describe what actually happened.

prompt: Why do specific numbers and constraints make an answer credible?
optionA: They make the story more interesting
optionB: They show the candidate has a good memory
optionC: They are hard to invent and easy to probe
optionD: They demonstrate technical competence
correctAnswerText: They are hard to invent and easy to probe
explanation: An interviewer can ask why that number. A vague answer has nothing to ask about, which is itself a signal.

prompt: You describe an impressive project your team delivered. What has the interviewer learned?
optionA: That your team was capable
optionB: That you worked somewhere interesting
optionC: That you understand the technology
optionD: That you can explain a project well
correctAnswerText: That your team was capable
explanation: Nothing about you. Saying what you personally decided and built is the entire purpose of the question.

prompt: What is an interviewer actually testing with a failure question?
optionA: Whether you learn from things going wrong
optionB: Whether you have taken real risks
optionC: Whether you are honest about mistakes
optionD: Whether you can handle pressure well
correctAnswerText: Whether you learn from things going wrong
explanation: Honesty is the entry ticket. What they are buying is somebody whose second year is better than their first.

prompt: Why does an interviewer ask "and why did you choose that?"
optionA: To see whether the reasoning is yours
optionB: To check the accuracy of the story
optionC: To extend the answer for more detail
optionD: To test whether you can justify it
correctAnswerText: To see whether the reasoning is yours
explanation: A rehearsed answer survives the first question and not the third. That is what the follow-ups are for.

prompt: What does an interviewer usually mean by whether somebody would fit?
optionA: Whether they would get on socially
optionB: Whether they are similar to the team
optionC: Whether they share the same interests
optionD: Whether they work the way this team works
correctAnswerText: Whether they work the way this team works
explanation: Written communication, giving review, disagreeing openly. Working style, not personality.

prompt: Why do the questions you ask count?
optionA: They fill the time at the end politely
optionB: They demonstrate you researched the company
optionC: They give the interviewer a chance to sell
optionD: They show what you care about in a job
correctAnswerText: They show what you care about in a job
explanation: Asking about code review and on-call says more about your seniority than most of your answers will.

prompt: Why is overstating your contribution a bad strategy?
optionA: Interviewers verify claims with references
optionB: The follow-up questions expose it quickly
optionC: It makes you sound arrogant to the panel
optionD: Other candidates will be more modest
correctAnswerText: The follow-up questions expose it quickly
explanation: Two levels of "how did you decide that?" and the story stops having answers. It is very visible.

prompt: Why is a university group project a legitimate answer?
optionA: Academic work is technically comparable
optionB: It is the only experience you can offer
optionC: The behaviour being assessed is the same
optionD: Interviewers expect less from students
correctAnswerText: The behaviour being assessed is the same
explanation: Disagreement, deadlines, somebody not delivering. The situation is real and the behaviour transfers.

prompt: Why does "what would you do differently?" score so heavily?
optionA: It shows how recently the work happened
optionB: It shows whether you reviewed your own work
optionC: It tests whether you can accept criticism
optionD: It reveals what went wrong in the project
correctAnswerText: It shows whether you reviewed your own work
explanation: Somebody with nothing to change has not thought about it since. That is the signal being read.

prompt: Which part of an answer should take the most time?
optionA: The final result achieved
optionB: The background to the situation
optionC: The lesson you took from it
optionD: What you personally did
correctAnswerText: What you personally did
explanation: Most candidates spend two minutes on context and twenty seconds on their actions. It should be the reverse.

prompt: What makes a good answer about disagreeing with a colleague?
optionA: That your position turned out to be correct
optionB: That you handled it without escalating
optionC: That the relationship was unaffected
optionD: How it was resolved and what happened after
correctAnswerText: How it was resolved and what happened after
explanation: An answer where you were right and they came round is less convincing than one where you changed your mind.

prompt: Which failure is the best one to talk about?
optionA: A real one where you changed how you work
optionB: The smallest one you can think of
optionC: One that was recovered before it mattered
optionD: One caused by circumstances outside control
correctAnswerText: A real one where you changed how you work
explanation: The change is the payload. Without it the answer is a confession rather than evidence.

prompt: The project was genuinely a team effort. How do you describe it?
optionA: Explain that the credit belongs to everybody
optionB: Set the team context, then say what you owned
optionC: Focus on your contribution and omit the rest
optionD: Describe the team’s work and your role in it
correctAnswerText: Set the team context, then say what you owned
explanation: Both halves. Claiming it all is dishonest; claiming none of it leaves the interviewer with nothing.

prompt: How do you strengthen "I made the page load faster"?
optionA: Give the before and after figures
optionB: Explain the technique that you used
optionC: Say how long the work took you
optionD: Describe how users responded to it
correctAnswerText: Give the before and after figures
explanation: Four seconds to 800ms. The number invites the follow-up question you want, which is how you did it.

prompt: You are asked about mentoring somebody and you never have. What do you say?
optionA: Describe how you would approach mentoring
optionB: Talk about being mentored by somebody else
optionC: Explain that you have not had the chance
optionD: Say so, and offer the closest thing you did
correctAnswerText: Say so, and offer the closest thing you did
explanation: Helping a classmate through a concept is the same behaviour at a smaller scale. Name it honestly and tell it.

prompt: What set of stories should you prepare?
optionA: One for every question you expect to be asked
optionB: One strong story you can adapt to anything
optionC: A few covering conflict, failure, difficulty and success
optionD: The most technically impressive work that you did
correctAnswerText: A few covering conflict, failure, difficulty and success
explanation: Four or five, each usable from several angles. Most behavioural questions are one of those four shapes.

prompt: What is a strong question to ask an interviewer?
optionA: What a typical day in the role involves
optionB: What the company’s plans are for next year
optionC: What the progression path looks like here
optionD: How the team handles code review and releases
correctAnswerText: How the team handles code review and releases
explanation: It is a real question about real working conditions, and the answer tells you something worth knowing.

prompt: You are asked something you have no answer for. What is best?
optionA: Ask them to move on to something else
optionB: Start talking and find an answer as you go
optionC: Take a moment, then say honestly where you are
optionD: Redirect to a question you can answer
correctAnswerText: Take a moment, then say honestly where you are
explanation: A pause reads as thinking. Talking while you search for a point reads as exactly that.

prompt: How should a story about a successful project end?
optionA: With how the project is used today
optionB: With the result, and what you would change
optionC: With the result and the praise received
optionD: With the technologies you learned from it
correctAnswerText: With the result, and what you would change
explanation: Even on a success. It is the difference between somebody who delivered and somebody who is still improving.

prompt: A candidate gives a polished five-minute answer and the interviewer learns nothing. Why?
optionA: It used too much technical detail
optionB: It focused on the outcome achieved
optionC: It described the project, not their actions
optionD: It was too long for the question asked
correctAnswerText: It described the project, not their actions
explanation: The commonest failure in behavioural interviewing, and it is entirely invisible to the candidate.

prompt: Asked for a time they handled a deadline, a candidate describes their general approach. What is lost?
optionA: The structure the interviewer expected
optionB: The chance to show their technical depth
optionC: Any evidence that it ever actually happened
optionD: The opportunity to mention the result
correctAnswerText: Any evidence that it ever actually happened
explanation: A general approach is a belief about yourself. An occasion is evidence, and only one of them was asked for.

prompt: A candidate answers a weakness question with "I care too much about quality". What does the interviewer conclude?
optionA: They have prepared a standard answer
optionB: They have not thought about their weaknesses
optionC: They are unwilling to answer the question
optionD: They are nervous about being judged
correctAnswerText: They are unwilling to answer the question
explanation: It is recognised instantly. The candidate has declined to engage, and that itself is the information.

prompt: A candidate’s answers become vague as the interviewer digs deeper. What does that suggest?
optionA: Their role was smaller than described
optionB: They have forgotten the details
optionC: The question moved outside their expertise
optionD: They are becoming nervous under pressure
correctAnswerText: Their role was smaller than described
explanation: Somebody who did the work gets more specific as you dig, not less. The pattern is very legible.

prompt: A candidate’s failure story is entirely about other people’s mistakes. What does that signal?
optionA: They worked in a poorly run organisation
optionB: They may not see their own part in outcomes
optionC: They were not given enough authority
optionD: They are protecting confidential detail
correctAnswerText: They may not see their own part in outcomes
explanation: It may all be true and it still answers nothing. An interviewer hears somebody who will blame this team too.

prompt: A candidate answers three questions in a forty-minute interview. What has that cost them?
optionA: The opportunity to ask their questions
optionB: The structure of the conversation
optionC: The interviewer’s patience with them
optionD: The chances to show a range of evidence
correctAnswerText: The chances to show a range of evidence
explanation: Twelve minutes on one story crowds out the four other things they could have demonstrated.

prompt: A story ends with what the candidate built and nothing more. What is the interviewer left wondering?
optionA: Who else was involved in it
optionB: How long the work took
optionC: Which technologies were used
optionD: Whether it actually worked
correctAnswerText: Whether it actually worked
explanation: An unfinished story reads as one that did not end well. Say the result even when it is mixed.

prompt: An answer is fluent and does not quite address the question asked. What has happened?
optionA: The candidate ran out of relevant stories
optionB: A prepared answer was used regardless
optionC: The candidate misheard the question
optionD: The question was ambiguously worded
correctAnswerText: A prepared answer was used regardless
explanation: Preparing stories is good; delivering one that does not fit is worse than a hesitant relevant answer.

prompt: A candidate is strongly critical of their previous employer. How is that read?
optionA: As a sign they have high standards
optionB: As honesty about a genuinely bad situation
optionC: As a reason they are looking to leave
optionD: As how they will describe this job later
correctAnswerText: As how they will describe this job later
explanation: It may well be justified. The interviewer still hears the conversation somebody will have about them.

prompt: A candidate has no questions at the end. How is that usually interpreted?
optionA: As confidence that they know enough
optionB: As limited interest in the actual job
optionC: As respect for the interviewer’s time
optionD: As nervousness at the end of the process
correctAnswerText: As limited interest in the actual job
explanation: Fair or not, it is read as not caring which job it is. Two prepared questions avoid it entirely.

prompt: Why is honesty the better strategy even from self-interest?
optionA: Interviewers can always detect dishonesty
optionB: References will contradict the claims
optionC: A job won on a false picture goes badly
optionD: It is easier than maintaining a story
correctAnswerText: A job won on a false picture goes badly
explanation: Being hired for skills you do not have is three unpleasant months and a difficult conversation.

prompt: During the interview you realise the job is not what you want. What is the sensible response?
optionA: End the interview politely and early
optionB: Mention your concerns to the interviewer
optionC: Continue as though nothing has changed
optionD: Ask the questions that would confirm it
correctAnswerText: Ask the questions that would confirm it
explanation: You may be wrong, and the information is worth having. It is an assessment in both directions.

prompt: How much do nerves count against a candidate?
optionA: Only if they affect the answers given
optionB: Little — interviewers expect and discount them
optionC: Heavily, since the role involves pressure
optionD: Not at all in a technical interview
correctAnswerText: Little — interviewers expect and discount them
explanation: Every interviewer has been nervous in an interview. What counts is whether the substance comes through.

prompt: What is an interviewer ultimately deciding?
optionA: Whether you will stay for long enough
optionB: Whether you are better than the others
optionC: Whether they want to work with you
optionD: Whether you are technically capable
correctAnswerText: Whether they want to work with you
explanation: Technical ability is necessary and not the decision. The decision is about the next two years of Tuesdays.

prompt: What does an interviewer expect from a graduate that they do not from a senior candidate?
optionA: Evidence of learning, rather than of scale
optionB: Enthusiasm about the company
optionC: Awareness of their own limitations
optionD: Technical depth in a chosen area
correctAnswerText: Evidence of learning, rather than of scale
explanation: Nobody expects you to have led a migration. They want evidence you get better quickly and notice things.

prompt: An interviewer is dismissive and interrupts throughout. What is that worth knowing?
optionA: It is information about working there
optionB: It is a deliberate test of composure
optionC: It reflects how busy they are today
optionD: It means you are not being considered
correctAnswerText: It is information about working there
explanation: Sometimes it is a bad day. Often it is the culture, and you have been shown it for free.

prompt: What single quality most reliably impresses in a behavioural interview?
optionA: Confidence and clarity when speaking
optionB: Breadth of technical experience described
optionC: Clear thinking about your own past decisions
optionD: Enthusiasm for the role being offered
correctAnswerText: Clear thinking about your own past decisions
explanation: Someone who can say why they chose something and what they would change now is unusual and very legible.

prompt: You were rejected after a behavioural round. What is most useful to do?
optionA: Consider whether the role suited you
optionB: Ask the company for detailed feedback
optionC: Write down which answers were weak
optionD: Prepare more stories for next time
correctAnswerText: Write down which answers were weak
explanation: Feedback is often generic and slow. Your own notes while it is fresh are more specific and available now.

prompt: Where is the line between good preparation and over-rehearsal?
optionA: Prepare the openings and improvise the rest
optionB: Write the answers down but do not memorise
optionC: Practise aloud, but only a few times
optionD: Know the stories, not the sentences
correctAnswerText: Know the stories, not the sentences
explanation: Knowing what happened lets you answer any angle. Knowing your wording means one angle and a wall.

prompt: What is the durable advice underneath all of this?
optionA: Prepare thoroughly for the common questions
optionB: Present your experience as impressively as you can
optionC: Do work worth talking about, then talk about it plainly
optionD: Learn the structure interviewers are trained on
correctAnswerText: Do work worth talking about, then talk about it plainly
explanation: The technique here is only how to say it. The substance has to come from having actually done things.

prompt: What are the three sets a dataset is usually split into?
optionA: Sample, population and holdout
optionB: Training, evaluation and production
optionC: Training, validation and test
optionD: Input, output and verification
correctAnswerText: Training, validation and test
explanation: Train fits the model, validation tunes it, test is looked at once. The third only works if it stays untouched.

prompt: What is overfitting?
optionA: Using a model that is too complicated
optionB: Learning the training data instead of the pattern
optionC: Training the model for far too many rounds
optionD: Having too little data to learn from
correctAnswerText: Learning the training data instead of the pattern
explanation: It memorises the examples, including their noise, and has learned nothing that transfers.

prompt: What is data leakage?
optionA: The dataset containing personal information
optionB: Training data being exposed outside the team
optionC: Data being lost between the pipeline stages
optionD: The model saw information it will not have in use
correctAnswerText: The model saw information it will not have in use
explanation: It produces an excellent score and a useless model, which is the worst combination available.

prompt: What is a baseline in a machine learning project?
optionA: The result published in the literature
optionB: The simplest thing your model must beat
optionC: The accuracy required by the business
optionD: The performance of the first model tried
correctAnswerText: The simplest thing your model must beat
explanation: Predict the most common class, or use a simple rule. Without one, no score means anything.

prompt: Why is accuracy often a poor metric?
optionA: Predicting the common case scores well
optionB: It is harder to calculate than others
optionC: It ignores how confident the model was
optionD: It cannot be compared between models
correctAnswerText: Predicting the common case scores well
explanation: One percent of transactions are fraud, so "never fraud" is 99% accurate and catches nothing.

prompt: Where does most of the time in a machine learning project go?
optionA: Training the model on the data
optionB: Deploying the model into production
optionC: Choosing and tuning the model
optionD: Getting the data into a usable state
correctAnswerText: Getting the data into a usable state
explanation: Collecting, cleaning, labelling and understanding it. Students consistently expect the opposite.

prompt: What is a feature?
optionA: A capability the model provides
optionB: A pattern the model discovered
optionC: An input the model learns from
optionD: A column in the original dataset
correctAnswerText: An input the model learns from
explanation: Often derived rather than raw. Choosing and building them is usually worth more than changing the model.

prompt: Why does a deployed model get worse over time?
optionA: The data it stores becomes corrupt
optionB: The code becomes out of date
optionC: The model degrades as it runs
optionD: The world it was trained on changes
correctAnswerText: The world it was trained on changes
explanation: The model is frozen and reality moves. That is why monitoring a model is not optional.

prompt: What must be recorded to reproduce a result?
optionA: The training time and the hardware
optionB: The name of who ran the experiment
optionC: The final accuracy and the model type
optionD: The data, the code and the settings used
correctAnswerText: The data, the code and the settings used
explanation: All three, versioned. A result you cannot reproduce is an anecdote rather than a finding.

prompt: What should you establish before building a model?
optionA: How much data you can gather
optionB: Whether a rule would do the job
optionC: What accuracy is achievable
optionD: Which algorithm suits the data
correctAnswerText: Whether a rule would do the job
explanation: A great many machine learning projects replace a handful of if statements that worked.

prompt: Why should the test set be looked at only once?
optionA: Repeated evaluation wears the data out
optionB: Tuning against it makes it another training set
optionC: It is needed for the final report
optionD: The test set is smaller than the others
correctAnswerText: Tuning against it makes it another training set
explanation: Every decision made after seeing it leaks a little into the model. After twenty, it measures nothing.

prompt: Why is leakage so often missed?
optionA: It affects only certain kinds of model
optionB: It only appears on large datasets
optionC: It requires special tools to detect
optionD: It shows up as an unusually good result
correctAnswerText: It shows up as an unusually good result
explanation: Nobody investigates a result that exceeded their hopes. Suspicion of a good number is the defence.

prompt: Why report both precision and recall?
optionA: One applies to training, one to testing
optionB: They measure different kinds of data
optionC: Together they are easier to explain
optionD: Each can be made perfect at the other’s cost
correctAnswerText: Each can be made perfect at the other’s cost
explanation: Flag everything for perfect recall; flag one certain case for perfect precision. Either alone is gameable.

prompt: Your model scores 87%. Is that good?
optionA: Unknowable without knowing the baseline
optionB: No, production models need higher
optionC: Yes, provided the test set was large
optionD: Yes, that is a strong result generally
correctAnswerText: Unknowable without knowing the baseline
explanation: If guessing the common class gives 86%, your model has contributed one percentage point of value.

prompt: Training accuracy is 99% and validation is 71%. What does the gap say?
optionA: The two sets came from different sources
optionB: The validation set is too small to trust
optionC: The model needs more training rounds
optionD: The model memorised rather than generalised
correctAnswerText: The model memorised rather than generalised
explanation: A large gap is the definition of overfitting, and it is visible before anything reaches production.

prompt: Why is more or better data usually worth more than a better model?
optionA: Data is cheaper to obtain than expertise
optionB: The model can only learn what the data contains
optionC: Larger datasets train more quickly
optionD: Models have become largely interchangeable
correctAnswerText: The model can only learn what the data contains
explanation: No architecture recovers a signal that is not present. Fixing the labels often beats a month of tuning.

prompt: Why can a model be unfair even with no protected attribute in the data?
optionA: The metric rewards unfair predictions
optionB: Other features stand in for it
optionC: The algorithm introduces its own bias
optionD: The training process amplifies noise
correctAnswerText: Other features stand in for it
explanation: Postcode carries income and ethnicity. Removing the column does not remove the information.

prompt: Why is a deployed model harder to monitor than ordinary code?
optionA: Its outputs cannot be logged usefully
optionB: Its performance depends on the hardware
optionC: It produces different results each time
optionD: It degrades without ever raising an error
correctAnswerText: It degrades without ever raising an error
explanation: Broken code throws. A model quietly becomes 20% worse and every response still looks like a valid answer.

prompt: Why is a random split wrong for time-series data?
optionA: The data points are not independent
optionB: The test set would be too similar
optionC: The model would train on the future
optionD: The classes would become imbalanced
correctAnswerText: The model would train on the future
explanation: Predicting Tuesday having seen Wednesday. In production you will never have that, so the score is fiction.

prompt: Why does how you frame the problem matter more than the model?
optionA: The wrong question cannot be answered well
optionB: Frames are harder to change than models
optionC: Framing determines the training time
optionD: The framing decides which model applies
correctAnswerText: The wrong question cannot be answered well
explanation: Predicting who will churn and predicting who can be retained are different problems with different uses.

prompt: You are detecting a rare disease. Which mistake matters more?
optionA: Both equally, so accuracy is appropriate
optionB: Neither, so any metric will serve
optionC: A false alarm, so precision is the priority
optionD: Missing a case, so recall is the priority
correctAnswerText: Missing a case, so recall is the priority
explanation: The metric follows the cost of each error. A missed diagnosis and an extra test are not comparable.

prompt: Your data has many records per customer. How should you split it?
optionA: By date, with the newest held back
optionB: Randomly across all of the records
optionC: By customer, so none appears in both
optionD: Evenly, keeping the classes balanced
correctAnswerText: By customer, so none appears in both
explanation: Otherwise the model recognises the customer rather than the pattern, and the score is measuring memory.

prompt: What is the right first model to build?
optionA: The simplest one that produces a number
optionB: The one the team has used before
optionC: The one the literature recommends
optionD: The most powerful one available
correctAnswerText: The simplest one that produces a number
explanation: It exercises the whole pipeline and gives every later result something to be compared against.

prompt: You scale your features before splitting the data. What is wrong?
optionA: The features will be scaled inconsistently
optionB: The scaling should come after training
optionC: The split will no longer be random
optionD: The training set learned from the test set
correctAnswerText: The training set learned from the test set
explanation: The mean and range came from all the data, including the test set. Fit the scaler on training only.

prompt: Your model is 82% accurate and you want to improve it. What do you do first?
optionA: Examine a sample of the errors by hand
optionB: Collect more data of the same kind
optionC: Tune the hyperparameters further
optionD: Try a more powerful model architecture
correctAnswerText: Examine a sample of the errors by hand
explanation: Fifty misclassified examples usually reveal a pattern, and the pattern tells you which fix is worth trying.

prompt: You have run forty experiments. What must you have recorded?
optionA: The settings and data behind each result
optionB: The time each experiment took to run
optionC: The accuracy achieved by each of them
optionD: The order the experiments were run in
correctAnswerText: The settings and data behind each result
explanation: Otherwise the best result is unrepeatable, which means it is not a result you can ship.

prompt: Only 2% of your examples are positive. What must you do?
optionA: Train for more rounds on the positives
optionB: Collect more of the negative examples
optionC: Remove some of the negative examples
optionD: Choose a metric that reflects the rare class
correctAnswerText: Choose a metric that reflects the rare class
explanation: Resampling may help too. Getting the metric right first is what stops you celebrating a useless model.

prompt: What must be identical between training and serving?
optionA: How the features are computed
optionB: The programming language used
optionC: The hardware the model runs on
optionD: The volume of data processed
correctAnswerText: How the features are computed
explanation: Training-serving skew. Two implementations of the same feature drift, and the model silently degrades.

prompt: What should you monitor for a model in production?
optionA: The number of predictions served
optionB: The input distribution and the outcomes
optionC: The memory the model consumes
optionD: The response time of each prediction
correctAnswerText: The input distribution and the outcomes
explanation: Inputs shifting is the early warning; outcomes are the truth, and they usually arrive weeks later.

prompt: You are predicting customer churn. What must be defined first?
optionA: Which customers are worth predicting for
optionB: What exactly counts as having churned
optionC: Which model will be used to predict it
optionD: How far ahead the prediction should be
correctAnswerText: What exactly counts as having churned
explanation: Thirty days inactive, or cancelled, or no purchase in a quarter. Different labels, different problems.

prompt: Your model scores 99.8% on a hard problem. What should you do?
optionA: Report the result and move to deployment
optionB: Assume leakage and go looking for it
optionC: Check that the model is not overfitting
optionD: Try it on a larger test set to confirm
correctAnswerText: Assume leakage and go looking for it
explanation: On a genuinely hard problem, a near-perfect score is evidence of a mistake rather than of success.

prompt: A churn model uses "account closed date" as a feature. What is wrong?
optionA: It is a date rather than a number
optionB: It is missing for most of the customers
optionC: It correlates too strongly with the label
optionD: It is only known after the thing being predicted
correctAnswerText: It is only known after the thing being predicted
explanation: It will not exist at prediction time. Ask of every feature whether you would have it when you need it.

prompt: The dataset contains near-duplicate records and the split was random. What follows?
optionA: The training set is smaller than reported
optionB: The classes are unevenly distributed
optionC: The model has effectively seen the test data
optionD: The model will underfit the problem
correctAnswerText: The model has effectively seen the test data
explanation: Deduplicate before splitting. A near-duplicate on the other side of the split is the answer handed over.

prompt: A team checked the test score after every change for two months. What is that score now?
optionA: A measure of how much they improved
optionB: A reliable measure of the final model
optionC: Equivalent to a validation score
optionD: An optimistic estimate, not a held-out one
correctAnswerText: An optimistic estimate, not a held-out one
explanation: Hundreds of decisions have been fitted to it by hand. Production will be worse than the number says.

prompt: A model that scored 91% offline performs far worse live. What would you check first?
optionA: Whether production traffic is larger
optionB: Whether the model was deployed correctly
optionC: Whether the model needs retraining
optionD: Whether the features are computed the same way
correctAnswerText: Whether the features are computed the same way
explanation: Training-serving skew is the commonest cause, and it is invisible in every offline evaluation.

prompt: A model is 90% accurate overall and 62% for one group of users. What does that indicate?
optionA: That group is inherently harder to predict
optionB: The overall metric was computed wrongly
optionC: The model needs more training rounds
optionD: The training data under-represented that group
correctAnswerText: The training data under-represented that group
explanation: An aggregate number hides it completely. Evaluating per group is how you find it before your users do.

prompt: A model deployed a year ago has never errored and business results have slowly fallen. What should you suspect?
optionA: The model is being called incorrectly
optionB: The business results have another cause
optionC: The model server needs to be restarted
optionD: The model no longer matches the current world
correctAnswerText: The model no longer matches the current world
explanation: Drift produces no error and no alert. It looks like the market changing, which is partly what it is.

prompt: A model cannot exceed 70% however it is tuned. What is worth checking?
optionA: Whether the features are being scaled
optionB: Whether there is sufficient training data
optionC: Whether the labels themselves are correct
optionD: Whether the model is powerful enough
correctAnswerText: Whether the labels themselves are correct
explanation: If two annotators disagree 30% of the time, no model can do better than the labels it is given.

prompt: A recommender is retrained on what users clicked, and its variety keeps narrowing. Why?
optionA: The model is overfitting the recent data
optionB: It only sees outcomes for what it showed
optionC: The catalogue has not been updated
optionD: Users are becoming more consistent
correctAnswerText: It only sees outcomes for what it showed
explanation: It never learns about what it did not recommend. The loop closes and the model trains on its own opinions.

prompt: The best result from last month cannot be reproduced. What was not captured?
optionA: The random seed used during training
optionB: The hardware the training ran on
optionC: The version of the libraries installed
optionD: The exact data and settings that produced it
correctAnswerText: The exact data and settings that produced it
explanation: All of the others are part of it. Without the data version and the settings, none of them helps.

prompt: When is machine learning the wrong tool?
optionA: When the rule can simply be written down
optionB: When the accuracy needed is very high
optionC: When the team has no specialist available
optionD: When the dataset has fewer than a million rows
correctAnswerText: When the rule can simply be written down
explanation: A model is a way of learning a rule you cannot state. Where you can state it, state it.

prompt: What should decide the threshold at which a model acts?
optionA: The relative cost of each kind of mistake
optionB: The value the model was trained with
optionC: The threshold used by similar systems
optionD: The point where accuracy is highest
correctAnswerText: The relative cost of each kind of mistake
explanation: A wrong film recommendation and a wrong loan refusal sit at very different points on that curve.

prompt: When is a simpler, less accurate model the better choice?
optionA: When the dataset is relatively small
optionB: When the team is less experienced
optionC: When the training time needs to be shorter
optionD: When somebody must be told why the answer was that
correctAnswerText: When somebody must be told why the answer was that
explanation: Lending, hiring, medicine. Two points of accuracy do not pay for being unable to justify a refusal.

prompt: What must accompany a reported accuracy figure?
optionA: The baseline, and where the model fails
optionB: The confidence interval of the estimate
optionC: The training time and the model size
optionD: The number of experiments that were run
correctAnswerText: The baseline, and where the model fails
explanation: A number without a baseline cannot be judged, and one without known failure modes will surprise somebody.

prompt: You have a week to improve a model. Where does it usually go furthest?
optionA: Into the data and the features
optionB: Into tuning the hyperparameters
optionC: Into trying newer architectures
optionD: Into training for much longer
correctAnswerText: Into the data and the features
explanation: Fixing labels, adding a feature that carries real signal, removing bad rows. Reliably the best return.

prompt: What is usually underestimated about putting a model into production?
optionA: The accuracy the business will demand
optionB: The compute the model will need to run
optionC: The time the model takes to train
optionD: Everything around the model outweighs the model
correctAnswerText: Everything around the model outweighs the model
explanation: Pipelines, feature stores, monitoring, retraining, rollback. The model is a small part of what you must run.

prompt: How should you decide when to retrain a model?
optionA: From measured drift, not a fixed schedule
optionB: When the business asks for improvements
optionC: Whenever new training data is available
optionD: On a regular schedule, such as monthly
correctAnswerText: From measured drift, not a fixed schedule
explanation: A schedule retrains when nothing changed and misses the week everything did. Measure and trigger on it.

prompt: A model makes decisions that disadvantage a group. Whose problem is it?
optionA: The source of the biased training data
optionB: Nobody’s, if the data was accurate
optionC: The team that built and deployed it
optionD: The business that specified the model
correctAnswerText: The team that built and deployed it
explanation: "The data was like that" is an explanation, not a defence. You chose to train on it and to ship the result.

prompt: What habit protects you most in machine learning work?
optionA: Distrusting results that exceed expectations
optionB: Trying many models before choosing one
optionC: Collecting as much data as you can
optionD: Reading the current research regularly
correctAnswerText: Distrusting results that exceed expectations
explanation: Nearly every serious error in this file presents as an unexpectedly good number that nobody questioned.

prompt: What is the discipline this whole workflow exists to protect?
optionA: Getting the model into production quickly
optionB: Efficient use of the available compute
optionC: Choosing the best model for the problem
optionD: Honest measurement of what the model can do
correctAnswerText: Honest measurement of what the model can do
explanation: Splits, baselines, metrics, leakage checks. Every practice here exists to stop you fooling yourself.
